claims.claim: CVE-2025-6514: critical command injection flaw in the widely used 'mcp-remote' package due to unvalidated authorization URLs (JFrog, 9 July 2025).
claims.check: CVSS score, mechanism (authorization_endpoint passed to open()), affected and fixed versions, discoverer, disclosure date, Windows vs macOS/Linux impact differences, precondition (connecting to an untrusted MCP server).
claims.what_is_true:
CVE record: assigned by JFrog; reserved 23 Jun 2025; published 9 Jul 2025, 12:41 UTC. CVSS 3.1 9.6 Critical (AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:R/S:C/C:H/I:H/A:H); CWE-78. Description: 'mcp-remote is exposed to OS command injection when connecting to untrusted MCP servers due to crafted input from the authorization_endpoint response URL.'

Mechanism, checked in the npm tarballs: through 0.1.14, redirectToAuthorization() built the URL from the server's OAuth metadata (new URL(metadata.authorization_endpoint)) and called await open(authorizationUrl.toString()). That passes it to the 'open' package, which launches the browser through the OS.
- 0.1.15 (11 Jun 2025) added a sanitizeUrl() wrapper: http/https only, components URL-encoded.
- 0.1.16 (17 Jun 2025) also encodes the username and password, and is the official fixed version.

Versions: 0.0.5 through 0.1.15 affected (GHSA-6xpm-ggf7-wc3p, published 9 Jul 2025).

People and disclosure: discovered by JFrog Security Research (team lead Or Peles); patched by maintainer Glen Maddern. Disclosed 9 Jul 2025 through JFrog's blog, press release and advisory JFSA-2025-001290844.

Platform differences, per coverage of JFrog's findings:
- Windows: arbitrary OS command execution with full parameter control.
- macOS and Linux: arbitrary executables can be launched, with limited parameter control.

Precondition: the MCP client must use mcp-remote to connect to an untrusted or malicious MCP server; the CVSS vector requires user interaction (UI:R). JFrog also advises connecting only to trusted servers over HTTPS. Peles called it 'the first time that full remote code execution is achieved in a real-world scenario on the client operating system' when connecting to an untrusted remote MCP server.
claims.suggested_rewrite: Initial Vector: CVE-2025-6514 (CVSS 9.6, disclosed by JFrog on 9 July 2025). mcp-remote 0.0.5–0.1.15 failed to sanitize the authorization_endpoint URL a remote server returns during OAuth before handing it to the OS to 'open'. Connect to a malicious MCP server and the login step becomes code execution on your machine. Fixed in 0.1.16.
claims.notes: This run's web-search budget ran out before I could read JFrog's blog directly, and jfrog.com is blocked for direct fetch. The platform-difference wording therefore relies on The Hacker News and SecurityBrief coverage of JFrog's findings. The CVE range ends at 0.1.15 even though 0.1.15 already had a partial sanitizer; cite 0.1.16 as the fix. The heading 'CVE-2025–6514' uses an en dash.

evidence.detail: Assigner JFROG; datePublished 2025-07-09T12:41:44Z. 'mcp-remote is exposed to OS command injection when connecting to untrusted MCP servers due to crafted input from the authorization_endpoint response URL'. CVSS 3.1 9.6 CRITICAL; CWE-78. Affected 0.0.5 to 0.1.15 inclusive. Patch commit geelen/mcp-remote 607b226a; references the JFrog blog and JFSA-2025-001290844.
GHSA-6xpm-ggf7-wc3p (alias CVE-2025-6514), published 2025-07-09T15:30:44Z. npm mcp-remote, introduced 0.0.5, fixed 0.1.16; severity CRITICAL.
Vulnerable code: authorizationUrl = new URL(metadata.authorization_endpoint), then redirectToAuthorization() calls 'await open(authorizationUrl.toString())' with no validation.

Fixed code: 'await open(sanitizeUrl(authorizationUrl.toString()))'. sanitizeUrl rejects non-http(s) protocols and unencoded hostnames, and URL-encodes username, password, path, query and hash. 0.1.15 had the same function without the username/password encoding.

JFrog Security Research announces CVSS 9.6 RCE: arbitrary OS command execution when clients such as Claude Desktop connect to an untrusted MCP server through mcp-remote. Affects 0.0.5–0.1.15, fixed in 0.1.16. Advises connecting only to trusted servers over HTTPS. Seen via search snippets.

Arbitrary OS command execution on Windows with full parameter control; on macOS and Linux, arbitrary executables with limited parameter control. Fixed in 0.1.16, released June 17, 2025. Or Peles: 'first time that full remote code execution is achieved in a real-world scenario on the client operating system'.

A malicious server sends a crafted 'authorization_endpoint' URL that mcp-remote processes. JFrog credits maintainer Glen Maddern for the patch. Windows exploit demonstrated with full parameter control.

claims.claim: Over 437,000 downloads were exposed to full RCE against MCP client implementations in production environments.
claims.check: The download figure and its source; whether 'full RCE ... in production environments' is supported or overstated; any evidence of in-the-wild exploitation.
claims.what_is_true:
The vulnerability: CVE-2025-6514 (GHSA-6xpm-ggf7-wc3p; JFrog CNA, published 9 Jul 2025) is OS command injection (CWE-78) in mcp-remote when it connects to an untrusted MCP server, via a crafted authorization_endpoint URL. CVSS 3.1 9.6 Critical, AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:R/S:C/C:H/I:H/A:H. Affected versions 0.0.5 to 0.1.15. The fix, 0.1.16, reached npm on 17 Jun 2025, three weeks before disclosure.

Impact per JFrog: arbitrary OS commands with full parameter control on Windows; arbitrary executables with limited parameter control on macOS and Linux. The target is the machine running mcp-remote, typically a desktop MCP client such as Claude Desktop. JFrog calls it the first full RCE on a client OS from a remote MCP server.

The figure: '437,000+' is the package's cumulative npm download count to date (The Hacker News, 10 Jul 2025). It spans all versions, including unaffected 0.0.1 to 0.0.4 and patched 0.1.16 to 0.1.18, and it counts repeated npx fetches and CI runs. It is not a count of installations or exposed systems. No source mentions production environments.

Exploitation:
- CISA ADP SSVC at publication: Exploitation none, Automatable no.
- Not in CISA KEV (catalog 2026.10.30, 1,766 entries). The only MCP-related KEV entry is LiteLLM CVE-2026-59822, added 2 Sep 2026.
- No credible in-the-wild report. Feedly's 'exploited by Clawdbot malware' tag cites no source.
claims.suggested_rewrite: Blast Radius: mcp-remote had been downloaded more than 437,000 times, across all versions, when JFrog disclosed the bug in July 2025. Any MCP client, Claude Desktop included, that used a vulnerable version (0.0.5 to 0.1.15) to connect to a malicious or untrusted MCP server could be made to run code on the user's own machine: arbitrary commands on Windows, arbitrary executables with limited arguments on macOS and Linux. The fix, 0.1.16, had shipped three weeks before disclosure. There's no public evidence of in-the-wild exploitation, and CISA's KEV catalog doesn't list it.
claims.challenge_reasoning:
I upheld the first pass's verdict and severity and confirmed its facts:
- The CVE record shows CVSS 9.6 with UI:R and CISA ADP 'Exploitation: none'.
- The GHSA gives the range 0.0.5 up to the 0.1.16 fix.
- The current KEV JSON does not list the CVE.
- The Hacker News headline confirms the 437,000+ figure.

I amended two things:
(a) New fact: the npm registry shows 0.1.16 shipped on 17 Jun 2025, and 0.0.1 to 0.0.4 predate the bug. So part of the cumulative 437,000 downloads were of non-vulnerable versions, which weakens 'downloads exposed' further.
(b) The first-pass rewrite said 'any MCP client ... that used it'. That implies every mcp-remote user was exposed, so I added the vulnerable range and the fact that the fix predated disclosure.

I also corrected the first pass's description of Feedly. Its tag claims exploitation by 'Clawdbot malware', with no primary source. Clawdbot is OpenClaw, a legitimate agent that post-dates the CVE. Either way the tag is unreliable.

On 'full RCE': that is JFrog's own framing, but full parameter control was shown only on Windows. 'In production environments' has no support.

Severity stays major. The underlying critical bug and the download count are real, but the sentence inflates exposure and setting.

IHVM agreement: I disagree with IHVM's 'confirmed' label. IHVM bundled this with the CVE facts (covered separately in A2-05) and itself says the 'downloads exposed to full RCE in production' framing should be softened. Here that framing is the whole claim, so partially_correct is the accurate verdict.
claims.notes: The number is real and fairly sourced, but 'downloads exposed to full RCE... in production environments' overstates it. Downloads are not exposed systems, exploitation needs a malicious server plus user action, full command control is Windows-only, and the affected hosts are desktop/developer clients. Feedly's CVE page carries an 'Exploited in the wild' tag, but its own text says the sources do not indicate active exploitation. Don't rely on it.

evidence.detail: JFrog CNA. Title 'OS command injection in mcp-remote when connecting to untrusted MCP servers'. Affected 0.0.5 to <=0.1.15. CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:R/S:C/C:H/I:H/A:H, 9.6 CRITICAL. CISA ADP SSVC: Exploitation none, Automatable no, Technical Impact total.
Alias CVE-2025-6514; CWE-78; CRITICAL; introduced 0.0.5, fixed 0.1.16.
Package created 2025-03-17; 0.0.5 published 2025-03-24; 0.1.15 on 2025-06-11; fixed 0.1.16 on 2025-06-17T05:06:24Z; 0.1.18 on 2025-07-07. The fix shipped three weeks before the 9 Jul disclosure.
Headline 'Critical mcp-remote Vulnerability Enables Remote Code Execution, Impacting 437,000+ Downloads'. The figure is a cumulative npm download count.

Read via search-result content. Shell commands with full parameter control shown on Windows; on macOS and Linux, execution of arbitrary executables with limited parameter control. JFrog calls it the first full RCE on a client OS when connecting to an untrusted remote MCP server.
catalogVersion 2026.10.30, 1,766 entries. CVE-2025-6514 absent. The only MCP-related entry is CVE-2026-59822 (BerriAI LiteLLM), added 2026-09-02.
Tags the CVE as exploited 'by Clawdbot malware' without any primary source. Clawdbot (OpenClaw) is a legitimate agent that appeared after the CVE. Unreliable.
The risk is when clients such as Claude Desktop connect to an untrusted MCP server via mcp-remote. JFrog advises upgrading to 0.1.16 and connecting only to trusted servers over HTTPS.

claims.claim: The Amazon Q case is presented as a real-world supply chain incident where a prompt was the payload.
claims.check: How AWS and researchers characterize it (supply chain compromise delivering a destructive prompt); whether the code could have executed in practice.
claims.what_is_true:
The characterization holds: a real compromise of an official release pipeline whose payload was a natural-language prompt for an AI agent.

The chain:
1. An over-scoped GitHub token in CodeBuild (AWS-2025-015), extracted through a CodeBuild memory dump (AWS-2025-016).
2. A commit to master added preparePackager() to scripts/package.ts.
3. On production (STAGE=prod) Linux release builds, preparePackager() curl-downloads scripts/extensionNode.bk from the 'stability' ref and writes it over src/extensionNode.ts.
4. On extension activation, that file runs childProcess.exec(`q --trust-all-tools --no-interactive "${PROMPT}"`) with the wiper prompt.
5. It shipped in the official v1.84.0 on 17 Jul 2025.

The tagged 1.84.0 source (packages/amazonq/src/extensionNode.ts) contains no prompt. Only the built artifact did.

Could it have executed? Per AWS, the injected code runs at launch, but a syntax error prevents a successful call to the Q Developer CLI, so as shipped the prompt never reached the agent. AWS calls the code 'inert' and says no customer resources were impacted. CISA's assessment lists Exploitation: none. The attacker claimed the defect was deliberate.

My inference: even a working version would have needed the Q Developer CLI installed and signed in on the machine, and AWS profiles configured locally, to do cloud damage.

JFrog described the injected code as a function that 'invokes Amazon's Q cli tool... utilizing a malicious prompt'.
claims.suggested_rewrite: This is the case where the prompt was the payload. The attacker never shipped a wiper binary. They shipped instructions for an AI agent already on the developer's machine, pre-approved for every tool with --trust-all-tools, through AWS's own release pipeline. Per AWS, only a syntax error in the injected code stopped it.
claims.notes: My inference: artifact signing, or an SBOM built from the tagged source, would not have caught this, because the malicious file came from AWS's own pipeline and never appeared in the tagged code. That is a strong argument for build-provenance attestation in the AIBOM. Frame the case as a near-miss, not an executed attack.

evidence.detail: Injected preparePackager(). It returns unless cwd includes 'amazonq' and process.env.STAGE === 'prod' (and the platform is Linux with curl), then downloads https://raw.githubusercontent.com/${REPO_NAME}/${TAG_NAME}/scripts/extensionNode.bk (TAG_NAME = 'stability') to src/extensionNode.ts. The v1.85.0 package.ts is byte-identical to v1.83.0.
The tagged source contains no PROMPT, childProcess or 'trust-all-tools'. The payload existed only in the build output.
Payload file: the destructive prompt, executed via `q --trust-all-tools --no-interactive` inside activateAmazonQNode().

'inert, injected code designed to call the Q Developer CLI... executes when the extension is launched... syntax error which prevents it from making a successful API call'. CAPEC-442 Infected Software. CISA ADP: Exploitation none.
Original report: Amazon shipped a version of Q with commands telling it to wipe users' computers. The person responsible called it a wiper 'designed to be defective as a warning'.
JFrog: the injected code 'invokes Amazon's Q cli tool... utilizing a malicious prompt'. Version 1.84.0 removed; per Amazon, no users impacted.

claims.claim: The official MCP Registry launched in preview on September 8, 2025, as a metaregistry: it hosts metadata, and the code still comes from npm, PyPI, Docker Hub, or GitHub Releases.
claims.check: Launch date; supported package types (npm, PyPI, NuGet, OCI/Docker, MCPB, remote servers) per the official blog/docs (blog.modelcontextprotocol.io is fetchable).
claims.what_is_true: The date and the design are right, but the list of code sources is incomplete. The MCP blog post 'Introducing the MCP Registry' (8 Sep 2025; David Soria Parra, Adam Jones, Tadas Antanavicius, Toby Padilla, Theodora Chu) launched registry.modelcontextprotocol.io 'in preview'. The registry hosts metadata only. The launch FAQ (registry tag v1.0.0) says it 'stores metadata about MCP servers and references to where they're hosted (npm, PyPI, NuGet, Docker Hub, etc.), but does not host the actual source code or packages.' The current docs call it 'the official centralized metadata repository for publicly accessible MCP servers'. The word 'metaregistry' never appears in the official docs, but it describes the design accurately. At launch, the v1.0.0 publishing guide supported npm (registry.npmjs.org only), PyPI, NuGet, Docker/OCI (docker.io only), and MCPB bundles hosted on GitHub or GitLab Releases (a SHA-256 hash was required). Remote servers were also supported; for those the registry stores only a URL and there is no package. The current docs add Cargo (crates.io) and more OCI registries: ghcr.io, quay.io, Google Artifact Registry (*.pkg.dev) and Azure Container Registry (*.azurecr.io). In the main-branch docs fetched on 1 Nov 2026, every registry doc page still says 'currently in preview', and the API has been frozen at v0.1 since 24 Oct 2025.
claims.suggested_rewrite: The official MCP Registry launched in preview on September 8, 2025. It is a metaregistry: it stores metadata, and the code still comes from npm, PyPI, NuGet, Docker Hub and other container registries, or GitHub and GitLab Releases. For remote servers there is no package at all, only a URL that someone else runs.
claims.notes: Remote servers matter for an AI-BOM: there is no artifact to hash or pin, so the BOM should record the URL and who operates it. The launch docs also contradict each other on OCI: the v1.0.0 FAQ lists GHCR as supported, while the v1.0.0 publishing guide says only docker.io is supported.

evidence.detail: 'Today, we're launching the Model Context Protocol (MCP) Registry—an open catalog and API for publicly available MCP servers...' and 'The MCP Registry is now available in preview.'

Launch-era FAQ: 'Is the MCP Registry a package registry? No. The MCP Registry stores metadata about MCP servers and references to where they're hosted (npm, PyPI, NuGet, Docker Hub, etc.), but does not host the actual source code or packages.' Also lists supported registries as npm, PyPI, NuGet.org and GHCR.

The v1.0.0 guide (the README at this tag targets the 'preview go-live on 8th September') has sections for npm, PyPI, NuGet, Docker/OCI ('currently only supports the official Docker registry (https://docker.io)') and MCPB ('currently only supports artifacts hosted on GitHub or GitLab releases'; 'MCPB packages must include a SHA-256 hash').
'Package registries — such as npm, PyPI, and Docker Hub — host packages with code and binaries. The MCP Registry hosts metadata that points to those packages.'
Current types: npm, PyPI, NuGet, Cargo (crates.io), Docker/OCI (docker.io, ghcr.io, quay.io, *.pkg.dev, *.azurecr.io), and MCPB ('artifacts hosted via GitHub or GitLab releases').
'2025-09-08 update: The registry has launched in preview' and '2025-10-24 update: The Registry API has entered an API freeze (v0.1)'. No GA announcement appears.

claims.claim: Namespace ownership is checked. Security scanning is not mandated.
claims.check: How namespace ownership is verified (GitHub OAuth/OIDC, DNS, HTTP); any security scanning, moderation or denylist policy of the official registry.
claims.what_is_true:
Both halves are accurate.

Ownership checks: the registry 'validates namespace ownership when publishing'.
- io.github.<user>/* and io.github.<org>/* names need GitHub OAuth (device flow) or GitHub Actions OIDC. Org namespaces need the Owner role.
- Reverse-DNS names (com.example/*) need either a DNS TXT record on the apex domain ('v=MCPv1; k=ed25519|ecdsap384; p=<key>') or an HTTP proof file at /.well-known/mcp-registry-auth.
- Each package type also carries an ownership marker: 'mcpName' in npm's package.json, 'mcp-name:' in a PyPI or NuGet README, the OCI label io.modelcontextprotocol.server.name, or for MCPB a URL containing 'mcp' plus a fileSha256. The registry does not validate that hash; clients do.
- For remote servers the registry 'does not verify that you control the remote URL'.

No security scanning by the registry itself:
- Launch FAQ: 'The MVP delegates security scanning to: underlying package registries; and subregistries'.
- Current docs: the registry 'focuses on namespace authentication and metadata hosting, while relying on the broader ecosystem for security scanning of actual server code.'
- Moderation policy: 'consumers should assume minimal-to-no moderation'. Maintainers remove illegal content, malware, spam and non-functioning servers, and can denylist entries (launch blog). They 'won't remove... Servers with security vulnerabilities'. A removed server is marked 'deleted', and its metadata stays retrievable.
claims.suggested_rewrite: The registry checks who owns a namespace (a GitHub login, or a DNS or HTTP challenge for a domain), not what the code does. It delegates security scanning to npm, PyPI, Docker Hub and downstream marketplaces, and its own moderation policy tells consumers to 'assume minimal-to-no moderation.'
claims.notes: Namespace verification proves control of a GitHub account or a domain. It does not prove the publisher is trustworthy or that a remote endpoint belongs to them.

evidence.detail: 'Publishing supports multiple authentication methods: GitHub OAuth, GitHub OIDC, DNS verification, HTTP verification... The registry validates namespace ownership when publishing.'

DNS TXT record 'v=MCPv1; k=ed25519; p=${PUBLIC_KEY}' on the apex; HTTP proof at '/.well-known/mcp-registry-auth'; 'To publish under an organization namespace... you must be an Owner of that organization.'

'The MCP Registry delegates security scanning to: Underlying package registries... Downstream aggregators... The MCP Registry focuses on namespace authentication and metadata hosting, while relying on the broader ecosystem for security scanning of actual server code.'

'The MCP Registry does not make guarantees about moderation, and consumers should assume minimal-to-no moderation.' It removes 'Malware, regardless of intentions'; it won't remove 'Servers with security vulnerabilities'.
'Is there security scanning? The MVP delegates security scanning to: underlying package registries; and subregistries'
'It does not verify that you control the remote URL, regardless of authentication method'

'Community members can submit issues to flag servers... containing spam, malicious code, or impersonating legitimate services. Registry maintainers can then denylist these entries and retroactively remove them from public access.'

claims.claim: By November 2025, the MCP Registry had nearly 2,000 entries.
claims.check: Official figure and date (e.g. MCP anniversary post, Nov 2025).
claims.what_is_true: The MCP blog post 'One Year of MCP: November 2025 Spec Release' (25 Nov 2025) says the registry 'now has close to two thousand entries since its announcement in September. That's a 407% growth from the initial batch of servers we onboarded that same month.' None of the MCP blog posts up to 29 Sep 2026 gives a later official count. 'Entries' are self-published listings, not vetted servers.
claims.suggested_rewrite: By late November 2025 it listed close to 2,000 entries, a 407% jump from the servers onboarded at launch (MCP blog, November 25, 2025).

evidence.detail: 'That's why we also launched the MCP Registry earlier this year. It's the central index for all available MCP servers that now has close to two thousand entries since its announcement in September. That's a 407% growth from the initial batch of servers we onboarded that same month.'
Full MCP blog feed (posts from Jul 2025 to Sep 2026). No post after 25 Nov 2025 gives an updated registry entry count.

claims.claim: Invariant Labs revealed that tool descriptions are trusted implicitly by AI agents but can contain hidden malicious instructions.
claims.check: Invariant Labs' 'Tool Poisoning Attacks' disclosure: date, what was shown, which clients.
claims.what_is_true:
Accurate. Invariant Labs' disclosure 'MCP Security Notification: Tool Poisoning Attacks' showed that instructions hidden in an MCP tool's description reach the model and are followed by the agent. Invariant's proof-of-concept repo (invariantlabs-ai/mcp-injection-experiments) has three demos:
1. Direct poisoning: an 'add' tool whose description makes the agent leak 'SSH keys and the mcp.json file itself', shown running in Cursor.
2. Tool shadowing: a malicious server changes how the agent uses a send_email tool from a different, trusted server, 'such that all emails sent by the agent are leaked to the attacker's server'.
3. WhatsApp takeover: shadowing plus 'a sleeper rug pull'. A benign 'random fact of the day' server swaps in a malicious tool on its second load and leaks messages through whatsapp-mcp. The stolen data is padded with spaces so the user does not see it.

Invariant then released mcp-scan. Its first PyPI release was on 7 Apr 2025, and it has since been renamed snyk-agent-scan. The disclosure dates from early April 2025; prior indexing gives 1 Apr 2025, but invariantlabs.ai cannot be reached from this sandbox, so the exact day is not re-confirmed. Cursor is the only client shown in the material I could fetch.
claims.suggested_rewrite: In April 2025, Invariant Labs showed that agents read and obey MCP tool descriptions, so a server can hide instructions in them that the user never notices. In Cursor, an innocent-looking 'add' tool leaked the user's SSH keys. A second demo hijacked a trusted send_email tool from another server so that every email went to the attacker.
claims.notes: invariantlabs.ai is blocked here, and the shared WebSearch budget was exhausted, so two details were not re-confirmed: the blog's exact publication day (1 April 2025 per prior indexing) and any list of affected clients beyond Cursor.

evidence.detail: 'we implement a simple MCP server that instructs an agent to leak sensitive files, when calling the add tool (in this case SSH keys and the mcp.json file itself)'; shadowing 'manipulates the agent's behavior of a send_email tool (provided by a different, trusted server), such that all emails sent by the agent are leaked to the attacker's server'; 'a shadowing attack combined with a sleeper rug pull'. Example executions are shown in Cursor.

The mcp-scan README links 'tool poisoning' to invariantlabs.ai/blog/mcp-security-notification-tool-poisoning-attacks and says it will 'detect and prevent MCP rug pull attacks, i.e. mcp-scan detects changes to MCP tools via hashing'.
Earliest release, 0.1.2, was uploaded 2025-04-07. The current summary reads 'This package has been renamed to snyk-agent-scan.'
'Further Reading' links 'MCP Security Notification Tool Poisoning Attacks' (invariantlabs.ai) and an April 9, 2025 Simon Willison post on MCP prompt injection.

claims.claim: The MCPTox benchmark found a 72.8% attack success rate against leading models.
claims.check: Whether 72.8% is the maximum for one model (which) or an average; number of agents/models, servers, tools and test cases; refusal rates; paper date and authors.
claims.what_is_true:
MCPTox is real. Zhiqiang Wang, Yichao Gao and 7 co-authors posted it as arXiv:2508.14925 on 19 Aug 2025, under the title 'MCPTox: A Benchmark for Tool Poisoning Attack on Real-World MCP Servers'. It was published at AAAI-26: Proceedings of the AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence 40(42), pp. 35811-35819, DOI 10.1609/aaai.v40i42.40895.

Setup:
- Built on 45 live, real-world MCP servers and 353 authentic tools.
- Malicious test cases were generated from 3 attack templates. arXiv v1 has 1,312 cases; the AAAI version has 1,348. Sources disagree on whether there are 10 or 11 risk categories.
- 20 LLM agents were evaluated.

Results:
- 72.8% is the single HIGHEST attack success rate, for o1-mini. Next were DeepSeek-R1 (70.9%) and Phi-4 (70.2%).
- The paper's average ASR across all model settings is 36.5%.
- Refusals were rare. The highest refusal rate, Claude-3.7-Sonnet's, was under 3%.
- More capable models were often MORE susceptible, because the attack exploits instruction-following.

So 'a 72.8% attack success rate against leading models' presents one model's worst case as a general rate. That figure is about twice the average.
claims.suggested_rewrite: The MCPTox benchmark (Wang et al., AAAI 2026) planted poisoned tool descriptions alongside 353 real tools from 45 live MCP servers and tested 20 LLM agents. The attacks succeeded 36.5% of the time on average and 72.8% of the time against the most vulnerable model, o1-mini, and no model refused even 3% of them.
claims.challenge_reasoning:
The first pass could not retrieve the paper and returned 'unverifiable'. Several independent search results quote the arXiv v1 abstract and table and the AAAI-26 version. They confirm the numbers the first pass expected, so the verdict becomes partially_correct.

The paper's abstract itself highlights 'o1-mini achieving an attack success rate of 72.8%'. The article dropped the model name and turned that worst case into a general rate. The average across model settings, 36.5%, is half the stated figure. I keep the severity at major because a reader would conclude that about three in four tool-poisoning attempts succeed against frontier models in general.

Two corrections to the first pass:
1. Its '1,312 cases across 10 risk categories' mixes versions. v1 is reported as 1,312 cases and 11 categories, and the AAAI version as 1,348 cases (category count reported inconsistently). My rewrite therefore avoids case and category counts.
2. Its rewrite says the poisoned descriptions came 'from 45 real MCP servers'. In fact the researchers generated the poison themselves and planted it among real servers' tools.

IHVM reaches the same verdict with the same numbers (o1-mini 72.8%, 36.5% average, refusals under 3%, 45/353, the 1,312 vs 1,348 discrepancy), so I mark agrees. Its fix cites 1,312, which is correct only if the arXiv version is the one cited.

Direct fetches of arxiv.org, ojs.aaai.org and alphaxiv.org failed here (sandbox network block), so the figures rest on search-result content quoting the papers, cross-checked across multiple results.
claims.notes: The verdict is 'unverifiable' only because the source could not be retrieved in this run; a follow-up search is needed. Confirm every number in the rewrite against the arXiv abstract before publishing. If the abstract matches the details above, the original sentence is partially correct: it turns the single worst-case model into a general result 'against leading models'. The severity rating assumes that likely outcome.

evidence.detail: arXiv v1 abstract (via search content): MCPTox is 'constructed upon 45 live, real-world MCP servers and 353 authentic tools'; 1312 malicious test cases; 'Our evaluation on 20 prominent LLM agents' found widespread vulnerability, 'with o1-mini achieving an attack success rate of 72.8%'.

AAAI-26 version (via search content): 'three distinct attack templates to generate a comprehensive suite of 1348 malicious test cases'; agents rarely refuse, 'with the highest refused rate (Claude-3.7-Sonnet) less than 3%'. Proceedings 40(42) 35811-35819.
Evaluation table (via search content): o1-mini 72.8%, DeepSeek-R1 70.9%, Phi-4 70.2% were the most susceptible; the paper reports an average ASR of 36.5% across all model settings.
Third-party summary repeating the 36.5% average and the three top per-model rates, and the 1,312-case count.

Context only: this is the tool-poisoning attack class that MCPTox measures. The MCPTox paper itself (arXiv:2508.14925, as cited by the author) could not be retrieved: arxiv.org is blocked by the sandbox and the WebSearch budget was exhausted.

claims.claim: The 'rug pull' exploits MCP's lack of schema verification after initial handshake; tools mutate their definitions post-approval.
claims.check: What the MCP spec provides (notifications/tools/list_changed; any integrity or pinning mechanism); who first described MCP rug pulls.
claims.what_is_true:
The substance is right, but the 'handshake' framing is out of date.

Every MCP spec version since 2025-03-26 lets servers change their tools at runtime. Servers declare 'listChanged', and 'When the list of available tools changes, servers that declared the listChanged capability SHOULD send a notification' (notifications/tools/list_changed). Tool definitions arrive via tools/list, not in the initialize handshake. Nothing in the spec signs, hashes, versions or pins a tool definition, or requires a client to re-approve one that changed. The spec only says clients 'MUST consider tool annotations to be untrusted unless they come from trusted servers'.

The current spec, 2026-07-28 (released 28 Jul 2026), 'officially retired the initialize/initialized exchange along with the Mcp-Session-Id header', so there is no handshake left at all. tools/list results now carry cache hints (ttlMs, cacheScope). The tool set 'MAY change over time... but MUST NOT vary per-connection or as a side effect of other requests'. There is still no integrity mechanism.

The earliest MCP 'rug pull' description in the sources I could fetch is Invariant Labs' April 2025 tool-poisoning work. Their 'sleeper rug pull' demo changes its tool interface on the second load, and their mcp-scan tool detects rug pulls 'via hashing'.

A CVE-backed case on the client side is CVE-2025-54136 (Cursor <=1.2.4, published 1 Aug 2025, fixed in 1.3). An already-approved MCP config could be silently swapped for a malicious command 'without triggering any warning or re-prompt'.
claims.suggested_rewrite: The rug pull works because MCP cannot verify that the tool you approved is still the tool you are running. Servers may change their tools at any time, and the spec only asks them to announce it with a notifications/tools/list_changed message. Nothing signs, hashes or pins a tool definition, and re-approval is left to each client.
claims.notes: The article cites a September 2026 source, so it postdates the 2026-07-28 spec, which has no handshake. Readers who know MCP will notice the 'after initial handshake' wording.

evidence.detail: 'When the list of available tools changes, servers that declared the listChanged capability SHOULD send a notification: notifications/tools/list_changed'; 'clients MUST consider tool annotations to be untrusted unless they come from trusted servers'. The Security Considerations section has no integrity or re-approval requirement.

'This set MAY be empty and MAY change over time (see List Changed Notification), but MUST NOT vary per-connection or as a side effect of other requests on the connection.' There is no signing, hashing or pinning mechanism.

'we've officially retired the initialize/initialized exchange along with the Mcp-Session-Id header (refer to SEP-2575, SEP-2567)'; 'Responses from tools/list... now carry ttlMs and cacheScope (SEP-2549).'
'a shadowing attack combined with a sleeper rug pull, i.e. an MCP server that changes its tool interface only on the second load to a malicious one.'
'detect and prevent MCP rug pull attacks, i.e. mcp-scan detects changes to MCP tools via hashing'

'Cursor's Modification of MCP Server Definitions Bypasses Manual Re-approvals': 'Once a collaborator accepts a harmless MCP, the attacker can silently swap it for a malicious command (e.g., calc.exe) without triggering any warning or re-prompt.' Fixed in 1.3.

claims.claim: A malicious MCP server provides a legitimate email-sending tool for weeks, building trust. Then an update adds a single line that BCCs every outgoing message to an attacker-controlled address. (Presented in the article as a hypothetical.)
claims.check: Whether this happened in the wild: package name, version that added the BCC, date, number of benign versions before, downloads, discoverer.
claims.suggested_rewrite: This is not hypothetical. In September 2025, an unofficial npm package called postmark-mcp shipped 13 clean releases in under two days. Then version 1.0.16 added one line that, according to Koi Security, which caught it, BCC'd every outgoing email to an attacker-controlled address. npm's record shows the package was pulled about a week later, on September 25.
claims.notes: Before publishing, confirm the BCC line, the attacker address, the 1.0.16 attribution and the download figures against Koi Security's report. The npm timeline and the date of the official package were verified directly. In the real case, trust came from borrowing the Postmark name before any official npm package existed, not from weeks of good behaviour.

evidence.detail: The official package was 'created' 2025-11-26T21:11:21Z (first version 1.0.0), two months after the impostor was pulled.
'Official Postmark MCP Server', npm badge for @activecampaign/postmark-mcp (the official package is scoped; the impostor was not).
The tool-shadowing demo manipulates a trusted send_email tool 'such that all emails sent by the agent are leaked to the attacker's server'.

claims.claim: Rug pull attacks: publishers launch benign tools to accumulate trust, star ratings, and downloads, then release an update containing malicious payloads, instantly compromising downstream automated agents.
claims.check: Documented real examples; whether compromise is 'instant' (depends on version pinning vs floating installs such as npx -y).
claims.what_is_true:
The pattern is documented, but 'instantly' overstates it.

Real cases:
1. postmark-mcp. The npm record shows clean versions on 15 and 16 Sep 2025, malicious 1.0.16 on 17 Sep, and removal on 25 Sep. Its trust came from a borrowed brand name rather than accumulated ratings.
2. CVE-2025-54136 (Cursor, 1 Aug 2025): an approved MCP server config could be silently swapped for a malicious command.
3. Invariant's 'sleeper rug pull' demo.

How far a malicious update spreads depends on pinning. Official setup instructions use floating installs: Postmark's README recommends 'npx -y @activecampaign/postmark-mcp', and the reference filesystem server uses 'npx -y @modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem'. Agents with unpinned installs pull a malicious release on their next launch. Pinned versions are unaffected until someone upgrades them. Remote MCP servers can change on the server side with no version at all. The official registry has no star ratings: its metadata is 'deliberately unopinionated', and ratings come from downstream marketplaces and GitHub.

claims.claim: Research by Anthropic and the UK AI Security Institute demonstrated that injecting as few as 250 poisoned documents into a pretraining corpus implants a persistent backdoor in models ranging from 600M to 13B parameters.
claims.check: Collaborators (incl. the Alan Turing Institute?), date, paper title, the backdoor behaviour studied (e.g. denial-of-service gibberish), whether 'persistent' is supported, and the caveats the authors state (anthropic.com is fetchable).
claims.what_is_true:
The study:
- Anthropic posted 'A small number of samples can poison LLMs of any size' on 9 Oct 2025.
- It describes a joint study by Anthropic's Alignment Science team, the UK AI Security Institute's Safeguards team AND the Alan Turing Institute. The article body names only the first two; its reference list has all three.
- The paper is Souly et al., 'Poisoning Attacks on LLMs Require a Near-constant Number of Poison Samples', arXiv:2510.07192, submitted 8 Oct 2025. It has 13 authors, with affiliations including OATML Oxford and ETH Zurich.

Verified results:
- Models of 600M, 2B, 7B and 13B parameters were pretrained on Chinchilla-optimal data (6B-260B tokens) with 100, 250 or 500 poisoned documents.
- 100 documents did not reliably backdoor any model. 250 or more did at every size, even though the largest model saw more than 20 times as much clean data.
- For the 13B model, 250 documents were about 420k tokens, or 0.00016% of training tokens.
- The backdoor was a narrow denial-of-service: the trigger <SUDO> makes the model output gibberish. Anthropic calls it 'unlikely to pose significant risks in frontier models' and says it is unclear whether the pattern holds for larger models or more harmful behaviours.

On 'persistent':
- The blog never uses the word.
- The paper reports that continued clean pretraining degrades such backdoors only slowly; some survive thousands of clean steps.
- Simulated alignment (supervised fine-tuning on clean data) was highly effective at mitigating them.
- Persistence through alignment was actually shown by an earlier paper, Zhang et al., 'Persistent Pre-Training Poisoning of LLMs' (ICLR 2025). Poisoning 0.1% of pretraining data let 3 of 4 attacks persist through post-training, and denial-of-service persisted at 0.001%.
claims.suggested_rewrite: Research by Anthropic, the UK AI Security Institute and the Alan Turing Institute (October 2025) showed that as few as 250 poisoned documents planted a backdoor in models from 600M to 13B parameters, even though the largest model trained on more than 20 times as much clean data. The backdoor was deliberately narrow (a <SUDO> trigger that makes the model output gibberish), and the paper found that further clean training, especially safety-style fine-tuning, weakens such backdoors. But the lesson holds: the attacker needs a roughly fixed number of documents, not a fixed share of the corpus.
claims.challenge_reasoning:
I re-fetched the primary Anthropic page today and checked search content quoting arXiv:2510.07192. Every number in the claim is correct. Two problems remain:
1. The in-text attribution drops the Alan Turing Institute, which the article's own reference entry includes.
2. 'Persistent' is not something the cited study claims.

However, 'persistent' is not flatly false. The paper finds that further clean pretraining wears these backdoors down only slowly. It is safety-style fine-tuning on clean data that strongly mitigates them. So the adjective overstates the result rather than inverting it, and the paragraph's real point is accurate: a near-constant absolute number of documents is enough, not a percentage. On that basis I rate it mostly_correct and minor, not partially_correct and major as the first pass did.

The first-pass rewrite also contains an error. It says the authors call it unclear 'whether it survives post-training'. Anthropic says nothing of the kind: it says attackers face the challenge of 'designing attacks that resist post-training', and the paper's own alignment experiments cut against persistence.

IHVM agrees on the core facts and also flags 'persistent'. But its statement that continued clean training 'degrades' the backdoor leaves out that the paper found the decay slow, and its verdict (partially-correct) is a notch harsher than the evidence supports, so I mark disagrees.

The word 'persistent' probably migrated from Zhang et al. (ICLR 2025), which Anthropic cites as prior work. If the author wants that word, they should cite that paper for it.

The heading's 'PEFT' is handled in A4-02. arxiv.org was blocked, so the paper-level persistence details come from multiple search summaries (AlphaXiv, Emergent Mind) quoting the paper; treat them as secondary.
claims.notes: The in-text attribution leaves out the Alan Turing Institute, although the article's own reference list includes it. 'Persistent' is the main problem: the 250-document result was measured on raw pretrained checkpoints, and the authors list resisting post-training as an open challenge. Background, not re-fetched: the Anthropic page links its 'previous work' to arXiv:2410.13722, which I believe is Zhang et al. 2024, 'Persistent Pre-Training Poisoning of Large Language Models'. That paper did test survival through post-training, so the word may have migrated from there. The web-search budget was exhausted at the start of this task, so this check relies on the fetched Anthropic page.

evidence.detail: Fetched today: 'In a joint study with the UK AI Security Institute and the Alan Turing Institute'; 'a collaboration between Anthropic's Alignment Science team, the UK AISI's Safeguards team, and The Alan Turing Institute'; 'We trained models of four different sizes: 600M, 2B, 7B, and 13B parameters'; '100, 250, and 500 malicious documents'; trigger '<SUDO>'; 'a narrow backdoor (producing gibberish text) that is unlikely to pose significant risks in frontier models'; 'Attackers also face additional challenges, like designing attacks that resist post-training'. The page does not call the backdoor persistent.

Abstract (via search content): models from 600M to 13B parameters on chinchilla-optimal datasets (6B to 260B tokens); '250 poisoned documents similarly compromise models across all model and dataset sizes'; the authors also show the same dynamics for poisoning during fine-tuning.

Summary (via search content): backdoors 'can be degraded through continued clean pretraining, but this process is slow and varies with poisoning methodology'; 'simulated alignment training (supervised fine-tuning on clean data) proved highly effective at mitigating backdoors'.
Summary (via search content): 'Some backdoors persist for thousands of clean training steps, indicating that simple post-training on clean data may not be sufficient for robust defense.'

Zhang, Rando et al., 'Persistent Pre-training Poisoning of LLMs' (ICLR 2025): 'Poisoning only 0.1% of a model's pre-training dataset is sufficient for three out of four attacks to measurably persist through post-training'; denial-of-service persists 'with a poisoning rate of only 0.001%'. This is where persistence was actually shown.

This is a different Anthropic study, and it is where 'persistent' backdoors were actually shown: "such backdoor behavior can be made persistent, so that it is not removed by standard safety training techniques, including supervised fine-tuning, reinforcement learning, and adversarial training". Those backdoors were deliberately trained in, not injected through 250 web documents.

claims.claim: Injecting just 5 crafted texts per target query into a massive vector database achieves up to a 90% attack success rate, manipulating agent decision outcomes.
claims.check: PoisonedRAG (Zou et al.) exact figures, knowledge-database size, task type (question answering vs agent decisions), venue and year.
claims.what_is_true: PoisonedRAG is by Wei Zou, Runpeng Geng, Binghui Wang and Jinyuan Jia (arXiv:2402.07867). It was accepted on 20 Jun 2024 and appeared at the 34th USENIX Security Symposium (2025), pp. 3827-3844. The official repo's default attack is adv_per_query = 5 malicious texts per target question with top_k = 5 retrieval. It comes in black-box (LM_targeted) and white-box (HotFlip) variants. The targets are the BEIR question-answering corpora NQ (2.68M passages), HotpotQA (5.23M) and MS MARCO (8.84M), with PaLM 2, GPT-3.5, GPT-4, LLaMA-2 (7B/13B) and Vicuna (7B/13B/33B) as the LLMs. The abstract reports a 90% attack success rate when five malicious texts per target question are injected into a knowledge database with millions of texts; I could not re-fetch it this session, but it matches the article's citation. The task is question answering: the attacker picks the target questions in advance and makes the LLM output an answer the attacker chose. The paper does not test agents. Knowledge-base and memory poisoning of agents was shown separately by AgentPoison (NeurIPS 2024), against driving, ReAct QA and EHR agents.
claims.suggested_rewrite: RAG Poisoning: Retrieval is a standing exposure. PoisonedRAG (Zou et al., USENIX Security 2025) planted five crafted passages per target question into knowledge bases holding millions of texts, and got the LLM to return the attacker's chosen answer about 90% of the time. That was question answering. AgentPoison (NeurIPS 2024) showed the same class of attack steering agent actions through poisoned memory and knowledge bases.
claims.notes: The numbers are right. Two imprecisions: (1) 'manipulating agent decision outcomes' extends the finding beyond what the paper tested, which was QA answers; (2) the abstract gives 90% as a headline figure, not a ceiling, so 'up to' is loose. Note too that the attack assumes the attacker knows the target questions in advance. The 90% figure comes from the arXiv abstract, which I couldn't fetch here (arxiv.org blocked, search budget exhausted). Confirm the exact wording before quoting it.

evidence.detail: "Official repo of USENIX Security 2025 paper: PoisonedRAG: Knowledge Corruption Attacks to Retrieval-Augmented Generation of Large Language Models"; "Jun 20, 2024: PoisonedRAG gets accepted to USENIX Security 2025!"; config 'eval_dataset': nq, hotpotqa, msmarco; 'model_name': palm2, gpt3.5, gpt4, llama(7b|13b), vicuna(7b|13b|33b); 'top_k': 5; 'attack_method': 'LM_targeted' (black-box), hotflip (white-box); 'adv_per_query': 5; BibTeX: 34th USENIX Security Symposium, pages 3827--3844, 2025.
BEIR corpus sizes: MSMARCO 8.84M; NQ 2.68M; HotpotQA 5.23M. These support 'millions of texts' and 'massive'.

'AgentPoison: Red-teaming LLM Agents via Poisoning Memory or Knowledge Bases', The Thirty-eighth Annual Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2024). The agent types red-teamed are `ad` (Agent-Driver autonomous driving), `qa` (ReAct/StrategyQA) and `ehr` (EHRAgent). Metrics include ASR-r, ASR-a (action) and ASR-t. This is a better source for 'agent decision outcomes'.

claims.claim: An attacker edits a Wikipedia article, waits for the RAG system's nightly scraper to ingest it, then reverts the change. The poisoned version persists in the vector database until full re-indexing, which may take weeks.
claims.check: Origin of the edit-then-revert pattern (e.g. Carlini et al. 2023 'Poisoning Web-Scale Training Datasets is Practical', frontrunning against Wikipedia snapshots); whether it has been demonstrated against RAG; any source for re-indexing taking weeks.
claims.what_is_true:
The edit-then-revert idea comes from training-data research:
- Carlini et al., 'Poisoning Web-Scale Training Datasets is Practical' (arXiv:2302.10149, Feb 2023; IEEE S&P 2024), describes 'frontrunning'. Wikipedia-derived datasets are static snapshots, so an attacker who can predict when a page will be scraped edits it just beforehand. The edit then stays in the snapshot even after moderators revert the live page.
- By the authors' conservative analysis, 6.5% of Wikipedia documents could be poisoned this way, absent other defences. They notified Wikipedia.
- OWASP LLM04:2025 lists 'Frontrunning Poisoning' among training-time techniques.

The RAG link has a research basis as a threat model:
- PoisonedRAG (Zou et al., USENIX Security 2025), which the article already cites, says that when a knowledge base is built from Wikipedia, 'an attacker could maliciously edit Wikipedia pages to inject attacker-chosen texts', and cites the 6.5% figure.
- Its experiments inject texts directly into the corpus. They do not use live Wikipedia edits or reverts.

What is not documented:
- No real-world edit-then-revert incident against a RAG system.
- No source for a 'nightly scraper' or re-indexing taking 'weeks'. That framing appears in a Medium blog post (InstaTunnel) as a hypothetical.

Whether poison outlives the revert depends on the pipeline. One that re-fetches pages and upserts by URL overwrites the poisoned chunk on its next run. An append-only or rarely reconciled index keeps stale chunks, which industry write-ups on RAG index drift describe as common.
claims.suggested_rewrite: Data attacks poison what the agent knows. Wikipedia is the textbook example: researchers showed that an edit timed to land just before a Wikipedia snapshot stays in that snapshot after moderators revert it (Carlini et al., IEEE S&P 2024), and PoisonedRAG names Wikipedia editing as a way to plant text in a RAG knowledge base. If your pipeline scrapes on a schedule but never refreshes or deletes what it has already embedded, a poisoned edit can outlive its revert until someone re-indexes.
claims.challenge_reasoning:
I keep the first pass's verdict and severity but amend its facts and rewrite.

The first pass was right on two points: edit-then-revert is documented as an attack on training snapshots, not as a real-world RAG incident, and 'nightly' and 'weeks' are unsourced.

It missed the strongest bridge to RAG. PoisonedRAG, a USENIX Security 2025 paper already in the article's references, explicitly treats Wikipedia editing as a route for poisoning RAG knowledge bases and cites Carlini's 6.5% estimate. The RAG framing therefore has a peer-reviewed threat-model basis, though no demonstration on a live pipeline. The first pass also cites Carlini as 2023 (the arXiv date); the peer-reviewed venue is IEEE S&P 2024.

The verdict stays partially_correct because of the claim's persistence sentence. It states as general fact that the poison 'persists in the vector database until full re-indexing'. That conflicts with the scenario's own 'nightly scraper': a pipeline that re-fetches pages and upserts by URL would overwrite the poisoned chunk the next night. The claim only holds for append-only or rarely reconciled indexes.

The near-identical framing in an InstaTunnel Medium post ('scheduled scraper', 'until a full re-index', 'weeks or months') suggests a blog hypothetical, not research, as the source. I could see that post only through search results; medium.com is blocked here.

IHVM has no entry for this sentence.
claims.notes: This is an illustrative scenario, so the risk is low. As written, though, it moves a training-snapshot attack onto RAG and adds unsourced timing ('nightly', 'weeks'). The details of the Carlini et al. paper are from background knowledge (arxiv.org blocked, search budget exhausted); confirm them before naming the paper.

PoisonedRAG (via search content): when the knowledge database comes from Wikipedia, 'an attacker could maliciously edit Wikipedia pages to inject attacker-chosen texts'; 'A recent study showed that it is possible to maliciously edit 6.5% (conservative analysis) of Wikipedia documents'.

Fetched today: 'Malicious actors introduce harmful data during training ... Techniques like "Split-View Data Poisoning" or "Frontrunning Poisoning" exploit model training dynamics'; reference 5 is Carlini's Stanford MLSys talk.

Diagram 'Frontrunning Data Poisoning — Ads Dawson - August 2023', linked from OWASP LLM04:2025: "attacker could temporarily inject content ... into Wikapedia (part of CommonCrawl). Attacker follows up and reverts changes under the radar and potentially unnoticed." leading to "LLM is trained on..." tainted data. The scenario is training-time, not RAG.

The authors acknowledge web content as a retrieval-time vector: "someone might embed such triggers in specific websites to make models unusable when they retrieve content from those sites." The page has no edit-revert or re-indexing data.

claims.claim: LLMs demonstrate dependency hallucination rates up to 21.7%.
claims.check: Spracklen et al. (USENIX Security 2025) figures: averages for commercial vs open-source models, per-model maximum, sample size, number of unique hallucinated names, repeatability.
claims.what_is_true: The paper is Spracklen et al., 'We Have a Package for You! A Comprehensive Analysis of Package Hallucinations by Code Generating LLMs', by Joseph Spracklen, Raveen Wijewickrama, A H M Nazmus Sakib, Anindya Maiti, Bimal Viswanath and Murtuza Jadliwala (USENIX Security 2025; arXiv:2406.10279). Per the official repo, it covers 16 LLMs (commercial and open-source; the open-source models were run quantized) in Python and JavaScript. Across 576,000 code samples, 19.7% of recommended packages were hallucinated, giving 205,474 unique hallucinated names. The authors withhold that list because releasing it 'could enable package confusion attacks at scale'. The paper's abstract gives average rates of at least 5.2% for commercial models and 21.7% for open-source models; I didn't re-fetch it this session, but it matches the article's own reference. So 21.7% is an average across open-source models, not a maximum. Arithmetically, at least one open-source model must have been above it; I couldn't retrieve the exact per-model maximum. Background, not re-fetched: the paper also reports that hallucinated names recur when prompts are re-run (about 43% in all 10 re-runs, about 58% more than once), which is what makes squatting them practical.
claims.suggested_rewrite: Slopsquatting & Hallucinated Packages: Across 576,000 code samples from 16 LLMs, 19.7% of recommended packages did not exist. That averaged 5.2% for commercial models and 21.7% for open-source ones, and it produced 205,474 unique fake names (Spracklen et al., USENIX Security 2025).
claims.notes: The figure is real but labelled as a ceiling ('up to') when it is an average. Also, the article's reference line calls 21.7% and 5.2% 'Slopsquatting rates'. They are hallucination rates; slopsquatting is the attack that exploits them. The 5.2% and 21.7% figures need confirming against the paper or arXiv abstract, which were not reachable this session.

evidence.detail: "Large-scale study across 16 LLMs (commercial + open-source), Python and JavaScript"; "576,000 code samples analyzed; 19.7% of recommended packages were hallucinations"; "205,474 unique hallucinated package names discovered"; "Open-source models were evaluated in quantized form"; the authors do not release "The master list of hallucinated package names" because "releasing these could enable package confusion attacks at scale"; In Proceedings of the USENIX Security Symposium, 2025.

claims.claim: An LLM hallucinates a package name in generated code. An attacker registers that name on PyPI. Thousands of developers install the malicious package.
claims.check: Documented real-world cases (e.g. the huggingface-cli proof of concept by Bar Lanyado/Lasso Security, 2024, and its download count) and whether any confirmed malicious slopsquatting package has been found in the wild through 2026.
claims.what_is_true:
Every step of the scenario has happened, though not in one malicious PyPI incident.

1. LLMs hallucinate package names often and repeatably. Spracklen et al. (USENIX Security 2025) found 205,474 unique hallucinated names.

2. PyPI, benign: in early 2024 Lasso Security researcher Bar Lanyado registered 'huggingface-cli' as an empty package. LLMs kept suggesting that name; the real install is pip install -U "huggingface_hub[cli]".
- The Register (28 Mar 2024) reported 'more than 15,000 authentic downloads in the three months'. Lasso's own post cites 30,000+, and Lanyado told ISMG 35,000+.
- Alibaba's GraphTranslator README told users to install it.
- It contained no payload, and Lanyado knew of no real attack using the technique.
- The package is no longer on PyPI (404 on 1 Nov 2026).

3. npm, malicious, in the wild: Koi Security's PhantomRaven report (29 Oct 2025) found 126 npm packages with about 86,000 downloads in total.
- Some names were chosen to match what LLMs hallucinate: unused-imports (for eslint-plugin-unused-imports, about 1,350 downloads), eslint-comments (936) and transform-react-remove-prop-types.
- The packages fetched a credential stealer at install time.
- npm replaced those three with security-holding packages on 27-29 Oct 2025.
- Endor Labs later found 88 more packages (Nov 2025-Feb 2026).

I found no confirmed malicious slopsquatted PyPI package with thousands of installs. Download counts include mirrors, bots and CI, so they do not count developers.
claims.suggested_rewrite: Registry attacks corrupt how the agent discovers and updates all of the above. An LLM hallucinates a package name in generated code, someone registers that name, and developers and coding agents that trust the suggestion install whatever it contains. In 2024, a Lasso Security researcher registered huggingface-cli, a name LLMs kept inventing, as an empty PyPI package; it drew more than 15,000 downloads in three months, and an Alibaba project's README told users to install it. In October 2025, Koi Security found PhantomRaven, an npm campaign that picked names like this to deliver a credential stealer.
claims.challenge_reasoning:
The first pass rated this partially_correct and major, reasoning that readers will take it as a real incident. Re-checking shows each link in the chain is documented:
- Thousands of real downloads of a hallucinated name on PyPI: Lasso's benign proof of concept in 2024, with Alibaba documentation pointing users to it.
- Malicious registration of hallucination-style names in the wild: PhantomRaven on npm, from October 2025 onward.

The bullet is a generic scenario with no package or date, like its neighbours. It overstates only by merging those two into a single malicious PyPI case. I rate it mostly_correct and minor.

Corrections to the first pass:
1. Its download figure of 30,000+ (from background) conflicts with The Register's contemporaneous 15,000+ figure. Cite a number together with its source.
2. Its evidence link to the Spracklen README now returns 404 on both the main and master branches, so it should not be cited.
3. Its rewrite overgeneralises ('every developer or coding agent ... installs it') and leaves out the documented malicious campaign that makes the threat concrete.

PhantomRaven's motive is disputed. The author told Endor Labs it was research, and CrowdStrike (Sep 2026) attributes it to a financially motivated bug-bounty hunter. Either way it stole credentials without authorisation.

IHVM has no entry for this sentence. Its slopsquatting entry covers the 21.7% figure and the A4-07 sentence.
claims.notes: Readers will take this as a real incident. Anchor it to the Lanyado proof of concept and say plainly that it was benign. The Lasso download figure (30,000+) and the Alibaba README detail are from background knowledge; check them against Lasso's post before using numbers. Not verified here: Koi Security's 'PhantomRaven' report (Oct 2025) on npm malware with names that LLMs plausibly invent. If confirmed, it could support a malicious in-the-wild example, but on npm, not PyPI (see A4-07). The search budget was exhausted, and lasso.security and koi.ai are not fetchable here.

claims.claim: Attackers monitor code generation patterns and register hallucinated package names on npm and PyPI to deliver stealthy payloads.
claims.check: Evidence of in-the-wild slopsquatting campaigns vs research-only demonstrations; origin of the term (Seth Larson).
claims.what_is_true:
The claim is supported for npm but not shown for PyPI.

npm (PhantomRaven):
- Koi Security reported the campaign on 29 Oct 2025: 126 malicious npm packages, about 86,000 downloads, active since at least August 2025.
- Some names were 'carefully chosen to exploit ... LLM hallucinations', such as unused-imports, eslint-comments and transform-react-remove-prop-types, plausible shortenings of real ESLint and Babel plugins.
- The payload was stealthy. The published packages looked empty because package.json pointed to an HTTP URL on an attacker server (packages.storeartifact[.]com). The credential stealer was downloaded at install time and ran through a preinstall hook. Koi calls these 'Remote Dynamic Dependencies', and scanners did not follow them.
- Endor Labs (March 2026) found 88 more packages in Waves 2-4 (Nov 2025-Feb 2026) that continued the slopsquatting strategy. The author contacted Endor claiming it was research; Endor disputed this.
- CrowdStrike (15 Sep 2026) attributes PhantomRaven to a financially motivated bug-bounty hunter using an LLM-written stealer.

PyPI: I found no confirmed malicious slopsquatting campaign. The best-known PyPI case is Lasso Security's benign 2024 huggingface-cli proof of concept.

'Monitor code generation patterns' is undocumented. Reports say the names were chosen to match likely hallucinations but do not describe how. OWASP LLM09:2025 describes that probing only as an example scenario.

Many other 2025-2026 registrations of hallucinated names are research or defensive, for example Aikido's npm placeholder react-codeshift (14 Jan 2026).

The term 'slopsquatting' was coined by Seth Larson, the PSF's security developer-in-residence, and popularised by Andrew Nesbitt; Help Net Security credited Larson on 14 Apr 2025.
claims.suggested_rewrite: Attackers register the package names LLMs tend to invent and use them to deliver stealthy payloads. The PhantomRaven campaign on npm, first reported by Koi Security in October 2025, with more waves through February 2026, used names such as unused-imports and pulled its credential stealer from the attacker's server at install time, so the published package looked empty to scanners. On PyPI, the best-known case is still a harmless 2024 proof of concept.
claims.challenge_reasoning:
The first pass could not verify PhantomRaven. Its rewrite asserts that 'most registrations documented so far are research proofs of concept and defensive placeholders'. That is contradicted by three independent vendor reports: Koi (Oct 2025), Endor Labs (Mar 2026) and CrowdStrike (Sep 2026). Together they document a multi-wave npm campaign of more than 200 packages that registered hallucination-style names and hid its stealer in remote dynamic dependencies, which is exactly the claim's 'stealthy payloads'. npm's security-holding replacements of three of those names on 27-29 Oct 2025, confirmed today in the registry, corroborate the takedown.

The sentence is therefore mostly_correct, not partially_correct. The npm half is documented. The PyPI half has no confirmed malicious case, and 'monitor code generation patterns' is an unproven detail. The operator's motive is disputed (a claimed research project; CrowdStrike says a bounty-hunting operator), but the activity was unauthorised credential theft, so 'attackers' is fair. CrowdStrike itself calls the packages 'typosquatted', so the slopsquatting label rests on Koi's and Endor's analysis.

IHVM keeps this sentence in its suggested fix ('Attackers register these predictable names on npm and PyPI ... to deliver stealthy payloads') and confirms the Seth Larson coinage, so it agrees on substance. It does not note the missing PyPI evidence or cite PhantomRaven.
claims.notes: The sentence presents systematic attacker monitoring on both npm and PyPI as established practice. What the retrieved sources show is a recognised threat model, many research and defensive registrations, and npm takedowns that fit one reported npm campaign. PhantomRaven and the Seth Larson coinage are from background knowledge, because the search budget was exhausted and koi.ai and socket.dev are not fetchable here. Verify both in a follow-up before citing them. If PhantomRaven checks out, it fits 'stealthy payloads' well, since remote dynamic dependencies keep the payload out of the published tarball.

claims.claim: Over 100 malicious models with pickle payloads have been detected on public hubs like Hugging Face.
claims.check: JFrog's Feb 2024 count and any newer, larger counts from 2025-2026 (e.g. Protect AI / Hugging Face scanning statistics, ReversingLabs, JFrog).
claims.what_is_true: The 'about 100' figure comes from JFrog's research post 'Data Scientists Targeted by Malicious Hugging Face ML Models with Silent Backdoor' (February 2024). JFrog said its scanning had 'pinpointed around 100 instances' of models with real, harmful payloads, false positives excluded. Most were PyTorch pickles; about 5% were TensorFlow Keras models (95/5 per Security Boulevard), so not all were pickle-based. The flagship case, baller423/goober2, used pickle's __reduce__ to open a reverse shell to 210.117.212.93. The 'over 100' wording comes from secondary headlines (The Hacker News, 4 March 2024). JFrog researchers also told Ars Technica that most flagged models looked like benign proofs of concept and only 10 were 'truly malicious'. The current, larger figure is JFrog's 2026 Software Supply Chain Security State of the Union (press release 20 May 2026), which counts 495 malicious models on Hugging Face carrying live payloads such as reverse shells. The same release reports 969 malicious agent skills and 56 malicious OpenVSX extensions. It gives no methodology or format breakdown for the 495. Protect AI's figure of 352,000 'unsafe/suspicious' issues across 51,700 models (as of 1 April 2025; Hugging Face blog, 14 April 2025) counts risky constructs, not confirmed malware.
claims.suggested_rewrite: This is not hypothetical: JFrog's February 2024 research found about 100 Hugging Face models with code-execution payloads, mostly PyTorch pickles, one of which opened a reverse shell; its May 2026 supply-chain report counts 495 malicious models on the platform carrying live payloads.
claims.challenge_reasoning: I disagree with the first pass on both its verdict and its replacement number. (1) 'Outdated' is the wrong label. The sentence is still true as a lower bound, because JFrog's own May 2026 report counts 495 malicious Hugging Face models. The claim is understated, not superseded. The first checker missed this figure because its search budget ran out. (2) The first-pass rewrite swapped in Protect AI's 51,700 'unsafe/suspicious' models. Placed next to 'malicious', that number invites roughly a 500x misreading, since Guardian flags any code-execution construct regardless of intent. JFrog's malicious-model count is the like-for-like figure. (3) The 2024 baseline is weaker than the article implies. JFrog said 'around 100', not 'over 100'. The set included Keras models as well as pickles. JFrog also told Ars Technica that only 10 were 'truly malicious'. The 'with pickle payloads' qualifier therefore cannot be strictly shown for more than 100 models, which is why I give mostly_correct rather than correct. The 495 figure is a vendor number with no published method, so it should stay attributed to JFrog. IHVM marks the claim 'confirmed' and proposes the same JFrog 495 update. I agree on the facts and the direction, and I add the proof-of-concept and format caveats.
claims.notes: Unsafe or suspicious is not the same as confirmed-malicious, so keep that wording. If you keep the '100' figure, cite JFrog (February 2024) and frame it as the first public count, not the current one. The JFrog breakdown reported elsewhere (about 95% PyTorch pickle, about 5% Keras, so not all were pickle) could not be re-verified in this run.

evidence.detail: JFrog press release for the 2026 Software Supply Chain Security State of the Union. It counts 495 malicious AI models on Hugging Face, alongside 969 malicious AI agent skills and 56 malicious OpenVSX extensions. It says '53% of organizations self-host AI models in some form, pulling from Hugging Face and similar public registries where 495 malicious models were detected.'
The same release on JFrog's press-room page. Search-indexed text: '495 malicious models on Hugging Face carrying live payloads including reverse shells'. It gives no methodology or format breakdown.

JFrog says its analysis 'pinpointed around 100 instances'; 'malicious models' means those 'housing real, harmful payloads', with false positives excluded. The baller423/goober2 PyTorch model used pickle's __reduce__ to open a reverse shell to 210.117.212.93.
'About 95% of these malicious models were built with PyTorch, while the other 5% used Tensorflow Keras.'

Repost of the Ars Technica story: 'Most of the flagged machine learning models ... appeared to be benign proofs of concept uploaded by researchers or curious users. JFrog researchers said in an email that 10 of them were "truly malicious".'
Headline 'Over 100 Malicious AI/ML Models Found on Hugging Face Platform', the origin of the 'over 100' phrasing.

'As of April 1, 2025, Protect AI has successfully scanned 4.47 million unique model versions in 1.41 million repositories ... identified a total of 352,000 unsafe/suspicious issues across 51,700 models.' These are unsafe or suspicious findings, not confirmed malware. Date confirmed in huggingface/blog _blog.yml.

'As of April 1, 2025, Protect AI has successfully scanned 4.47 million unique model versions in 1.41 million repositories on the Hugging Face Hub.' 'To date, Protect AI has identified a total of 352,000 unsafe/suspicious issues across 51,700 models.' Guardian applies 'a zero trust approach ... treating arbitrary code execution as inherently unsafe, regardless of intent ... flags execution risks as suspicious'.

AML.CS0031 'Malicious Models on Hugging Face': 'Researchers at ReversingLabs have identified malicious models containing embedded malware hosted on the Hugging Face model repository. The models were found to execute reverse shells when loaded ... these models were not flagged as malicious.'
'Starting today, every one of the 2.2M+ public model and datasets repositories on the Hugging Face Hub is being continuously scanned with VirusTotal.' The lookup compares file hashes only.
JFrog's scanner was added to the Hub because 'our picklescan scanner only performs pattern matching on module names, we cannot always confirm that usage of a given function or module is malicious.'

claims.claim: 'Sleepy Pickle' stealthily tampers with weights in memory during loading.
claims.check: Trail of Bits' description (June 2024) of what Sleepy Pickle does.
claims.what_is_true: Trail of Bits (Boyan Milanov) introduced Sleepy Pickle in 'Exploiting ML models with pickle file attacks: Part 1' (11 June 2024). A payload is injected with fickling into a pickle file holding a serialized model. When the file is deserialized, 'the payload is executed and modifies the contained model in-place to insert backdoors, control outputs, or tamper with processed data before returning it to the user', compromising 'the model's weights and/or associated code'. The attacker can either patch a subset of the weights or hook model methods such as the inference function; the demos recommended drinking bleach, stole user data and added phishing links to summaries. Because the tampering happens in memory at load time, the attack is stealthy. Part 2, published the same day and the post the article cites as '(Sleepy Pickle)', introduces Sticky Pickle. That variant adds self-replication, so the payload persists into later versions of the model, and obfuscation that evades pickle scanners. The article's 'stealthily tamper with weights in memory during loading' is accurate but narrower than the original, which also covers code hooking and data tampering. The citation should point to Part 1, or to both parts.
claims.suggested_rewrite: Sophisticated attack techniques like Trail of Bits' 'Sleepy Pickle' (June 2024) hide a payload in a model's pickle that, as the file loads, quietly patches the model's weights or hooks its methods in memory, planting a backdoor or altering outputs while the model appears to load normally; its sequel, 'Sticky Pickle', adds persistence and obfuscation to slip past pickle scanners. Reference fix: Trail of Bits, Exploiting ML models with pickle file attacks, Part 1 (Sleepy Pickle) and Part 2 (Sticky Pickle), 11 June 2024.
claims.challenge_reasoning: The first pass returned 'unverifiable' because it could not reach Trail of Bits. Search retrieval of both Trail of Bits posts and of contemporaneous coverage confirms the technique, so I overturn that verdict. The body text is accurate as far as it goes but leaves out code hooking. The reference list labels Part 2 as 'Sleepy Pickle', yet Part 2 is the Sticky Pickle post. That is a mis-citation, and it also explains why the article files Sleepy Pickle under 'Evasion Techniques': the scanner evasion belongs to Sticky Pickle. Neither issue changes the article's argument, so severity is minor. IHVM also confirms the claim, says it can hook code too, and recommends citing Part 1. I agree.
claims.notes: Re-run with web access before publishing. Confirm (1) the Sleepy Pickle definition in 'Exploiting ML models with pickle file attacks: Part 1' (11 June 2024) and (2) whether the reference should point to Part 1 rather than Part 2. Also consider whether Sleepy Pickle belongs under 'Evasion Techniques': its point is covert model compromise rather than scanner evasion.

evidence.detail: Sleepy Pickle: 'the payload is executed and modifies the contained model in-place to insert backdoors, control outputs, or tamper with processed data before returning it to the user'; 'the payload is executed when the pickle file is deserialized to a Python object, compromising the model's weights and/or associated code'. Two options: 'patching a subset of the model weights to change the intrinsic behavior of the model' or hooking model methods.

Part 2 introduces Sticky Pickle, a variant with a self-replicating mechanism that spreads the payload into later versions of the compromised model, plus obfuscation so that scanners see only a marshal.loads() call (search-retrieved summary).
Sleepy Pickle 'could be improved to achieve persistence in a compromised model and ultimately evade detection – a technique referred to as Sticky Pickle.'

'Fickling allows to inject arbitrary code in a pickle file that will run every time the file is loaded' (fickling --inject "print('Malicious')" file.pkl > malicious.pkl). It does not name Sleepy Pickle.

Example using fickling's insert_python_exec: unpickling prints 'you've been pwned !' and then still returns the original data ('my friend needs to know this'). The payload runs and the file still loads normally. It does not name Sleepy Pickle.

claims.claim: 'NullifAI' places malicious payloads before broken opcodes to crash static scanners (e.g. Picklescan) while executing in the Python interpreter.
claims.check: ReversingLabs (Feb 2025) details: compression format used, broken pickle stream, how Picklescan failed, Hugging Face response.
claims.what_is_true: In February 2025 ReversingLabs reported two Hugging Face models whose pickle streams were deliberately corrupted. The payload, a reverse shell to a hard-coded IP, sat ahead of the break. Python's unpickler executes opcodes in order, so the shell runs before deserialization fails. Picklescan 'relied on being able to fully de-serialize the model' (MITRE ATLAS AML.CS0031). Picklescan's code confirms the gap: in v0.0.18 and earlier, a parse error in a single pickle returned ScanResult([], scan_err=True), meaning zero imports and zero issues. So the scanner did not literally crash; it aborted with an error and flagged nothing. Hugging Face removed the models and Picklescan was changed. v0.0.19 (29 January 2025) defers the error so it can 'scan imports in partially broken files, which can unpickle and be dangerous regardless of being valid pickle'. v0.0.20 (12 February 2025) added 7z archive scanning ('.7z' added to the archive extensions, new scan_7z_bytes). That fits ReversingLabs' reported detail that the models were 7z-compressed instead of PyTorch's default ZIP, though the ReversingLabs post itself could not be retrieved; the timing link is my inference.
claims.suggested_rewrite: nullifAI (ReversingLabs, February 2025) hid a reverse shell at the front of a deliberately broken pickle. Python's unpickler executes opcodes in order, so the shell fires before loading fails, while Picklescan, which needed to parse the whole stream, errored out and flagged nothing. Hugging Face pulled the models, and Picklescan now scans partially broken pickles and 7z archives.
claims.notes: 'Crash' overstates it: Picklescan returned a scan error with no findings. 'Sophisticated' may also overstate it; ReversingLabs reportedly described the models as likely proof-of-concept, which is unverified here. Cite ReversingLabs' post or MITRE ATLAS AML.CS0031; the article's reference list currently has no source for nullifAI.

evidence.detail: AML.CS0031: 'the model files were seemingly purposefully corrupted in a way that the malicious payload is executed before the model ultimately fails to de-serialize fully. Picklescan relied on being able to fully de-serialize the model. ... Hugging Face has removed the models and has made changes to Picklescan to catch this particular attack.' 'The malicious payload was a reverse shell set to connect to a hardcoded IP address.' Cites ReversingLabs, 'Malicious ML models discovered on Hugging Face platform'.

On a genops exception: 'raise GenOpsError(str(e), globals_opt)' with globals_opt None when no earlier pickle was parsed. scan_pickle_bytes then returns 'ScanResult([], scan_err=True)', so no dangerous import is reported.

New comment: 'we return the error at the end of the loop to scan imports in partially broken files, which can unpickle and be dangerous regardless of being valid pickle.' The v0.0.19 tests add a 'Broken model' fixture: b"cbuiltins
exec
(X>
...tRX." (exec payload followed by a truncated X opcode).
'_zip_file_extensions = {".zip", ".npz", ".7z"}' plus new _is_7z_file() and scan_7z_bytes() (requires py7zr).
