claims.claim: Require signed AIBOMs (CycloneDX 1.6+ ML-BOM or SPDX 3.0 AI profile).
claims.check: Whether each format supports signing natively (CycloneDX JSF / XML signature; SPDX 3.0 none) and common practice (cosign, in-toto attestations).
claims.what_is_true: Both formats can carry signed AIBOMs, but in different ways. CycloneDX signs natively: enveloped JSON Signature Format (JSF) signatures can sit at BOM level and on individual components, services and compositions. The property exists in the 1.4 schema and later; 1.6 describes it as 'Enveloped signature in JSON Signature Format (JSF)'. JSF algorithms include RS/PS/ES 256-512, Ed25519, Ed448 and HS. SPDX 3.0.1 defines no digital-signature construct. Its integrity mechanism is the Element property verifiedUsing (IntegrityMethod, e.g. hashes), and the spec's chapters (scope, conformance, serializations, annexes) have no signing section. SPDX AIBOMs are therefore signed outside the document, typically as in-toto attestations (predicate types https://cyclonedx.org/bom and https://spdx.dev/Document/v3) signed with Sigstore `cosign attest`. Its --type flag accepts spdx, spdxjson, cyclonedx or a custom predicate URI. Per the third-party encoding, the G7 minimum elements include 'SBOM author signature'. For SPDX, use the AI and Dataset profiles together. Caveat: k8s-aibom, which the article names in the same step as the reference implementation, does not sign the BOMs it emits.
claims.suggested_rewrite: Require signed AIBOMs. CycloneDX 1.6+ (ML-BOM) supports enveloped JSF signatures natively. SPDX 3.0.1 (AI and Dataset profiles) has no built-in signature, so ship it as an in-toto attestation signed with Sigstore (cosign attest). Google's k8s-aibom doesn't sign its output yet, so add that step yourself.
claims.notes: The recommendation is sound and achievable in both formats. Spell out the mechanism so readers don't assume SPDX has built-in signing. Add a note that the cited reference tool's output still has to be signed downstream.

evidence.detail: Top-level 'signature': {'$ref': '#/definitions/signature', 'description': 'Enveloped signature in [JSON Signature Format (JSF)]'}. compositions also carry 'signature'. The 1.4 schema already has the top-level signature property.
Official valid example carries ES256 JSF signatures at /signature (whole BOM), /components[0]/signature, /services[0]/signature and /compositions[0]/signature.

'An IntegrityMethod provides an independently reproducible mechanism that permits verification of a specific Element ... enables a recipient to determine if anything in the original Element has been changed'. Element.md exposes it as 'verifiedUsing'. No signature class appears in the model or the spec chapters (mkdocs nav: Scope, References, Symbols, Terms, Conformance, Model and serializations, Annexes A-E).

'Predicate type: SPDX. Type URI: https://spdx.dev/Document/v3 ... This can represent software artifacts, software supply chains, AI models and more.' cyclonedx.md: 'Type URI: https://cyclonedx.org/bom ... The predicate contains a JSON-encoded CycloneDX BOM.'
'--type string specify a predicate type (slsaprovenance|slsaprovenance02|slsaprovenance1|link|spdx|spdxjson|cyclonedx|vuln|openvex|custom) or an URI (default "custom")'.
G7AI-MD-05 'SBOM author signature: A cryptographic signature or integrity method that allows verification of SBOM authorship.'

k8s-aibom output is not yet signed: '...before AICR signs runtime observations'; 'signing observed bytes proves what the signer captured, not that every upstream heuristic or workload declaration was true'.

claims.claim: CycloneDX 1.7 added citations, patent assertions and broader crypto coverage, but nothing agent-specific.
claims.check: Release date of 1.7 and the complete list of additions (citations, patents, distribution constraints/TLP, isExternal, CBOM changes, formulation changes, etc.); whether anything agent/MCP/tool-specific was added.
claims.what_is_true: CycloneDX 1.7 was released on 21 October 2025. Diffing bom-1.7.schema.json against 1.6 gives these additions. (1) A new top-level `citations` array (definition `citation`). (2) Patents: `definitions.patents` (patent / patentFamily), `patentAssertions` on components and services, and the externalReference types `citation`, `patent`, `patent-assertion` and `patent-family`. (3) `metadata.distributionConstraints.tlp` (TLP). (4) `component.isExternal` and `component.versionRange` (vers syntax). (5) licenseChoice restructured into one array that mixes licenses and expressions, with `licensing` split into its own definition. (6) `externalReference.properties`. (7) Streebog-256 and Streebog-512 hash algorithms. (8) A large CBOM expansion: a new cryptography-defs registry (`algorithmFamily`, `ellipticCurve`, with `curve` deprecated), a `key-wrap` primitive, certificate lifecycle fields (certificateState, creation/activation/deactivation/revocation/destruction dates, serialNumber, fingerprint, certificateExtensions, certificateFileExtension), `relatedCryptographicAssets`, protocol types dtls, quic, 5g-aka, eap-aka, eap-aka-prime and prins, IKEv2 transform definitions, and cipherSuite tlsGroups and tlsSignatureSchemes. (9) The formulation description was broadened to cover any referenceable object. The 1.7 release added no new component.type values, and services gained only `patentAssertions`. Nothing in it is agent-, tool- or MCP-specific. Patch releases followed: 1.7.1 (published by 4 June 2026) and an XSD-only 1.7.2.
claims.suggested_rewrite: CycloneDX 1.7 (21 October 2025) added citations, patents and patent assertions, a BOM-level TLP label, external components with version ranges, and a much bigger CBOM. None of it is agent-specific: there are no new component types and no tool or MCP constructs.
claims.notes: The claim is accurate but undersells 1.7. TLP distribution constraints, external components with version ranges and the license restructure are also new. Elsewhere the document says 1.7 'expanded formulation workflows' and that 1.7 deepened ML-BOM. Both are overstated (see additional findings).

evidence.detail: OWASP announcement says v1.7 was released 21 October 2025. Its headline areas are advanced cryptography (CBOM), intellectual property (patents and patent families) and data provenance (structured citations).

Recursive diff against bom-1.6.schema.json shows additions limited to: citations; definitions.patents; patentAssertions on component and service; metadata.distributionConstraints; component isExternal and versionRange; externalReference properties plus types citation, patent, patent-assertion and patent-family; hash-alg Streebog-256/512; and cryptoProperties additions (algorithmFamily, ellipticCurve, key-wrap, certificate lifecycle fields, relatedCryptographicAssets, protocol types dtls/quic/5g-aka/eap-aka/eap-aka-prime/prins, tlsGroups, tlsSignatureSchemes). component.type enum is unchanged at 13 values.

CycloneDX-maintained diff says: 'CycloneDX 1.7 is the 2nd Edition (December 2025) and adds citations, patents, distribution constraints, and a standardized cryptography registry'. It also lists External Components (isExternal, versionRange), the License Choice restructure, 'Formulation Scope. Extended beyond components and services to cover any referenceable BOM object', CBOM deprecations and Streebog hashes.
The specification's release history lists CycloneDX 1.7 dated 21 October 2025.

claims.claim: CycloneDX 1.7's modelCard.properties field exists in the JSON schema but not in the XML schema, which a maintainer confirmed is a bug, so converting between the two loses data.
claims.check: Inspect both schemas for modelCard properties; search for the GitHub issue and maintainer response.
claims.what_is_true: The claim was true for the original CycloneDX 1.7 release (21 Oct 2025, XSD version="1.7.0") but has been fixed since 2 June 2026. In 1.7.0, XSD modelCardType held only modelParameters, quantitativeAnalysis and considerations, and the Protobuf ModelCard stopped at field 4 (bom_ref, modelParameters, quantitativeAnalysis, considerations). The JSON schema has had modelCard.properties since 1.5, and the 1.5.0 and 1.6.0 XSDs had the same gap. Spec issue #726 ('[Defect]: modelCard missing `properties` in XML & ProtoBuf') says the bug 'exists since v1.5' and is 'in v1.7 still'. In cyclonedx-python-lib PR #914, a ModelCard with properties validated as JSON 1.7 but failed XML 1.7 ('... properties is not expected'). Maintainer jkowalleck replied that it was a bug, 'caused CycloneDX/specification#726', and proposed omitting the property for XML only. The 1.7.1 patch (GitHub release 2 June 2026, with backports 1.6.2 and 1.5.1) fixed it via PR #743. It added an optional //modelCard/properties XML node (bom:propertiesType, 0..1) and the Protobuf field `repeated Property properties = 5` (release notes call it 'ModelCard.property'). Parsed XSDs confirm properties in 1.5.1, 1.6.2, 1.7.1 and 1.7.2. 1.7.1 also changed considerations user, useCase, technicalLimitation and performanceTradeoff in XML from maxOccurs=1 to unbounded, closing a second JSON-to-XML loss. The 1.7.0-to-1.7.1 JSON diff is editorial only, so the defect was XML/Protobuf-only. cyclonedx-python-lib 11.8.0 and @cyclonedx/cyclonedx-library 10.1.0 added 1.7.1 support on 4 June 2026. The JS library added 1.7.2 support on 17 Sept 2026. 1.7.2 fixed another XML-only gap (protocol relatedCryptographicAssets, PR #1019), so JSON/XML drift is a recurring pattern.
claims.suggested_rewrite: Its original 1.7.0 release defined modelCard.properties in JSON but not in the XML or Protobuf schemas, a gap dating back to 1.5 that a maintainer confirmed as a bug (spec issue #726), so JSON-to-XML conversion lost data until the 1.7.1 patch fixed it on 2 June 2026. Validators still pinned to the 1.7.0 XSD reject the field.
claims.challenge_reasoning: I re-checked the first pass against primary files, and its facts hold. I parsed the XSDs at their git tags. modelCardType has no properties element in 1.5.0, 1.6.0 or 1.7.0, and gains it in 1.5.1, 1.6.2, 1.7.1 and 1.7.2. The proto diff from 1.7.0 to 1.7.1 adds `repeated Property properties = 5`. The XSD diff also confirms the first pass's second finding (four considerations elements moving from maxOccurs 1 to unbounded). The first pass could not pin the fix date. The GitHub releases page (via search) shows 1.7.1 published 02 Jun, which fits both reference libraries shipping 1.7.1 support on 4 June 2026 (PyPI and npm timestamps, plus changelogs). The claim is therefore outdated, not false: current 1.7.x schemas carry the field in JSON, XML and Protobuf. I made three amendments. (1) The rewrite now gives the fix date and notes that Protobuf was also affected. (2) The first-pass wording 'Maintainers called it a bug (spec issue #726)' blurs who said what: one maintainer (jkowalleck) confirmed it in python-lib PR #914 and pointed at spec issue #726. The claim's 'a maintainer confirmed' is accurate. (3) I lowered severity from major to minor. The corrected past-tense statement still supports the author's point that the extension point wobbled, so the original gets the timing wrong but not the substance. Both instances still need fixing. For the second ('Even the extension point wobbles: modelCard.properties validates in JSON but the 1.7 XML schema rejects it.'), use: 'Even the extension point wobbled: until the 1.7.1 patch in June 2026, modelCard.properties validated in JSON but the 1.7 XML schema rejected it.' IHVM agrees on substance: issue #726, the maintainer quote, XML plus Protobuf affected, the gap dating from 1.5, and the fix in 1.7.1/1.6.2/1.5.1 on 2 June 2026. It labels the claim 'partially-correct' where I use 'outdated'. It also follows the release notes in naming the Protobuf field 'ModelCard.property', while the .proto file names it `properties`. I could not independently confirm IHVM's #726 close date (22 May 2026): github.com is blocked, and the shared search budget ran out.
claims.notes: The document asserts this twice: in the Format-specific section, and as 'modelCard.properties validates in JSON but the 1.7 XML schema rejects it'. Both are stale as of the 1.7.1 patch. I could not pin the exact 1.7.1 tag date because GitHub pages are blocked; both reference libraries shipped 1.7.1 support on 4 June 2026. claims.claim: CycloneDX 1.7 citations already carry an optional signature.
claims.check: citation object fields in the 1.7 JSON schema.
claims.what_is_true: In bom-1.7.schema.json, the `citation` definition has these properties: bom-ref, pointers (JSON Pointers), expressions (JSONPath/XPath), timestamp, attributedTo, process, note and signature. `signature` ($ref to the JSF signature) is optional and described as 'A digital signature verifying the authenticity or integrity of the attribution.' Only `timestamp` is required. At least one of attributedTo or process must be present, and exactly one of pointers or expressions. The XSD citationType has no explicit signature element. XML citations would be signed with an XML-DSig element placed in its xs:any ##other slot.
claims.suggested_rewrite: Citations can already carry a JSF signature (citation.signature in the 1.7 JSON schema), but it's optional, and it signs the attribution, not the source it points to.
claims.notes: This contradicts the document's other line that 1.7 'doesn't bind citations to cryptographic evidence, it's a reference, not a proof'. The binding exists but is optional, and it signs the attribution record, not the cited source.

claims.claim: CycloneDX's native signing is JSF; JSF enveloped signatures are rarely used, and ecosystems sign with Sigstore/DSSE instead.
claims.check: JSON schema signature definition (JSF) and XML signing (XML-DSig); evidence on real-world usage.
claims.what_is_true: The JSON schema's `signature` is an 'Enveloped signature in JSON Signature Format (JSF)' ($ref jsf-0.82.schema.json). It can be attached to the BOM root, components, services, compositions, annotations, standards, citations and every level of declarations. JSF supports simple signatures, multi-signatures (`signers`) and signature chains (`chain`). XML BOMs use enveloped W3C XML Signature (ds:Signature) placed through the XSD's ##other extension slots. CycloneDX's own use-case documentation lists XML Signature, JWS and JSF. Tooling evidence: the official cyclonedx-cli `sign bom` and `verify all` handle only XML ('Only XML BOMs are currently supported for signing'). cyclonedx-python-lib marks bom.signature as not supported. Sigstore cosign supports `attest --type cyclonedx` (an in-toto statement with a CycloneDX predicate, in a DSSE envelope). I found no usage survey; 'rarely used' is inferred from tooling.
claims.suggested_rewrite: CycloneDX's native signing is enveloped: JSF for JSON, XML Signature for XML. Even CycloneDX's own CLI signs and verifies only XML, and the Python library doesn't implement signatures at all. In practice teams sign BOMs out of band with Sigstore (cosign attest --type cyclonedx: an in-toto statement in a DSSE envelope), which the spec doesn't define.
claims.notes: Native signing is JSF for JSON only; XML uses XML-DSig. The neighbouring line 'Signing is bytes-level and single-party' is wrong on the second point, because JSF supports multisignature and signature chains. What's missing is claim-level composition and Sigstore/DSSE alignment, not multi-party signing. The search budget ran out before I could look for usage statistics.

signature oneOf: 'signers' ('Multiple Signatures (multisignature)'), 'chain' ('Signature Chains (signaturechain)'), or a simple signer.

'CycloneDX supports existing standards, including XML Signature, JSON Web Signature (JWS), and JSON Signature Format (JSF).' The XML example uses ds:Signature with the xmldsig#enveloped-signature transform.

claims.claim: CycloneDX already has a substantial claims-and-evidence structure (attestations), including evidence expiry.
claims.check: declarations object (assessors, attestations, claims, evidence with created/expires, targets, affirmation); the version that introduced it.
claims.what_is_true: Top-level `declarations` was introduced in 1.6 as CycloneDX Attestations (CDXA); it is absent in 1.5. It has six parts plus a signature. (1) assessors: thirdParty flag and organization. (2) attestations: an assessor plus a map from requirement to claims and counterClaims, with conformance (score 0 to 1, rationale, mitigationStrategies), confidence (score, rationale) and a signature. (3) claims: target, predicate, mitigationStrategies, reasoning, evidence, counterEvidence, externalReferences and a signature. (4) evidence: propertyName, description, data (attachment/url, classification, sensitiveData, governance), created, `expires` ('when the evidence is no longer valid'), author, reviewer and a signature. (5) targets: organizations, components, services. (6) affirmation: statement, signatories, signature. Requirements come from top-level `definitions.standards` (also new in 1.6). The keys are unchanged in 1.7.
claims.suggested_rewrite: CycloneDX already has a real claims-and-evidence model. Declarations (CDXA, since 1.6) map standards requirements to claims, counter-claims and evidence, with conformance and confidence scores, third-party assessors, signed affirmations and expiring evidence (evidence[].expires).

evidence.detail: properties.declarations: assessors, attestations, claims, evidence, targets, affirmation, signature. evidence[].expires: 'The date and time (timestamp) when the evidence is no longer valid.'
declarations and definitions.standards are present in 1.6, with the same keys and evidence created/expires. Both are absent from bom-1.5.schema.json.

claims.claim: CycloneDX's own AI/ML guide acknowledges that some information, including tokenizers, prompt templates, training workflow details and runtime topology, may require properties or external references in v1.7.
claims.check: Find the CycloneDX AI/ML-BOM guide (authoritative guide) and the exact wording.
claims.what_is_true: The guide is the OWASP CycloneDX Authoritative Guide to AI/ML-BOM from the CycloneDX AI/ML Working Group: First Edition 2026-03-03, First Edition r1 ('Updates to appendices and examples') 2026-06-10. Search excerpts of the PDF show three relevant points. (1) It says v1.7 may not have specific objects or fields for some AI/ML metadata, and directs producers to reserved AI/ML property names registered in the CycloneDX Property Taxonomy. (2) Its 'Tokenizers and prompt templates' section covers 'Descriptive details of specific tokenizers (e.g., libraries, files, configurations) and prompt templates used to train and/or interact with the model during runtime', and says 'It is best practice to treat tokenizers and prompt (or chat) templates as annotated components'. (3) It uses externalReferences to link a model's repository and originating model card. The official taxonomy (cdx:ai-ml) reserves cdx:ai-ml:model:tokenizer and cdx:ai-ml:model:template:prompt/chat (each defined as a boolean marker). It also reserves cdx:ai-ml:tokenizer:hyperparameter:* (including chat_template, eos_token, vocab_size). Its own tokenizer example sets the boolean marker to 'LLMTokenizer' and uses an undefined name, cdx:ai-ml:tokenizer:parameter:vocab_size. The schema stores property names and values as plain strings, and registration is optional. I found no guide text saying training workflow details or runtime topology need properties. Runtime topology has a native v1.7 field: formulation workflow and task runtimeTopology, 'A graph of the component runtime topology for workflow's instance'. Formulation natively covers 'how a model was trained', but the 1.7 taskType enum (copy, clone, lint, scan, merge, build, test, deliver, deploy, release, clean, other) has no training or fine-tuning value. A secondary summary says normative AI/ML workflow task types and fine-tuning taxonomies are slated for CycloneDX v2.0.
claims.suggested_rewrite: CycloneDX's own AI/ML-BOM guide (first edition March 2026, revised June 2026) acknowledges that v1.7 may lack fields for some AI/ML metadata and points producers to reserved cdx:ai-ml properties. It models tokenizers and prompt or chat templates as separate components tagged with those properties, and links model repositories and model cards through external references. Training runs fit in formulation, but v1.7's task types have no training or fine-tuning value. These mechanisms are useful, but the registered names are mostly markers and free-form strings that no schema validates, so implementers still need richer shared definitions and validation rules to make the data interoperable.
claims.challenge_reasoning: The first pass called this unverifiable. I'd move it to partially_correct, because search excerpts of the guide PDF support the core attribution: the guide does say v1.7 may lack specific fields for some AI/ML metadata and sends producers to reserved properties. It also recommends annotated components for tokenizers and prompt or chat templates, and uses external references for model repositories and model cards. The specific four-item list does not hold up. 'Tokenizers, prompt templates' matches the guide's annotated-component guidance. 'Training workflow details' is half-right: formulation is a native home (the SBOM guide says formulation shows 'how a model was trained'), but no training task type exists, and v2.0 is said to add AI/ML task taxonomies (secondary source only). 'Runtime topology' is contradicted by the schema, which has a native runtimeTopology field on workflows and tasks. I also challenge the first-pass rewrite. Its line 'two producers' annotations won't line up without shared definitions' ignores that the official Property Taxonomy already defines shared names for tokenizers, chat/prompt templates and tokenizer hyperparameters. The author's point survives in narrower form: those names are a registry, not schema-validated, and the taxonomy's own tokenizer example contradicts its boolean definition and uses an undefined name. Limitations: I could not read the guide's full text. cyclonedx.org is blocked for fetch, only the frontispiece, preface, introduction and history chapters were retrievable from the guides repo, and the shared web-search budget ran out mid-check. Guide quotes therefore come from search-engine excerpts. Severity is minor: it is a supporting sentence, and a reword fixes it. IHVM does not cover this claim.
claims.notes: I could not locate the exact passage. cyclonedx.org is blocked for direct fetch, the shared web-search budget ran out during this check, and only two chapters of the guide's Markdown source could be retrieved. The guide is real. The specific acknowledgment, especially 'runtime topology', may be an AI-assisted paraphrase. The guide's verified stance (model tokenizers and templates as annotated components) differs a little from 'may require properties or external references'. Cite the section precisely, or use the rewrite.

evidence.detail: 'The content in this guide results from the work of the CycloneDX AI/ML Working Group'; 'First Edition (Revision 1), 10 June 2026'; version table: First Edition 'Initial Release' 2026-03-03; First Edition r1 'Updates to appendices and examples' 2026-06-10.

Search excerpts: v1.7 'may not have specific objects or fields' for certain AI/ML metadata, so the guide uses reserved AI/ML property names from the CycloneDX Property Taxonomy. TOC lists 'Tokenizers and prompt templates' and 'Using CycloneDX AI/ML properties'.

claims.claim: CycloneDX services[] has endpoints, authenticated, x-trust-boundary and data flow, but no tool input/output schema, no description text used by models, no definition hash, and no MCP-style annotations.
claims.check: Service object fields in 1.7 (endpoints, authenticated, x-trust-boundary, trustZone, data[].flow, etc.).
claims.what_is_true: The 1.7 service fields are: bom-ref, provider, group, name, version, description, endpoints, authenticated, x-trust-boundary, trustZone (since 1.5), data[], licenses, patentAssertions (1.7), externalReferences, services (nested), releaseNotes, properties, tags and signature. data[] items have flow (inbound, outbound, bi-directional, unknown), classification, name, description, governance, source and destination. Services have no input/output schema, no `hashes` (so no definition digest) and no annotation vocabulary. Services do have a generic free-text `description` ('Specifies a description for the service'). Nothing designates it as the model-facing tool description or pins it to a digest, though a JSF signature over the service object is possible.
claims.suggested_rewrite: Services are endpoint-centric. services[] has endpoints, authenticated, x-trust-boundary, trustZone and data[].flow: fine for REST, thin for tools. There's no input/output schema, no hashes field (so no definition digest to catch a rug-pull) and no MCP-style annotations (read-only, destructive, idempotent, open-world). There's only a generic description string, and nothing marks it as the text the model reads or pins it.

claims.claim: CycloneDX dependencies[] (ref, dependsOn, provides) carry no edge semantics such as invokes or delegatesTo, and no way to mark an edge as runtime-resolved.
claims.check: Dependency object fields in 1.7.
claims.what_is_true: The 1.7 `dependency` object has only `ref` (required), `dependsOn[]` and `provides[]`. provides means components or services 'that define a given specification or standard, which are provided or implemented by this dependency object'. It sets additionalProperties:false and has no `properties`, so edges can't even be annotated. There are only two edge kinds and no runtime-resolution marker. claims.claim: CycloneDX's dependency model is a flat list with no graph relationships; multi-model pipelines (ensemble, cascade, router to specialist) are awkward to represent.
claims.check: Whether dependencies form a graph via refs, and what relationship mechanisms exist (dependsOn, provides, pedigree ancestors/descendants/variants, compositions, formulation).
claims.what_is_true: CycloneDX models a directed dependency graph, serialized flat by design. The SBOM guide says 'A dependency graph is capable of representing both direct and transitive relationships' and that the graph 'SHOULD be codified to be one node deep, meaning no nested child graphs. All relations are on the same level.' The 1.7 schema's dependency definition refers to 'the graph' and 'the dependency graph' and recommends compositions to indicate unknown dependency graphs. CycloneDX's own skill describes dependencies as 'a directed graph'. There are only two edge types: 'As of CycloneDX v1.6, there are two types of dependencies: dependsOn and provides'. dependsOn is a uniqueItems array, with no order, role or condition. Other relationship mechanisms exist. The guide says: 'CycloneDX has a rich set of relationships ... These include assemblies, dependencies, and pedigree', plus bom-ref references. Pedigree has ancestors, descendants and variants (typed lineage, usable for derived-from). Compositions describe completeness. serviceData flows carry direction (inbound, outbound, bi-directional, unknown) with source and destination BOM-Links. Formulation workflows and tasks have taskDependencies, inputs, outputs and runtimeTopology graphs. BOM-Link links across BOMs. What's missing is vocabulary for runtime invocation semantics such as routes-to, falls-back-to or ensemble-member. Ensembles, cascades and router-to-specialist pipelines can therefore be represented only lossily, not natively.
claims.suggested_rewrite: Coarse graph relationships. CycloneDX does have a dependency graph, serialized as a flat, one-level list with only two edge types, dependsOn and provides. An ensemble, a cascade and a router-to-specialist pipeline all collapse to 'depends on', with no order, condition or role on the edge. Assemblies, pedigree, service data flows and formulation workflows add structure, but none of them marks an edge as a routing choice, a fallback or an ensemble member.
claims.challenge_reasoning: I uphold partially_correct with an amended rewrite. Primary sources refute 'no graph relationships'. The 1.7 schema, the SBOM guide's Relationships chapter and CycloneDX's own skill all call dependencies a graph, and the guide lists assemblies, dependencies and pedigree as native relationships. 'Flat list' is literally right, because the guide prescribes one-node-deep serialization, but a flat adjacency list is still a graph. The 'awkward for multi-model pipelines' judgment is defensible: there are two edge types, dependsOn is an unordered set, and there are no roles or conditions. I challenge two parts of the first-pass rewrite. 'Its edges are untyped' overstates: there are two edge types, so 'coarse' is more accurate. 'Pedigree, compositions and formulation add structure, not edge semantics' is partly wrong. Pedigree ancestors, descendants and variants are typed lineage relations, and serviceData flows carry direction with source and destination. The real gap is runtime invocation semantics. The doc already states this correctly elsewhere ('dependencies[].dependsOn/provides carries no edge semantics (invokes, delegatesTo, ...)'), so the two passages should be reconciled. Severity is major: in a section aimed at standards bodies, a CycloneDX practitioner would refute 'no graph relationships' from the spec's own wording. IHVM does not cover this claim.
claims.notes: 'No graph relationships' is wrong and easy for a CycloneDX practitioner to refute. The defensible point is 'untyped edges'.

evidence.detail: 'CycloneDX has a rich set of relationships ... Some relationships are declared through the natural use of the CycloneDX format. These include assemblies, dependencies, and pedigree.' 'A dependency graph is capable of representing both direct and transitive relationships. In CycloneDX representation dependencies, a dependency graph SHOULD be codified to be one node deep, meaning no nested child graphs. All relations are on the same level.' 'As of CycloneDX v1.6, there are two types of dependencies: dependsOn and provides.'

definitions.dependency: 'Components or services that do not have their own dependencies must be declared as empty elements within the graph. Components or services that are not represented in the dependency graph may have unknown dependencies ... It is recommended to leverage compositions to indicate unknown dependency graphs.' dependsOn and provides are uniqueItems arrays of refLinkType. serviceData has flow (inbound, outbound, bi-directional, unknown), source and destination ('The URI, URL, or BOM-Link of the components or services the data is sent to'). pedigree has ancestors, descendants, variants, commits, patches and notes. workflow has taskDependencies and runtimeTopology.

'CycloneDX can represent component pedigree including ancestors, descendants, and variants which describe component lineage from any viewpoint'; ancestors 'Describes zero or more components from which a component is derived.'

Official CycloneDX skill: 'Dependencies. The dependencies array models a directed graph with ref (the component) and dependsOn (its direct dependencies). The provides field documents which specifications a component implements.'

claims.claim: CycloneDX VEX has no vocabulary for 'not affected: tool disabled / guardrail enforced / human approval required'.
claims.check: vulnerabilities[].analysis.justification enum values in 1.7 (e.g. protected_by_mitigating_control, requires_configuration) and whether they could express these.
claims.what_is_true: CycloneDX 1.7 VEX lives in vulnerabilities[].analysis. Its fields are state, justification, response, detail, firstIssued and lastUpdated, with no reference or properties field. state values are resolved, resolved_with_pedigree, exploitable, in_triage, false_positive and not_affected ('Justification should be specified for all not_affected cases'). The justification enum is unchanged from 1.7.0 through 1.7.2: code_not_present; code_not_reachable ('The vulnerable code is not invoked at runtime'); requires_configuration ('Exploitability requires a configurable option to be set/unset'); requires_dependency; requires_environment; protected_by_compiler; protected_at_runtime ('Exploits are prevented at runtime'); protected_at_perimeter; protected_by_mitigating_control ('Preventative measures have been implemented that reduce the likelihood and/or impact of the vulnerability'). Response values: can_not_fix, will_not_fix, update, rollback, workaround_available. Generic terms therefore exist for all three cases. Tool disabled maps to requires_configuration or code_not_reachable, guardrail enforced to protected_at_runtime, and human approval required to protected_by_mitigating_control. What's missing is agent-specific values and any structured link from the justification to the specific control (guardrail component, policy version, approval gate). The schema directs the explanation to free-text detail: it 'should include specific details on why the component or service is not impacted'. The only other place is untyped vulnerability-level properties. Ratings (CVSSv2, CVSSv3, CVSSv31, CVSSv4, OWASP Risk Rating, SSVC, other) score severity and do not express not-affected. CycloneDX 2.0 is not released: the spec README lists 1.7 (21 Oct 2025) as the latest release, and master has no bom-2.0 schema.
claims.suggested_rewrite: VEX can only say 'not affected' here in generic terms: requires_configuration (or code_not_reachable), protected_at_runtime and protected_by_mitigating_control roughly cover 'tool disabled', 'guardrail enforced' and 'human approval required', but the analysis object has no field that names the guardrail, policy version or approval gate, so that evidence ends up in free-text detail or untyped properties.
claims.challenge_reasoning: I uphold partially_correct with an amended rewrite. The schema check confirms that the 1.7 justification enum, unchanged through 1.7.2, has generic values that map onto each of the author's three cases. 'No vocabulary' is therefore overstated, and a VEX practitioner would cite protected_by_mitigating_control or protected_at_runtime. code_not_reachable also fits 'tool disabled', which the first pass missed. The defensible gap is precision and evidence binding: analysis has no reference field, and the schema itself sends the reason to free-text detail. I challenge two parts of the first-pass rewrite. 'Only in CVE-era terms' is inaccurate, because the justification enum is generic rather than CVE-specific. 'That evidence lives in free-text detail' leaves out untyped vulnerability-level properties as the other, non-standard place. The original's mention of 'ratings' misses the point, since ratings score severity and never express not-affected. Context: the IHVM register reports that CycloneDX's August 2026 2.0 announcement plans VEX determinations with attached evidence. That suggests the project itself sees bare not_affected assertions as a gap. 2.0 is unreleased, so the 1.7 gap is current. I could not re-verify that announcement myself because the shared search budget ran out. IHVM has no entry for this specific claim. Severity is major: the overstatement sits in the section that motivates the doc's AI-VEX proposal, where the target audience would catch it.
claims.notes: 'No vocabulary' is overstated. A VEX practitioner would cite protected_by_mitigating_control. The real gap is precision and evidence binding.

evidence.detail: definitions.impactAnalysisJustification enum and meta:enum as quoted (code_not_reachable 'The vulnerable code is not invoked at runtime'; requires_configuration 'Exploitability requires a configurable option to be set/unset'; protected_at_runtime 'Exploits are prevented at runtime'; protected_by_mitigating_control 'Preventative measures have been implemented that reduce the likelihood and/or impact of the vulnerability'). analysis properties: state, justification, response, detail, firstIssued, lastUpdated. detail: 'If a vulnerability is not exploitable, this field should include specific details on why the component or service is not impacted by this vulnerability.' scoreMethod enum: CVSSv2, CVSSv3, CVSSv31, CVSSv4, OWASP, SSVC, other.
The impactAnalysisJustification definition is byte-identical to current master, so the enum is unchanged from 1.7.0 through 1.7.2.
Release History table's latest row: 'CycloneDX 1.7 | 21 October 2025'. schema/bom-2.0.schema.json returns 404 on master, so CycloneDX 2.0 is not released.

claims.claim: modelCard.quantitativeAnalysis.performanceMetrics names benchmarks as strings with no benchmark version, dataset hash, harness identity or configuration.
claims.check: performanceMetrics fields in the 1.7 modelCard.
claims.what_is_true: A 1.7 `performanceMetric` has type (string, 'The type of performance metric', e.g. accuracy or F1), value (string), slice (string) and confidenceInterval {lowerBound, upperBound} (strings). It sets additionalProperties:false and has no properties field, and the definition is unchanged since 1.6. There is no benchmark name or version field, no dataset reference or hash, no harness identity and no configuration. Evaluation datasets can be listed separately in modelParameters.datasets ('The datasets used to train and evaluate the model', inline or by ref to a data component that can carry hashes), but nothing ties an individual metric to a dataset. Strictly, there is no benchmark field at all; benchmark identity ends up in free-text type or slice.
claims.suggested_rewrite: Evals sit in quantitativeAnalysis.performanceMetrics as bare strings: type, value, slice and a confidence interval. There's no benchmark version, no dataset reference or hash, no harness identity or config, and no properties field to add them. Eval datasets can be listed in modelParameters.datasets, but nothing ties a score to one.

evidence.detail: definitions.performanceMetric properties: type, value, slice, confidenceInterval{lowerBound, upperBound}; additionalProperties false. modelCard.modelParameters.datasets: 'The datasets used to train and evaluate the model.'

claims.claim: CycloneDX 1.7 distribution controls (TLP) are only labels.
claims.check: distributionConstraints / TLP field in 1.7.
claims.what_is_true: 1.7 adds `metadata.distributionConstraints` with a single field, `tlp` (tlpClassification enum CLEAR, GREEN, AMBER, AMBER_AND_STRICT, RED; default CLEAR). It is 'The Traffic Light Protocol (TLP) classification that controls the sharing and distribution of the data that the BOM describes.' It applies to the whole BOM, not to individual components or fields. It carries no encryption, redaction or verification mechanism.
claims.suggested_rewrite: CycloneDX 1.7's distribution control is one BOM-wide TLP label (metadata.distributionConstraints.tlp, CLEAR to RED). It isn't per component or per field, and it enforces nothing. Neither it nor SPDX's dataset confidentiality level lets a consumer verify a redacted copy.

claims.claim: CycloneDX 2.0 has a declared-behavior model covering an agent's permitted actions, callable tools and human-approval points.
claims.check: Is CycloneDX 2.0 released, in draft, or proposed as of Nov 2026? Dates; what it (or its drafts) contain about agents and behaviour.
claims.what_is_true: CycloneDX 2.0 had not been released as of 1 Nov 2026. CycloneDX's 5 Aug 2026 post 'CycloneDX 2.0 Delivers Transparency Reaching Far Beyond Bill of Materials' says 2.0 is 'due this fall with Ecma International approval anticipated in December'. On the agent claim, the post says: 'The declared behavior specifies what an agent is allowed to do, which tools it may call, and where human approval is needed.' It pairs this with observed behaviour, a record of what the delivered system actually does that a test suite or independent assessor can check. In the repo, the 2.0-dev branch README lists 'CycloneDX 2.0 | to be announced', and there is no 2.0 tag (the latest spec tags are 1.7, 1.7.1 and 1.7.2). The GitHub 2.0 milestone showed 'Status: Draft (not ready)' with a 30 June 2026 due date, which has passed. In the draft schema the behaviour model is generic, not agent-specific. cyclonedx-behavior-2.0.schema.json defines behavior instances and graphs (activity or state-machine nodes, with transitions that carry guards). Each has an 'acknowledgment' of 'declared' ('explicitly declared, designed, or expected') and/or 'observed'. Behaviours sit under blueprints[].behaviors, and their values come from a separate behavior taxonomy with 740 entries. Agent-relevant values include ai:agent:invokesTool, ai:agent:requestsUserApproval, ai:agent:actsOnBehalfOfUser, safety:autonomousBehavior:enforcesHumanInLoop, safety:autonomousBehavior:respectsDecisionBoundary and safety:humanInteraction:requestsConfirmation. The 2.0 draft has no agent component type. An agent is a party kind or role 'agent' or a blueprint asset type 'agent'. Nothing in the draft makes a declaration deny-by-default or binds it to an enforced policy.
claims.suggested_rewrite: CycloneDX 2.0 (draft, due late 2026, with Ecma approval expected in December) adds a declared-behaviour model. In the project's words, it 'specifies what an agent is allowed to do, which tools it may call, and where human approval is needed', and an observed-behaviour record sits beside it. It's the first real move. But it is a generic behaviour taxonomy (ai:agent:invokesTool, ai:agent:requestsUserApproval), not an enforceable, deny-by-default permission set.
claims.notes: The announcement and the draft schema both support the claim's content. The only problem is tense: 2.0 is announced and in draft, not shipped. A cdxgen tracking issue (#4589) reportedly calls the 2.0 schema 'ratified', which conflicts with the primary sources ('to be announced'; Ecma approval 'anticipated in December'). Primary sources were preferred. The announcement quotes come from search-tool extracts because cyclonedx.org could not be fetched directly.

evidence.detail: Search-result extract: 'The declared behavior specifies what an agent is allowed to do, which tools it may call, and where human approval is needed.' Also: 'CycloneDX 2.0, due this fall with Ecma International approval anticipated in December.'

claims.claim: CycloneDX 2.0's reworked VEX has attached evidence, an eight-point exploitability scale, and conflicting attributed assertions in one document.
claims.check: Any CycloneDX 2.0 draft or announcement text about VEX changes.
claims.what_is_true: This matches the 2.0 draft schema, which is still unreleased. vulnerability.evidence has presence[], occurrences[], callStacks and data[] (supporting material). Each presence entry is 'A single, attributable determination about the presence, absence, or exploitability of the vulnerability'. It carries status (affected, unaffected or unknown), justification, exploitability, exploitMaturity, confidence (required, 0 to 1), methods, tools, assertion (parties plus role) and timestamp. The schema says: 'Determinations are perspectival: several entries may concern the same reference from different vantages, each attributed through `assertion`, so a supplier assertion of unaffected and a consumer assertion of affected can coexist.' exploitabilityLevel has exactly eight values: component-present, code-present, code-reachable, runtime-reachable, attacker-reachable, preconditions-satisfiable, proven-exploitable and exploited. These indicate 'increasing confidence in exploitability rather than a strictly cumulative sequence'. A separate exploitMaturity scale covers the wider threat landscape: not-defined, unreported, proof-of-concept, functional, active. A schema rule makes 'proven-exploitable' and 'exploited' cite at least one demonstrative method (exploitation, penetration-testing, dynamic-analysis, instrumentation or runtime-protection) whose result is not 'not-detected' or 'inconclusive'. The 5 Aug 2026 announcement describes the eight-point scale. It also says a supplier and an independent party can disagree in one document, each claim attributed to its author.
claims.suggested_rewrite: CycloneDX 2.0's reworked VEX (draft) is the right structure to extend. Evidence attaches to each determination, an eight-level exploitability scale runs from 'component-present' to 'exploited', and conflicting supplier and consumer assertions sit in one document, each attributed.
claims.notes: This is spec content in the draft schema, not commentary. Readers should be told 2.0 is a draft (see B2-01).

evidence.detail: $defs: vulnerabilityEvidence, presenceEvidence, exploitabilityLevel (8-value enum), exploitMaturity (5-value enum). presenceEvidence text: '...a supplier assertion of unaffected and a consumer assertion of affected can coexist.' allOf $comment: '...the strongest claims cannot be a bare assertion.'

Search-result extract: 'Exploitability moves beyond a simple yes or no answer to an eight-point scale that ranges from the component being present to the attacker being able to reach it, and finally to the vulnerability having been exploited in the wild.' Also: 'both claims being included in the same CycloneDX document, each one assigned to its author'.

claims.claim: CycloneDX 2.0 attaches technique, tool, confidence, evidence location, timestamp and asserting party to each determination.
claims.check: Same: CycloneDX 2.0 draft/spec text.
claims.what_is_true: This is faithful to the announcement but overstated against the draft schema. The 5 Aug 2026 announcement says: 'Every determination in a 2.0 document carries its basis: the technique, the tool, the confidence, the location of the evidence, the timestamp, and the party asserting it.' In the draft schema, identity, license, copyright and vulnerability-presence determinations each offer methods[]. Each method holds a technique, a per-technique confidence, a result (detected, not-detected or inconclusive) and an optional rule. Each determination also offers tools[], assertion.parties[] (party plus role), a timestamp and an overall confidence. License and copyright entries carry their own occurrences (location). Identity and vulnerability determinations share occurrences and callStacks at the parent evidence object rather than having them per determination. Only confidence on vulnerability presence entries, and technique plus confidence inside each method, are required. Tools, assertion, timestamp and occurrences are optional. So 2.0 lets each determination carry its basis; it does not guarantee it. The technique vocabulary has 28 values, including 'attestation' ('A determination asserted by a party ... rather than derived from direct analysis') and 'unknown'.
claims.suggested_rewrite: 2.0 (draft) lets each determination carry its basis: technique, tool, confidence, evidence location, timestamp and asserting party.
claims.notes: The claim repeats the announcement word for word in substance. The normative draft schema makes most of these fields optional, and location is not per determination for identity or vulnerability findings.

evidence.detail: Search-result extract: 'Every determination in a 2.0 document carries its basis: the technique, the tool, the confidence, the location of the evidence, the timestamp, and the party asserting it.'

analysisMethod requires 'technique' and 'confidence'. 'assertion' is 'Attribution of an evidence determination to the parties involved'. partyAttribution has party plus role (supplier, auditor, asserter, ...). analysisTechnique has 28 values, including 'attestation'.

componentIdentityEvidence (required: scheme) has confidence, concludedValue, methods, tools, assertion and timestamp. licenseEvidence and copyrightEvidence also have occurrences ('The locations at which the license was detected').

cdxgen issue 'Emit attributed claims on component evidence at CycloneDX 2.0': '2.0 adds attributed claims, which record the technique, tool, confidence, evidence and author behind each determination.'

claims.claim: There is an active CycloneDX discussion (#973) on whether ML-BOM should support a runtime assertion record that links static AI artifact documentation to specific AI-supported decisions.
claims.check: CycloneDX/specification issue or discussion #973: title, author, date, content, status.
claims.what_is_true: CycloneDX/specification discussion #973 exists. Its title is 'Proposal for a runtime AI Assertion Record / chain-of-reliance extension to ML-BOM'. GitHub user tbarrett002-boop opened it in the 'Ideas, Proposals, RFCs' category. It opens: 'Opening a discussion on whether CycloneDX / ML-BOM should support a runtime chain-of-reliance record that links static AI artifact documentation to specific AI-supported decisions.' It treats ML-BOM as the static manifest and proposes AACIF (AI Assertion and Chain Integrity Framework). AACIF is a runtime AI Assertion Record that carries the evidence behind an AI-supported judgment through retrieval, inference, tool use, human review and audit. The author says they are 'not asking CycloneDX to adopt AACIF in full'. The narrower question is whether CycloneDX, ML-BOM, CDXA or related work should support such a record or a chain-of-reliance extension. Proposed next steps: map AACIF fields to existing ML-BOM structures, identify fields that arise only at runtime, and pilot on one high-consequence workflow. The indexed snapshot showed no replies or maintainer response, so 'active' is not supported. The open date was not retrieved. AACIF also appears in a public comment to the PCAOB, alongside a note by Thom Barrett.
claims.suggested_rewrite: An open CycloneDX discussion (#973) proposes a runtime 'AI Assertion Record' that links static ML-BOM documentation to specific AI-supported decisions. It's a community proposal with no maintainer response yet, not spec.
claims.notes: The only problem is 'active': no responses were visible. The exact open date could not be retrieved because GitHub is blocked and the web-search budget ran out. The draft's paragraph 'ML-BOM is the manifest. Consequential AI risk often materializes after the manifest ends...' appears to paraphrase #973's framing closely and should be attributed to it (inference from the search extracts; the full text was not visible).

evidence.detail: Title as above. Search extracts: '...whether CycloneDX / ML-BOM should support a runtime chain-of-reliance record that links static AI artifact documentation to specific AI-supported decisions.' Also: 'They are not asking CycloneDX to adopt AACIF in full.' Opened by tbarrett002-boop in Ideas, Proposals, RFCs; no replies in the indexed snapshot.
A PCAOB public comment describes AACIF as 'the runtime chain-of-reliance record' (seven boundary assertions across a twelve-layer AI decision chain) and refers to a companion note by Thom Barrett.

claims.claim: CycloneDX issue #1015 proposes tool-manifest and policy-bundle digests on the agent component, so evidence records can point at a specific BOM snapshot.
claims.check: CycloneDX/specification issue #1015: title, author, date, content, status.
claims.what_is_true: CycloneDX/specification issue #1015 is titled 'Behavior evidence gap: linking agent actions back to BOM components'. It is open, labelled as an enhancement, and was described in a WasmAgent PR as a proposed core enhancement under the behaviour capability. It was filed by the maintainer of WasmAgent/agentbom, who calls themselves an early implementer of the CycloneDX Agent BOM proposal (issue #895). The issue argues that the current design, including the Blueprints RFC's runtime evidence, attests what an agent is, not what it did. In its words: 'An agent BOM that can only attest "these tools were loaded" but cannot anchor "and these are the actions that were taken under this tool set" leaves a critical gap.' It proposes explicit digest anchor fields on the agent component, such as a tool-manifest digest, a policy-bundle digest and a model snapshot, so that external behaviour records can point at a specific BOM snapshot. It also proposes an evidence-envelope schema. The example records include a per-action record linking run, model, policy-bundle digest and tool-manifest digest, plus a hash-chained memory record. No maintainer decision was found. WasmAgent PR #233 reports secondhand that Steve Springett said the Blueprints working group had briefly discussed possible v2.1 work. The same PR explicitly disclaims adoption, endorsement or any v2.1 commitment. The 'agent component' it assumes does not exist: neither CycloneDX 1.7 nor the 2.0 draft has an agent component type.
claims.suggested_rewrite: CycloneDX issue #1015 (open, not accepted) proposes exactly this: tool-manifest and policy-bundle digests on the agent component, so external evidence records can point at a specific BOM snapshot.
claims.notes: The filing date was not retrieved; one search snapshot said 'about 82 days ago' with no fixed anchor date.

evidence.detail: Search extracts: the issue proposes 'adding explicit digest fields to the agent component, such as for a tool manifest and a policy bundle, so external behavior records can point at a specific BOM snapshot'; quotes the 'critical gap' sentence; status open.

Records #1015 as an open proposed core enhancement. Lists claims the record must not make: 'adoption, endorsement, Ecma acceptance, v2.1 commitment, standardization'. Reports Springett's comment on possible v2.1 work.
'AgentBOM aligns with the emerging CycloneDX Agent BOM proposal (upstream issue #895)... an early reference implementation of it.'

claims.claim: cdxgen turns instruction files, skills and MCP config into namespaced properties, emitting categories, tool names, scopes and counts rather than raw text that may hold secrets.
claims.check: cdxgen documentation or release notes on AI-BOM, MCP, skills and agent instruction file support.
claims.what_is_true: cdxgen's docs and its 13.6.0 source confirm this. agentFormulationParser.js matches AGENTS.md, AGENT.md, CLAUDE.md, GEMINI.md, QWEN.md, .cursorrules, .windsurfrules, .clinerules, .github/copilot-instructions.md, .github/instructions/** and *.prompt/*.mdc. It emits a 'file' component for each, whose properties are derived signals only: cdx:file:kind, cdx:agent:hasMcpReferences, cdx:agent:hiddenEndpointCount, cdx:agent:mcpPackageRefs, sanitized cdx:agent:hiddenMcpUrls and hiddenMcpHosts, cdx:agent:providerNames, cdx:agent:authHints, and cdx:agent:credentialExposure. Credential risk is reported through cdx:agent:credentialRiskIndicators, which holds the names of the matched patterns, not the secret values. Agentic CLI host scans emit 'redacted structural counts', and the docs note that 'the rules are not copied' and 'transcripts are never read'. Raw instruction bodies are never copied. The exact wording 'categories, tool names and scopes rather than raw text that may hold secrets' comes from the plan in issue #4593 for 2.0 output.

claims.claim: Dependency-Track still ingests only CycloneDX 1.6 or earlier.
claims.check: Current Dependency-Track release and the CycloneDX versions it supports as of Nov 2026.
claims.what_is_true: The claim was true until late August 2026. Dependency-Track's CycloneDxValidator mapped specVersion 1.2 to 1.6 and threw 'Unrecognized specVersion' for 1.7. Users reported that error (issue #5974), and an April 2026 write-up describes 1.7 uploads failing schema validation, with --spec-version 1.6 as the workaround. v5.1.0 added CycloneDX 1.7 ingestion ('Add CycloneDX 1.7 support', PR #6703). Its GitHub release is dated 27 Aug 2026 and the project announcement 31 Aug 2026. The 4.x line got a backport in v4.14.4, whose release notes are dated 14 Sep 2026 ('Add support for ingestion of CycloneDX 1.7 BOMs - [apiserver/#6966]'). Validator source by tag: 4.14.3 and 5.0.5 have no case for '1.7'; 5.1.0, 5.2.1, 4.14.6, the 4.14.x branch and main all map '1.7' to VERSION_17. On 1 Nov 2026 the latest tags are v5.2.1 and v4.14.6 (release notes dated 25 Oct 2026); tags 5.2.2, 5.3.0 and 4.14.7 do not exist. v4 is in maintenance mode and reaches end-of-life in December 2026. CycloneDX 1.7 shipped on 21 Oct 2025, so support arrived about 10 to 11 months later. CycloneDX 2.0 has not been released, so whether Dependency-Track supports it is not yet a question.
claims.suggested_rewrite: Dependency-Track only started accepting CDX 1.7 in v5.1.0 (August 2026) and its v4.14.4 backport (September 2026), about ten months after 1.7 shipped;
claims.challenge_reasoning: I re-checked this against Dependency-Track's own release notes and its validator source at each tag. The first pass is right that the claim is outdated, but its rewrite has two problems. (1) It names v4.14.4 (September 2026) first and gives v5.1 no date, which reverses the order: 5.1.0 shipped first (27 Aug 2026), and 4.14.4 was the backport, as the maintainer said in discussion #5802. (2) It adds 'it rejects 2.0 outright'. The validator's default branch would indeed reject an unknown specVersion, but CycloneDX 2.0 is unreleased (the spec repo's master README still lists 1.7 as the latest release), so this is a moot criticism and a new claim the author did not make. Severity stays major: it is a present-tense statement about a widely used OWASP tool, easy to check and now false. claims.claim: CycloneDX tools have faster and more stable resolution times for GitHub issue reports than SPDX tools, partly because the simpler model is easier to implement (arXiv study).
claims.check: Find the study and its actual finding.
claims.what_is_true: The study exists: Zhimin Zhao, Abdul Ali Bangash, Tongxu Ge, Arshdeep Singh, Zitao Wang and Bram Adams, 'The State of the SBOM Tool Ecosystems: A Comparative Analysis of SPDX and CycloneDX', arXiv 2512.21781 (December 2025). The authors' replication package says it was accepted for publication in Empirical Software Engineering (2026). In search-engine extracts, the arXiv text analyses 13,281 closed issues in 90 CycloneDX tool repositories and 13,352 in 191 SPDX tool repositories, and states that CycloneDX tools have 'a faster and more stable resolution time'. Secondary summaries give inconsistent magnitudes (SPDX about 71% higher, or a mean of 88 vs 130 days). The accepted version's replication data (26,853 issues since 2018, collected 1 May 2025) show CycloneDX tools faster in most issue categories, for example bug fixes at a mean of 61.8 vs 96.9 days. The effect sizes are negligible to small (Cliff's delta), and SPDX tools resolve licensing issues faster (111.5 vs 153.5 days). I found no support for 'partly because the simpler model is easier to implement' in the abstract, the project page or the replication data. The abstract says CycloneDX-using projects show higher developer engagement while SPDX has a larger, more mature tool ecosystem. The project page groups shorter resolution times with higher contributor activity and more frequent commits as 'reflecting stronger recent momentum'. The issue data come almost entirely from SPDX 2.x tooling: only 5 of 456 SPDX tool repositories advertised SPDX 3.0 support. That makes the data weak evidence for any SPDX 3.0 'complexity tax'.
claims.suggested_rewrite: Complexity tax. SPDX 3.0's RDF/linked-data heritage makes it powerful for semantic querying but creates a barrier to adoption, and uptake has been slow: a study of the SBOM tool ecosystems (Zhao et al., arXiv 2512.21781, accepted in Empirical Software Engineering) found only 5 of 456 SPDX tool repositories advertising SPDX 3.0 support in May 2025. The same study found that CycloneDX tools close GitHub issues faster on average than SPDX tools, though the authors read that as a sign of stronger momentum in CycloneDX projects (more contributors, more frequent commits), not of a simpler model, and SPDX tools resolve licensing issues faster.
claims.challenge_reasoning: The first pass could not find the paper. I found it, along with its replication package on raw GitHub. The measured half of the claim matches the paper's own wording, but three caveats apply. The effect sizes are mostly negligible or small. SPDX is faster on licensing issues. Reported magnitudes differ between versions and summaries, so the rewrite avoids a headline percentage. The causal half ('partly because the simpler model is easier to implement') is attributed to the study but appears to be the author's inference; the authors frame the gap as momentum and developer engagement. The author also uses the finding to support a point about SPDX 3.0's RDF complexity, but the issue data predate meaningful SPDX 3.0 tool support. In the scan, 9 repositories were flagged, and 4 of those are spec, meeting or license-list repositories, which leaves the 5 tools the authors cite. Pith's automated review flags a confound only for RQ4 (adopter projects, 'unbalanced search pools'), not for RQ3. Limitation: the shared web-search budget ran out and arxiv.org cannot be fetched here, so I did not read the full discussion section. If that section argues the complexity point, the causal clause could be restored with a page citation. The verdict moves from unverifiable to partially_correct. IHVM does not cover this claim.
claims.notes: This is a search-budget limitation, not evidence that the paper is fabricated. A follow-up search is needed, for example 'SPDX CycloneDX GitHub issue resolution time empirical study arXiv' and 'SBOM standards tool ecosystems comparison issue resolution'. Until the paper is found and its exact finding confirmed, cite it by title and arXiv ID and remove the causal explanation.

claims.claim: SPDX 3.0 is ISO/IEC 5962 ('Good: ISO 5962, AI Profile + Dataset Profile').
claims.check: Which SPDX version ISO/IEC 5962:2021 corresponds to, and the ISO status of SPDX 3.0 as of Nov 2026.
claims.what_is_true: ISO/IEC 5962:2021 is SPDX 2.2.1. That version was 'V2.2 reformatted for submission to ISO via the PAS process', with no technical changes. Its foreword says it 'was adopted, under the PAS procedure, by Joint Technical Committee ISO/IEC JTC 1'. SPDX 3.x is a Linux Foundation project specification published under the Community Specification License 1.0, not an ISO standard. On 1 Nov 2026, the SPDX 3 model README on both main and develop still says 'The prior version of this format ... is an ISO/IEC standard (ISO/IEC 5962:2021)'. The spec site's version index lists v3.1-RC1, v3.1-dev, v3.0.1 ('latest'), v2.3.1 and v2.2.2; unlike 2.2.1, no 3.x edition is ISO-formatted. The AI and Dataset profiles exist only in 3.x, so no ISO standard covers them. A related point on 'great for EU AI Act': the AI profile's safetyRiskAssessment uses the EU general product-safety risk methodology (Regulation 765/2008), and the spec itself notes that 'this categorization differs from the one proposed in the EU AI Act's provisional agreement'.
claims.suggested_rewrite: Good: an ISO pedigree (ISO/IEC 5962:2021 is SPDX 2.2.1; SPDX 3.x, including the AI and Dataset profiles, is not an ISO standard), AI and Dataset profiles that help with EU AI Act documentation (though the AI profile's safety-risk levels follow the EU general product-safety methodology, which the spec says differs from the AI Act's), and typed relationships.
claims.challenge_reasoning: The first pass's verdict and facts hold up; I re-fetched every primary source. I amended its rewrite in two places. First, 'is not an ISO standard yet' implies an ISO process for 3.x that I found no evidence of. Second, 'AI and Dataset profiles that suit EU AI Act documentation' clashes with the spec's own caveat that its risk categorization differs from the AI Act's (the first pass quoted that caveat in its notes but did not carry it into the rewrite). Severity stays major: the line presents SPDX 3.0, and implicitly its AI profile, as ISO-standardised, which matters to procurement- and compliance-minded readers. Limitation: the ISO catalogue and news could not be checked (the search budget was exhausted and iso.org is not fetchable). The conclusion rests on SPDX's own repositories, which still call 5962:2021 'the prior version' and contain no ISO-formatted 3.x edition. IHVM does not cover this claim.
claims.notes: Searching for 'as of Nov 2026' ISO news was impossible: this run's shared web-search budget was used up before I could query ISO, LF or news sources. The ISO-status conclusion rests on the SPDX repositories alone, so check the ISO/IEC 5962 catalogue entry before publishing. A related caveat on 'great for EU AI Act': the spec says the AI profile's safetyRiskAssessment categories follow the EU general product-safety methodology and 'differ from the one proposed in the EU AI Act's provisional agreement'.

claims.claim: SPDX 3.0 already has Agent, invokedBy and delegatedTo; the relationship types usesTool, invokedBy, delegatedTo and trainedOn exist; LifecycleScopedRelationship has a runtime scope.
claims.check: RelationshipType vocabulary (and how many values it has) and LifecycleScopeType values in 3.0.1.
claims.what_is_true: Core RelationshipType has 59 values in both SPDX 3.0 and 3.0.1. They include usesTool ('The from Element uses each to Element as a tool, during a LifecycleScopeType period'), invokedBy ('The from Element was invoked by the to Agent, during a LifecycleScopeType period'), delegatedTo, trainedOn and testedOn. delegatedTo reads: 'The from Agent is delegating an action to the Agent of the to Relationship (which must be of type invokedBy)'. So SPDX delegation points from an Agent to an invokedBy edge, not straight at another Agent. Agent is a Core class. LifecycleScopedRelationship subclasses Relationship and adds an optional scope from LifecycleScopeType, whose values are design, development, build, test, runtime and other. Every Relationship also has optional startTime and endTime (a validity window) and completeness, and as an Element it carries its own creationInfo/createdBy. SPDX has no permission, condition or grant qualifiers on edges. 3.1-RC1 grows the vocabulary to 76 values.
claims.suggested_rewrite: Relationship vocabulary is build-era. SPDX 3.0.1 has 59 relationship types, including usesTool, invokedBy, delegatedTo (which points at an invokedBy edge) and trainedOn. LifecycleScopedRelationship can scope an edge to runtime, and CDX has nothing comparable. Edges can carry a validity window (startTime/endTime) and their own creator, but nothing for permission, condition or who granted what.
claims.notes: The claim is right, but the same draft paragraph (lines 1536-1540) says edges carry no 'validity window'. That is wrong: Relationship.startTime and endTime exist. The missing qualifiers are permission, condition and grantor semantics. Line 260 ('SPDX gives you DEPENDS_ON, CONTAINS - too coarse') uses SPDX 2.x names and contradicts this claim.

evidence.detail: Lists 59 entries, including 'delegatedTo: The from Agent is delegating an action to the Agent of the to Relationship (which must be of type invokedBy), during a LifecycleScopeType...', 'invokedBy: ...invoked by the to Agent', 'trainedOn' and 'usesTool: The from Element uses each to Element as a tool, during a LifecycleScopeType period.'
SPDX 3.0.0 also has 59 entries, with delegatedTo, invokedBy, usesTool, trainedOn and testedOn present. 3.0.1 later fixed typos such as hasInputs and hasPrerequsite.
Entries: design, development, build, test, 'runtime: A relationship has specific context implications during the execution phase of an element.', other.
'SubclassOf: Relationship'; property scope: LifecycleScopeType, 0..1.
Relationship properties: from (1..1), to (1..*), relationshipType (1..1), completeness (0..1), startTime (0..1), endTime (0..1).

claims.claim: In SPDX Core, Agent means an actor (Person, Organization, SoftwareAgent, Tool) that creates elements.
claims.check: Agent subclasses; whether Tool is an Agent subclass or a separate Element.
claims.what_is_true: In SPDX 3.0.1 Core, Agent (SubclassOf Element, concrete) 'represents anything that has the potential to act on a system. This could be a person, organization, software agent, etc. This is not to be confused with tools that are used to perform tasks.' Its only subclasses are Person, Organization and SoftwareAgent ('a software program that is given the authority (similar to a user's authority) to act on a system'). Tool is a separate class (SubclassOf Element): 'an element of hardware and/or software utilized to carry out a particular function'. Creation is recorded through CreationInfo.createdBy (Agent, minCount 1) and CreationInfo.createdUsing (Tool, minCount 0). Agents are not only creators. They also fill Artifact.suppliedBy and originatedBy, the invokedBy and delegatedTo relationships, and the vulnerability roles (foundBy, reportedBy, fixedBy, publishedBy, coordinatedBy, exploitCreatedBy, republishedBy). The generated 3.1-RC1 and 3.1-dev ontologies keep exactly the same three Agent subclasses, keep Tool under Element, and have no AIAgent class. The AI working group's unmerged proposal, PR #1257 ('ai agent v2'), defines AIAgent as 'SubclassOf: /Core/SoftwareAgent' and links it to its model with a usesModel relationship to an AIPackage. The earlier PR #1113 also subclassed SoftwareAgent.
claims.suggested_rewrite: Semantic overloading of "Agent". In SPDX Core, an Agent is anything that can act on a system: a Person, Organization or SoftwareAgent that creates, supplies or invokes things. Tools are a separate Element class, recorded with createdUsing, and the spec warns against confusing the two. The AI working group's unmerged AIAgent proposal (PR #1257, not in 3.1-RC1) subclasses SoftwareAgent and points to the model with a usesModel relationship to an AIPackage, so the principal and the artifact stay two linked elements; neither 3.0.1 nor 3.1-RC1 says how to describe one thing as both.
claims.challenge_reasoning: I confirmed the first pass's facts against the model files and by parsing the generated 3.0.1, 3.1-RC1 and 3.1-dev ontologies. Listing Tool under Agent is the exact confusion the Agent definition warns against, and 'that creates elements' is too narrow. I amended the rewrite because the author's next sentence ('Subclassing AIAgent from SoftwareAgent...') describes what the working group's open proposal actually does (raw pull ref of PR #1257). That proposal answers the principal-versus-artifact question with two linked elements (usesModel to an AIPackage) rather than dual typing, and none of it is in the RC. Severity stays major: a design document for an Agent BOM that miscasts the core class hierarchy invites wrong modelling, such as typing MCP tools as Agents. IHVM does not cover the Agent definition, but it independently reports that AIAgent lives in open PR #1257 and not in 3.1-RC1, which matches what I found.
claims.notes: The draft continues: 'Subclassing AIAgent from SoftwareAgent is elegant... the RC gives no dual-typing'. Neither the 3.1-RC1 nor the current 3.1-dev ontology contains an AIAgent class, so present any AIAgent design as a proposal, not RC content.

evidence.detail: 'The Agent class represents anything that has the potential to act on a system. This could be a person, organization, software agent, etc. This is not to be confused with tools that are used to perform tasks.' SubclassOf: Element; Instantiability: Concrete.
'A Tool is an element of hardware and/or software utilized to carry out a particular function.' SubclassOf: Element.
'A SoftwareAgent is a software program that is given the authority (similar to a user's authority) to act on a system.' SubclassOf: Agent.
createdBy: type Agent, minCount 1; createdUsing: type Tool, minCount 0.
invokedBy: 'The from Element was invoked by the to Agent'; delegatedTo: 'The from Agent is delegating an action to the Agent of the to Relationship'; foundBy/fixedBy/reportedBy etc. point to Agents.
Parsed: subclasses of Core/Agent are Organization, Person and SoftwareAgent only; Core/Tool subClassOf Core/Element; no AIAgent. The v3.1-dev ontology gives the same result.

Proposal (not merged into develop): 'SubclassOf: /Core/SoftwareAgent'; 'usesModel: Describes a relationship from the AIAgent to an AIPackage that represents the underlying AI model the agent relies on'.
In the generated 3.1-RC1 ontology, the only subclasses of Core/Agent are Organization, Person and SoftwareAgent. No class subclasses SoftwareAgent, and no AIAgent class exists.

claims.claim: In the AI profile, informationAboutTraining, limitation, modelExplainability and modelDataPreprocessing are plain strings, safetyRiskAssessment is an enum, and the profile has 20 AIPackage fields (5 required) and 18 dataset fields (6 required).
claims.check: Field list, types and cardinalities for AIPackage and DatasetPackage in 3.0.1 (count them).
claims.what_is_true:
SPDX 3.0.1 AIPackage defines 15 properties of its own, all optional (minCount 0).
- Eight are xsd:string: domain, informationAboutApplication (0..1), informationAboutTraining (0..1), limitation (0..1), modelDataPreprocessing (0..*), modelExplainability (0..*), standardCompliance and typeOfModel.
- Three are enumerations: autonomyType and useSensitivePersonalInformation (both PresenceType), and safetyRiskAssessment (SafetyRiskAssessmentType 0..1, with values serious, high, medium and low).
- Three are DictionaryEntry lists: hyperparameter, metric and metricDecisionThreshold.
- One is a structured class: energyConsumption.

AIPackage also makes five inherited properties mandatory: releaseTime, suppliedBy, downloadLocation, packageVersion and primaryPurpose. That gives 20 fields, 5 required.

DatasetPackage defines 13 properties of its own. Only datasetType (1..*) is required. It makes five inherited properties mandatory: builtTime, originatedBy (exactly 1), releaseTime, downloadLocation and primaryPurpose. That gives 18 fields, 6 required.

Counting every inherited property, the spec pages list 42 properties (8 required) for AIPackage and 40 (9 required) for DatasetPackage.
claims.suggested_rewrite: The AI profile is documentary. AIPackage adds 15 optional fields and makes five inherited Package fields mandatory (releaseTime, suppliedBy, downloadLocation, packageVersion, primaryPurpose): 20 fields, 5 required. DatasetPackage adds 13 fields (only datasetType required) plus five mandatory inherited ones: 18 fields, 6 required. informationAboutTraining, limitation, modelExplainability and modelDataPreprocessing are plain strings, and safetyRiskAssessment is a four-level enum (serious/high/medium/low). None of it is machine-verifiable.
claims.notes: The 20/5 and 18/6 figures depend on counting the class's own properties plus the five inherited properties it tightens. None of the 15 AI-specific fields is mandatory. My reading of the generated 3.0.1 JSON Schema and SHACL is that they do not encode the five inherited requirements (see additional findings). 3.1-RC1 cuts the requirements on both classes to primaryPurpose only.

claims.claim: SPDX makes profiles other than Core optional; conformance is per profile; AI-profile conformance does not entail Software-profile conformance.
claims.check: SPDX 3.0.1 conformance clause text.
claims.what_is_true: SPDX 3.0.1 clause 5 (Conformance) defines 'nine compliance points': Core, Software, Security, Licensing, Dataset, AI, Build, Lite and Extension. 'The Core Profile is mandatory. All others are optional.' 'Conformance to the Core Profile compliance point is mandatory for all other SPDX profiles.' For the AI profile: 'Conformance to the AI Profile compliance point does not entail support for the Software, Licensing, Security, Dataset, Build, Lite, or Extension profiles of the SPDX.' Every other profile has an equivalent sentence. The spec never calls profiles non-composable; it says the Extension profile 'is expected to be used in combination with the other profiles'. There is a tension here: AIPackage and DatasetPackage subclass Software/Package, and their required fields include Software-profile properties (downloadLocation, packageVersion, primaryPurpose). The 3.1-dev clause lists fourteen compliance points, adding Hardware, Service, SupplyChain, Operations and FunctionalSafety, and still makes only Core mandatory.
claims.suggested_rewrite: Profile fragmentation. Only Core is mandatory, and conformance is per profile: 'Conformance to the AI Profile compliance point does not entail support for the Software, Licensing, Security, Dataset, Build, Lite, or Extension profiles' (SPDX 3.0.1, clause 5). So two 'SPDX 3.0 conformant' tools can each drop what the other depends on.
claims.notes: Lines 1156-1158 of the draft call conformance 'explicitly non-composable'. That overstates the spec, which only says conformance to one profile 'does not entail support for' the others.

evidence.detail: 'The Core Profile is mandatory. All others are optional.' ... 'Conformance to the AI Profile compliance point does not entail support for the Software, Licensing, Security, Dataset, Build, Lite, or Extension profiles of the SPDX.'
3.1-dev: 'defines the following fourteen compliance points', which include the Service profile; 'The Core profile is mandatory. All others are optional.'

claims.claim: SPDX 3.0.1 has no native Service class.
claims.check: Whether any service concept exists in 3.0.1.
claims.what_is_true: The generated SPDX 3.0.1 OWL/SHACL ontology defines 90 classes and vocabularies across Core, Software, Security, Licensing, Dataset, AI, Build and Extension. None models a network service or endpoint. SoftwarePurpose has 29 values and none is a service; the nearest are 'application' and 'platform' ('a runtime environment'). 3.1-RC1 (2026-01-24) adds a Service profile with a SoftwareService class, 'Software provided as a service over a network'. Its RC1 properties are serverAuthenticationProtocol, provider and serviceHostingCountry. 3.1 is not final.
claims.suggested_rewrite: Missing service primitives. SPDX 3.0.1 has no service class: none of its 90 classes and vocabularies models a network service, and SoftwarePurpose has no service value. MCP servers, inference endpoints and vector databases end up as Packages with no endpoint, authentication or trust-boundary metadata. The 3.1 RC's SoftwareService adds a provider, hosting country and authentication protocol, but still no endpoint or trust boundary.

evidence.detail: Parsed the full owl:Class list (90 entries): there is no Service, endpoint or server class.
29 entries from application to test; no service value. 'platform: The Element represents a runtime environment.'
Service/SoftwareService: 'Software provided as a service over a network.' Paths: serverAuthenticationProtocol, provider, serviceHostingCountry.
