claims.claim: SPDX 3.0 integrity is Hash and PackageVerificationCode only, with no in-document signature mechanism; a contentIdentifier exists.
claims.check: IntegrityMethod subclasses; any signing support; ContentIdentifier class/property (gitoid, swhid) in 3.0.1.
claims.what_is_true: In SPDX 3.0.1, the abstract IntegrityMethod class has three subclasses: Core/Hash (algorithm plus hashValue), Core/PackageVerificationCode, and Software/ContentIdentifier (contentIdentifierType gitoid or swhid, value xsd:anyURI). The generated 3.1-RC1 and 3.1-dev ontologies have the same three. They attach through Element.verifiedUsing and SoftwareArtifact.contentIdentifier. The spec describes PackageVerificationCode as 'provided for compatibility with SPDX 2.X' and says its use 'is discouraged except for scenarios where the contentIdentifier property ... can not be used'. SWHID covers 'files, trees (also known as directories or folders), commits', so it can identify a whole directory. Nothing hashes a single large file in chunks. 3.0.1 defines a canonical JSON serialization (no whitespace, name/value pairs ordered by name) but no RDF graph canonicalization. It has no signature class, no key or signer fields and no signing clause. The HashAlgorithm vocabulary oddly lists crystalsDilithium, crystalsKyber and falcon, but only as algorithm labels on a Hash. ExternalRefType offers only references, such as secureSoftwareAttestation (NIST SSDF). The 3.1-RC1 spec has no signing or attestation clause either; its contents stop at clause 6. Only the post-RC1 develop branch adds clause 7 'Signing' and clause 8 'Attestation'. Clause 7 uses ITU-T X.590 JSS in a top-level 'signatures' property, and 'sub-objects of the document ... are not allowed to be signed. Only the object at the root of the document can contain a signature'. Clause 8 makes SPDX 3 JSON an in-toto predicate (type https://spdx.dev/Document/v3).
claims.suggested_rewrite: Integrity and signing. SPDX 3.0.1 has three integrity methods: Hash, PackageVerificationCode (kept for 2.x compatibility) and ContentIdentifier (gitoid or SWHID). A SWHID can identify a whole directory of weight shards, but nothing hashes a single multi-GB file in chunks, nothing canonicalizes prompts or tool schemas, and there's a canonical JSON form but no graph canonicalization. Neither 3.0.1 nor 3.1-RC1 has in-document signing. The 3.1 development draft written after RC1 adds JSS signatures and an in-toto predicate type, but only the document root can be signed, so a merged graph can't carry either party's signature.
claims.challenge_reasoning: The first pass's verdict and core facts hold up; I re-derived them from the model files and by parsing the ontologies. I made two corrections. (1) Its rewrite says 'The 3.1 draft adds whole-document JSS signatures'. That is true only of the develop branch: the 3.1-RC1 contents (mkdocs nav) end at clause 6 with no signing or attestation clause. This matters because the author's section is titled 'Gaps in SPDX 3.0.1 / 3.1-RC', so 'no in-document signing' is still accurate for the RC. (2) I lowered severity from major to minor. The claim's error is leaving ContentIdentifier out of 'Hash and PackageVerificationCode only', and the document itself names SPDX's contentIdentifier later. The substantive gaps (no in-document signing in any released or RC version, no chunked hashing) stand. I also added the SWHID-directory nuance from the spec's own vocabulary text, and noted that PQC algorithm names in HashAlgorithm do not amount to a signing mechanism. IHVM does not cover this claim.
claims.notes: 'Hash and PackageVerificationCode only' leaves out ContentIdentifier, which clashes with the draft's own later mention of SPDX's contentIdentifier (line 1623). 'No in-document signing' is accurate for 3.0 and 3.0.1. 'No canonicalization' needs narrowing: 3.0.1 has a canonical JSON form, but no RDF graph canonicalization and nothing for prompts or tool schemas. My own inference, which I did not check against the SWHID spec: SWHID directory identifiers are git-tree (Merkle) hashes, so a directory of weight shards can already get a Merkle-style root, but nothing provides chunked hashing of a single large file.

evidence.detail: Parsed: subclasses of Core/IntegrityMethod are Core/Hash, Core/PackageVerificationCode and Software/ContentIdentifier; no signature class. The v3.1-RC1 and v3.1-dev ontologies give the same result.

'A ContentIdentifier is a canonical, unique, immutable identifier of the content of a software artifact ... It can be used for verifying its identity and integrity.' SubclassOf: /Core/IntegrityMethod.
gitoid and swhid; swhid identifies 'files, trees (also known as directories or folders), commits, and other objects'.

'This verification method is provided for compatibility with SPDX 2.X. Use of this verification code method is discouraged except for scenarios where the contentIdentifier property on Artifact can not be used.'
'Canonical serialization is in JSON format ... No whitespace outside of strings ... The name/value pairs are ordered by name.' No signing text.

RC1 nav: clauses 1 to 6 ('6. Model and serializations') plus annexes; no Signing or Attestation clause. By contrast, develop/mkdocs.yml has '7. Signing': signing.md and '8. Attestation': attestation.md.

'SPDX 3 JSON documents may be signed using ITU-T X.590 JSON Signature Schema (JSS) ... sub-objects of the document ... are not allowed to be signed. Only the object at the root of the document can contain a signature'.
'SPDX 3 JSON documents can be used as an in-toto attestation predicate (version 1.2.0 or later) by using the predicate type https://spdx.dev/Document/v3.'
Lists crystalsDilithium, crystalsKyber and falcon as HashAlgorithm entries; Hash has only algorithm and hashValue (no key, signer or signed-content fields).

claims.claim: AIPackage and DatasetPackage are subclasses of Software/Package, forcing version/downloadLocation/supplier semantics onto weights and corpora.
claims.check: Class hierarchy and which of those properties are required.
claims.what_is_true: AIPackage and DatasetPackage are both 'SubclassOf /Software/Package', with the chain Package > SoftwareArtifact > Artifact > Element. In SPDX 3.0 and 3.0.1, AIPackage's external property restrictions require packageVersion, downloadLocation, suppliedBy, releaseTime and primaryPurpose (minCount 1); all 15 of its own properties are optional. DatasetPackage requires downloadLocation, builtTime, originatedBy (exactly one), releaseTime and primaryPurpose, plus its own datasetType. packageVersion and suppliedBy stay optional for datasets, since Package and Artifact define them as minCount 0. That gives 20 fields with 5 required for AIPackage, and 18 fields with 6 required for DatasetPackage. These requirements live in the spec's model text only. Neither the published 3.0.1 SHACL shapes (no minCount 1 on AIPackage; only datasetType on DatasetPackage) nor the 3.0.1 JSON Schema (AIPackage requires only spdxId and creationInfo; DatasetPackage adds dataset_datasetType) enforce them. 3.1-RC1 (2026-01-24, PR #1158) relaxes both classes so that primaryPurpose is the only required inherited property; datasetType remains required. 3.1-RC1 and develop still subclass Software/Package.
claims.suggested_rewrite: Package-centric inheritance is a straitjacket. AIPackage and DatasetPackage subclass Software/Package. The 3.0.1 spec requires every model to declare packageVersion, downloadLocation, suppliedBy, releaseTime and primaryPurpose, and every dataset to declare downloadLocation, originatedBy, builtTime, releaseTime and primaryPurpose (version and supplier stay optional for datasets). 3.1-RC1 drops all of those requirements except primaryPurpose, but weights and corpora are still typed as software packages.
claims.challenge_reasoning: I confirmed this against the class files at tags 3.0, 3.0.1, 3.1-rc1 and develop, the 3.1-RC1 changelog, and the parsed ontologies. The first pass is right. The inheritance critique holds for models, but 'forcing version/supplier onto corpora' is wrong, because datasets are forced to carry downloadLocation, originatedBy, builtTime and releaseTime instead. I extended its JSON Schema observation: the generated SHACL also omits these minimums, so the 'forcing' exists in the spec text, not in the official validators. I included primaryPurpose in both lists so the '3.1-RC1 drops all except primaryPurpose' contrast is accurate, and I fixed the spelling to 'straitjacket'. IHVM agrees: it counts 20 AIPackage fields (5 required) and 18 dataset fields (6 required) in 3.0.1, and lists the #1158 relaxation in 3.1-RC1.
claims.notes: The inheritance critique holds for AIPackage in 3.0.1. 'Forcing version/supplier onto corpora' is wrong: datasets are forced to carry downloadLocation, originatedBy, builtTime and releaseTime instead. The draft's 3.1 recommendation to 'decouple AIPackage from strict package semantics' is half done in RC1: requirements are relaxed, but the subclassing remains.

evidence.detail: 'SubclassOf: /Software/Package'. External properties restrictions minCount 1: /Core/Artifact/releaseTime, /Core/Artifact/suppliedBy, /Software/Package/downloadLocation, /Software/Package/packageVersion, /Software/SoftwareArtifact/primaryPurpose.
'SubclassOf: /Software/Package'. External restrictions minCount 1: builtTime, originatedBy (maxCount 1), releaseTime, downloadLocation, primaryPurpose; own property datasetType minCount 1.
downloadLocation and packageVersion: minCount 0, maxCount 1 on Package itself.
SPDX 3.0 has the same five required external properties (minCount 1, maxCount 1).

'3.1-RC1 (2026-01-24)... Changed: Relax property and relationship requirements of /AI/AIPackage and /Dataset/DatasetPackage classes - #1158'. RC1 class files keep only primaryPurpose minCount 1 and still 'SubclassOf: /Software/Package'.
ai_AIPackage requires only spdxId (Element_props adds creationInfo); dataset_DatasetPackage_props requires only dataset_datasetType; software_Package_props has no required list.
SHACL shape for ai:AIPackage has no sh:minCount 1 property; dataset:DatasetPackage has sh:minCount 1 only on datasetType; AIPackage and DatasetPackage rdfs:subClassOf software:Package.
Rendered spec page. External cardinality updates: builtTime 1, originatedBy 1..1, releaseTime 1, downloadLocation 1, primaryPurpose 1. 'All properties' table: packageVersion 0..1, suppliedBy 0..1.

claims.claim: The SPDX Security profile covers CVSS v2/v3/v4, EPSS, an exploit catalog, SSVC and VEX.
claims.check: Security profile classes.
claims.what_is_true:
The SPDX 3.0.1 Security profile has a Vulnerability class (subclass of Artifact) and an abstract VulnAssessmentRelationship (assessedElement, publishedTime, modifiedTime, withdrawnTime, suppliedBy). Its concrete subclasses are:
- CvssV2VulnAssessmentRelationship
- CvssV3VulnAssessmentRelationship (covers v3.0 and v3.1)
- CvssV4VulnAssessmentRelationship
- EpssVulnAssessmentRelationship
- ExploitCatalogVulnAssessmentRelationship (ExploitCatalogType: kev, other)
- SsvcVulnAssessmentRelationship (SsvcDecisionType: act, attend, track, trackStar)

There is also an abstract VexVulnAssessmentRelationship with four concrete subclasses: VexAffected, VexNotAffected, VexFixed and VexUnderInvestigation. VexJustificationType has 5 values.
claims.suggested_rewrite: Security profile is vuln-centric: CVSS v2/v3/v4, EPSS, exploit catalog (CISA KEV), SSVC and four VEX status relationships. That's the same mismatch as CDX.

evidence.detail: 'Provides a CVSS version 4 assessment for a vulnerability.' SubclassOf: VulnAssessmentRelationship. Sibling files exist for CvssV2, CvssV3, Epss, ExploitCatalog, Ssvc and the four Vex* classes.
'describes if a vulnerability is listed in any exploit catalog such as the CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog.'
Entries: act, attend, track, trackStar.

'The Security profile contains information about vulnerabilities and their assessments based on CVSS (versions 2, 3, and 4), EPSS, Exploit Catalog, SSVC, and VEX (affected, not affected, under investigation, and fixed categories).'

claims.claim: There is no formal documentation for how VEX objects are implemented in SPDX 3.0.
claims.check: SPDX 3.0 VEX documentation or guides.
claims.what_is_true: SPDX 3.0/3.0.1 defines VEX normatively in the Security profile. The abstract VexVulnAssessmentRelationship sets the rules: the from end must be a Security/Vulnerability and the to end must be the VEX product elements. Four concrete subclasses map to the VEX statuses: VexAffected (affects, actionStatement required in 3.0.1), VexNotAffected (doesNotAffect, needs a justificationType or impactStatement, citing the Minimum Elements for VEX), VexFixed (fixedIn) and VexUnderInvestigation (underInvestigationFor). Each class page has a JSON example. The informative 'Using SPDX' security guide explains linking out to CSAF VEX through externalRef type vulnerabilityExploitabilityAssessment. For the embedded approach it defers to the spdx.dev blog post 'Capturing Software Vulnerability Data in SPDX 3.0'. The VexNotAffected example uses unprefixed 'publishedTime' and an array for 'suppliedBy', but the 3.0.1 JSON-LD context defines 'security_publishedTime'. So formal documentation exists, implementation guidance is thin, and the examples contain serialization slips.
claims.suggested_rewrite: VEX is thinly documented, not undocumented. SPDX 3.0.1 normatively defines four VEX status relationships (affected, not affected, fixed, under investigation) with constraints and examples. What's missing is implementation guidance: the 'Using SPDX' guide mostly covers linking out to CSAF VEX, and the spec's own VEX examples contain serialization slips (e.g. 'publishedTime' where the JSON-LD context expects 'security_publishedTime').
claims.challenge_reasoning: I re-fetched the five 3.0.1 VEX class files, the 3.0.1 JSON-LD context and the Using-SPDX security guide. All exist, and the normative definitions plus examples refute 'no formal documentation'. I also confirmed the first pass's serialization-slip observation: the example at line 43 uses 'publishedTime', and the context only defines 'security_publishedTime'. The 'gaps in documentation' half is defensible. The doc attributes the claim to an Interlynk source, which I could not retrieve. The shared web-search budget was exhausted, so I had no search access. The ihvm register has no entry on this.
claims.notes: The shared web-search budget ran out before I could find the GitHub issue behind this claim, so its source is unidentified and may be mis-cited. 'No formal documentation' is contradicted by the normative spec. 'Gaps in documentation' is defensible: how-to guidance is thin, and the spec's own examples contain serialization slips (my comparison).

Abstract parent of the SPDX-VEX status relationships (fetched; 1497 bytes).
Context defines "security_publishedTime", not 'publishedTime'.

claims.claim: SPDX 3.0 serializes as JSON-LD with SHACL validation, a heavy validation path for CI.
claims.check: Serialization formats and validation approach in 3.0.1.
claims.what_is_true:
Clause 6 of SPDX 3.0.1 says the model is RDF-based, so data 'can be serialized in any of the multiple RDF serialization formats, including but not limited to' JSON-LD, Turtle, N-Triples and RDF/XML. A JSON-LD context is published, and the canonical serialization is JSON. A JSON-LD document conforms if it passes two checks:
- 'Structural validation' against the SPDX JSON Schema.
- 'Semantic validation' against the SPDX OWL ontology, which 'incorporates SHACL shape restrictions'.

The SPDX validation guide recommends ajv or check-jsonschema for structure and pyshacl for semantics ('currently only one preferred tool'). It says the JSON Schema lets documents be parsed 'as more simplistic JSON documents using a basic JSON parser', but that schema validation 'is unable to ensure that a document is semantically correct'. 3.1-dev renames the format 'SPDX 3 JSON' (PR #1019).
claims.suggested_rewrite: JSON-LD plus SHACL is a heavy validation path for CI: full SPDX 3.0.1 conformance needs a JSON Schema check (fast, e.g. ajv) and a semantic SHACL check (pyshacl over an RDF graph), and the schema alone won't catch semantic errors.
claims.notes: 'Heavy' fairly describes the SHACL/RDF step that full conformance requires. Leaving out the lightweight JSON Schema path overstates the burden for basic CI checks.

evidence.detail: 'any SPDX data can be serialized in any of the multiple RDF serialization formats, including but not limited to: JSON-LD... Turtle... N-Triples... RDF/XML' and 'Structural validation: ...against the SPDX JSON Schema... Semantic validation: ...against the SPDX OWL ontology... also incorporates SHACL shape restrictions'.

'There are two mechanisms for validating SPDX 3 JSON-LD documents: validating the structure against the JSON Schema, and validating the semantics against the SHACL model.' ajv is 'the recommended validation tool'; pyshacl is the only preferred SHACL tool.
'Clarified: Serialization and validation documents - #1019 - Use "SPDX 3 JSON" name (instead of "SPDX 3 JSON-LD").'

claims.claim: SPDX's dataset confidentialityLevel is only a label.
claims.check: confidentialityLevel field and its values.
claims.what_is_true:
DatasetPackage.confidentialityLevel has type ConfidentialityLevelType, cardinality 0..1, and 'Describes the levels of confidentiality of the data points contained in the dataset.' Its values follow the Traffic Light Protocol:
- red: share only with named recipients.
- amber: specific organizations and their clients, on a need-to-know basis.
- green: a community of peers and partners.
- clear: no restriction.

SPDX defines no access-control, enforcement or redaction-verification semantics for the field.
claims.suggested_rewrite: CycloneDX 1.7's distribution controls and SPDX's dataset confidentialityLevel (a Traffic Light Protocol label: red, amber, green or clear) are only labels. Neither lets a consumer verify a redacted copy.

evidence.detail: 'Describes the different confidentiality levels as given by the Traffic Light Protocol.' Entries: red, amber, green, clear.
'Describes the levels of confidentiality of the data points contained in the dataset.' Range: ConfidentialityLevelType.

claims.claim: SPDX 3.1 (release candidate published in January 2026) adds AI Agent, Prompt and RAG classes. Elsewhere the same document says 'Agent/Prompt/RAG sit in RC' and also 'I saw no agent, tool or prompt classes in the RC1 changelog'.
claims.check: SPDX 3.1 RC dates and contents regarding AI agents, prompts, RAG; GA status as of Nov 2026; which of the document's contradictory statements is true.
claims.what_is_true: SPDX 3.1-RC1 is dated 2026-01-24, so the January date is right. RC1 adds no AIAgent, Prompt or RAG class. Its AI changes are the deprecation of autonomyType in favour of Core isoAutomationLevel, relaxed AIPackage/DatasetPackage requirements, and new ML relationship types (RelationshipType grew from 59 to 76). After RC1, the develop branch added one AI class, AI/InteractionTemplate, a Core/Artifact subclass for prompt and chat templates. Its description references an /AI/AIAgent class that does not exist. AIAgent.md, Prompt.md and RAG.md all return 404 on develop, and the v3.1-dev TTL contains no 'AIAgent'. As of 2026-11-01, 3.1 is not GA: the develop changelog reads '3.1-dev (TBA)', and versions.json lists only v3.1-RC1 and v3.1-dev, with 'latest' still aliased to v3.0.1. Per the ihvm register, which I could not independently check, AIAgent, Prompt and RAG are open working-group PRs (#1257, #1249, #1115) tracked in issue #1091. Of the document's statements, only 'I saw no agent, tool or prompt classes in the RC1 changelog' is true.
claims.suggested_rewrite: SPDX 3.1 is still a release candidate (RC1, 24 January 2026). It swaps autonomyType for a seven-level isoAutomationLevel and relaxes AIPackage requirements, but adds no agent, prompt or RAG classes. Since RC1 the development branch has added one prompt-template class (InteractionTemplate), which already points to an AIAgent class that hasn't been defined. Agent and RAG classes are still proposals, so agents aren't covered yet.
claims.challenge_reasoning: I re-probed the develop model directly. AIAgent.md, Prompt.md, RAG.md and RetrievalAugmentedGeneration.md all return 404, InteractionTemplate.md returns 200, the develop CHANGELOG still reads '3.1-dev (TBA)', the v3.1-dev TTL has zero 'AIAgent' matches, and versions.json keeps 'latest' on v3.0.1. These checks confirm the first pass. The ihvm register reaches the same verdict (no agent, prompt or RAG classes in RC1, no GA) and adds the open PR numbers. It does not mention that InteractionTemplate was already merged to develop, a nuance I keep. Lines ~63, ~1046, ~1076 and ~1612 all need consistent fixes. Web search was unavailable (budget exhausted), and the GitHub API was denied.
claims.notes: The document contradicts itself. Lines ~63 ('adds AI Agent, Prompt and RAG classes'), ~1046 ('Agent/Prompt/RAG sit in RC') and ~1076 ('For SPDX 3.1 GA: Ship it -- the Agent/Prompt/RAG model is the right direction') are all wrong. Line ~1866 ('no agent, tool or prompt classes in the RC1 changelog') is right. The RC1 changelog defers profile-specific additions to the profile docs, so the changelog alone isn't proof; the normative RC1 TTL confirms the absence. Fix all three passages consistently. Verified from primary files fetched from raw.githubusercontent.com; the web search budget was exhausted, so secondary coverage (talks, blog posts announcing planned agent work) was not searched.

claims.claim: In SPDX 3.1, autonomyType is deprecated in favour of a Core isoAutomationLevel.
claims.check: 3.1 changelog or model files.
claims.what_is_true: SPDX 3.1-RC1 deprecates /AI/autonomyType. Its page reads 'DEPRECATED in SPDX 3.1. Use /Core/isoAutomationLevel instead.' The replacement is a new Core property, isoAutomationLevel (PR #1064). Its range is the IsoAutomationLevel enumeration of seven levels based on ISO/IEC 22989:2022 and aligned with SAE J3016, LASR and the DPV AutomationLevel: notAutomated (L0), assistiveAutomation (L1), partialAutomation (L2), conditionalAutomation (L3), highAutomation (L4), fullAutomation (L5), autonomous (L6). AIPackage gains isoAutomationLevel with cardinality 0..1. The old autonomyType was a PresenceType: yes, no or noAssertion. All of this is RC-stage (3.1 not GA). It is still one value per system, not per action.
claims.suggested_rewrite: 3.1-RC1 deprecates autonomyType in favour of a Core isoAutomationLevel: a seven-level scale from notAutomated to autonomous, taken from ISO/IEC 22989. It's finer-grained, but still one value per system, not per action.
claims.notes: Line ~1048 says autonomyType is 'already deprecated'. That is accurate for the RC, but say 'deprecated in 3.1-RC1' so readers don't assume it's final. Line ~634's description of autonomyType (yes/no/noAssertion) is correct for 3.0.1; it should mention the 3.1 replacement.

evidence.detail: 'Added: /Core/isoAutomationLevel property - #1064 - A spectrum of system automation capability.' Under 'Deprecations since 3.0.1': '/AI/autonomyType property - New documents should use /Core/isoAutomationLevel instead.'
'**DEPRECATED in SPDX 3.1.** Use /Core/isoAutomationLevel instead.' Range: /Core/PresenceType (yes, no, noAssertion).
'The 7-level enumeration is based on ISO/IEC 22989:2022...' Entries run from notAutomated (Level 0) to autonomous (Level 6).
New AIPackage property: '/Core/isoAutomationLevel - type: /Core/IsoAutomationLevel - minCount: 0 - maxCount: 1'.

claims.claim: In SPDX 3.1, AIPackage and DatasetPackage requirements were relaxed.
claims.check: 3.1 changelog or model files.
claims.what_is_true: The 3.1-RC1 changelog says: 'Changed: Relax property and relationship requirements of /AI/AIPackage and /Dataset/DatasetPackage classes - #1158'. AIPackage in 3.0.1 required five external properties: releaseTime, suppliedBy, downloadLocation, packageVersion and primaryPurpose. In 3.1-RC1 only primaryPurpose stays required. claims.claim: pkg:huggingface purls leave revision, format and quantization ambiguous.
claims.check: purl-spec definition of the huggingface type (namespace, name, version semantics, qualifiers); raw file may be at https://raw.githubusercontent.com/package-url/purl-spec/main/PURL-TYPES.rst or types/huggingface-definition.json.
claims.what_is_true: The purl-spec 'huggingface' type defines three fields. Namespace is the 'model repository username or organization' (required, case-sensitive). Name is the 'model repository name' (required, case-sensitive). Version is the 'model revision Git commit hash' (OPTIONAL, case-insensitive, lowercased). The default repository is https://huggingface.co, and the repository_url qualifier can override it. The type defines no qualifiers for file, format or quantization, and its test suite uses only repository_url. So a revision can be pinned exactly when the commit SHA is given, but it is optional, and nothing at the type level separates one weight file or quantization from another in the same repo. A purl names a repo snapshot, not the artifact that was loaded. The draft ECMA-427 2nd edition (Annex B, informative) recommends generic file_name and checksum qualifiers that could disambiguate, but no type or profile requires them for Hugging Face.
claims.suggested_rewrite: Model identity is mushy. A pkg:huggingface purl names a repo, not an artifact. Its version (the commit SHA) is optional, and the type defines no qualifiers for file, format or quantization, so one purl can cover the safetensors original and every GGUF quant in the repo. Fix: require the commit SHA, and pin the exact weight file with file_name and checksum qualifiers (ECMA-427 2nd ed., Annex B).
claims.notes: The author's later fix asks for 'purl qualifiers for revision/format/quantization'. Revision is not a qualifier: it is already the version component, defined as the commit hash. Only format and quantization lack a home. This verdict rests on the normative type definition. The claim that real-world SBOMs often omit the version is plausible, but this session did not measure it.

claims.claim: An OpenSSF model-signing manifest hashes each file in the model, and model signing intends to carry model-card information in its signed predicates.
claims.check: OpenSSF model signing (sigstore/model-transparency) spec and docs.
claims.what_is_true: OpenSSF Model Signing (OMS) is maintained in sigstore/model-transparency and published on PyPI as model-signing. Version 1.0.0 shipped on 4 April 2025, and the latest release is 1.1.1 (10 October 2025). OMS produces a Sigstore bundle containing a DSSE envelope, which in turn contains an in-toto Statement v1 with predicateType https://model_signing/signature/v1.0. Every file (method 'files') or file shard (method 'shards') is hashed and listed in predicate.resources as a name, algorithm and digest. Ignored paths such as model.sig and .git are excluded. The single subject carries the model name and one SHA-256 computed over all the resource digests in sorted order, which other metadata can use to refer to the model. On model cards, the README says 'The idea is to use the predicates to store (and therefor sign) model card information in the future.' The v1.0 code says 'Future extensions ... (e.g., incorporating model cards, etc.) can be added as part of the predicate. For v1.0 of the predicate the only supported fields ... are "serialization" and "resources". Any other field should be ignored by verifiers.' So model-card signing is a stated plan, not a shipped feature.
claims.suggested_rewrite: Bind to an OpenSSF Model Signing (OMS) bundle. Its v1.0 predicate lists a digest for every file (or shard), and its subject carries one SHA-256 over all of them, which is the model's content identity. OMS plans to carry model-card data in signed predicates but v1.0 does not yet, so BOMs should point at that once it ships rather than restate it unsigned.
claims.notes: The README still describes subjects as per-file (path, digest) pairs. That matches the deprecated v0.2 format (https://model_signing/Digests/v0.1). In v1.0, per-file digests sit in predicate.resources and the subject holds one aggregate digest. For BOM binding, the subject digest is the value to record. claims.claim: Cisco's Model Provenance Kit performs per-tensor/architecture fingerprinting.
claims.check: Existence, date, what it does.
claims.what_is_true: Cisco's Model Provenance Kit exists. It belongs to Cisco AI Defense, lives at github.com/cisco-ai-defense/model-provenance-kit, is Apache-2.0 and ships a 'provenancekit' CLI. On PyPI it is cisco-ai-provenance-kit 1.0.0, uploaded 4 May 2026, and the main branch is at 1.1.0. It is a lineage tool: it 'determines whether a machine learning model derives from a known base model family by comparing multi-signal fingerprints extracted from weights, tokenizers, and architecture metadata.' It uses eight signals. MFI covers architecture config plus two structural hashes. TFV and VOA cover the tokenizer. Five weight-level signals: EAS (embedding anchor self-similarity), NLF (norm-layer weight vectors), LEP (per-layer Frobenius norm of weight tensors), END (embedding-norm histogram) and WVC (layer-by-layer subsampled cosine of weight tensors). Its reference database covers about 150 base models from 45+ families. Its definition of provenance deliberately links fine-tunes, distillations, quantizations, pruned, merged and LoRA-merged derivatives to their parents. So it does fingerprint architecture and weight tensors, but as similarity statistics for family and lineage matching. It does not produce per-tensor content digests and is not built to detect a trojaned layer.
claims.suggested_rewrite: Whole-blob hashes tell you a file changed, not which layer changed or whether it's still the model it claims to be. Weight-level fingerprinting exists: Cisco's Model Provenance Kit (May 2026) links derivatives to base families using per-layer weight statistics plus tokenizer and architecture signals. But it's a lineage tool, not a trojan detector, and no completeness scorer or standard asks for either.
claims.notes: The sentence is roughly accurate on its own ('architecture fingerprinting' is right; 'per-tensor' really means per-layer statistical summaries). It misleads in context. The paragraph cites MPK against single-layer trojans, but MPK is designed to keep matching a model to its base family through fine-tuning, quantization and merging, so a backdoored fine-tune would very likely still match its parent. That is an inference from the documented design; MPK has no trojan-detection evaluation. The premise needs care too: a whole-file digest does change when any layer changes. What it cannot do is localize the change or judge an unseen model. Per-tensor digest manifests address localization; MPK addresses lineage.

evidence.detail: 'Model Provenance Kit is a Python toolkit and CLI for detecting model provenance. It determines whether a machine learning model derives from a known base model family by comparing multi-signal fingerprints extracted from weights, tokenizers, and architecture metadata.' Reference DB: '~150 base models spanning 45+ model families'.

Signal table rows include 'MFI | Metadata Family Identification | Architecture config + two structural hashes', 'LEP | Layer Energy Profile | Per-layer Frobenius norm of weight tensors' and 'WVC | Weight-Value Cosine | Layer-by-layer subsampled cosine similarity of weight tensors'.
cisco-ai-provenance-kit 1.0.0, author 'Cisco', Apache-2.0, files uploaded 2026-05-04T19:07:49.

In scope as linked lineage: 'C3 Mechanical transformation | B was produced from A's weights by a non-training operation (quantization, pruning, merging, format conversion)'. Also fine-tuning (SFT, RLHF, DPO) and LoRA merges.

claims.claim: MCP tool annotations express read-only, destructive, idempotent and open-world behaviour.
claims.check: readOnlyHint, destructiveHint, idempotentHint, openWorldHint: spec version introduced, and the spec's guidance that annotations are untrusted hints.
claims.what_is_true: MCP introduced ToolAnnotations in spec revision 2025-03-26 (PR #185). The four behavioural hints are unchanged through 2026-07-28 and the current draft. readOnlyHint ('does not modify its environment', default false). destructiveHint ('may perform destructive updates', default true, meaningful only when readOnlyHint is false). idempotentHint ('repeated calls ... no additional effect', default false, meaningful only when readOnlyHint is false). openWorldHint ('may interact with an "open world" of external entities', default true). Every spec version since 2025-03-26 carries the warning: 'For trust & safety and security, clients MUST consider tool annotations to be untrusted unless they come from trusted servers.' MCP's 16 March 2026 blog post stresses that 'every property is a hint', that 'an untrusted server can lie', and that annotations 'aren't enforcement'. Five SEPs propose more annotations: #1913, #1984, #1561 unsafeOutputHint, #1560 secretHint and #1487 trustedHint.
claims.suggested_rewrite: No tool input/output schema, no description text, no definition hash, and no MCP-style annotations (readOnlyHint, destructiveHint, idempotentHint, openWorldHint; in the spec since 2025-03-26 and, per the spec, untrusted unless the server is trusted).
claims.notes: For BOM capability modelling, the defaults are pessimistic: a tool with no annotations is treated as destructive and open-world. Self-declared hints should be recorded as unverified claims.

evidence.detail: 'Added comprehensive tool annotations for better describing tool behavior, like whether it is read-only or destructive (PR #185)'.

claims.claim: RFC 8785 (JSON Canonicalization Scheme) can canonicalize tool definitions for hashing.
claims.check: RFC 8785 status and date.
claims.what_is_true: RFC 8785, the 'JSON Canonicalization Scheme (JCS)', defines a canonical JSON form for cryptographic hashing and signing. Primitives are serialized as ECMAScript JSON.stringify() would serialize them. Data is constrained to the I-JSON (RFC 7493) subset. Object properties are sorted lexicographically and recursively, and array order is preserved. Maintained implementations include the cyberphone reference implementation, Trail of Bits' rfc8785 for Python (PyPI 0.1.4) and erdtman's canonicalize for npm. The A2A protocol spec (latest release 1.0.0) requires RFC 8785 canonicalization of Agent Cards before signing, a direct precedent for canonical hashing of agent and tool definitions. RFC 8785 was published in June 2020 as an Informational RFC on the Independent Submission stream (Rundgren, Jordan, Erdtman); this publication detail was not re-fetched in this session.
claims.suggested_rewrite: Fix: hash each tool definition in canonical form: RFC 8785 (JCS) over name, description, schema and annotations, the same canonicalization A2A mandates for signed Agent Cards.
claims.notes: Caveats worth a line in the spec. JCS does not normalize Unicode, so NFC and NFD variants of a description hash differently, which is arguably what you want. It requires I-JSON, so numbers beyond IEEE-754 double precision are unsafe. It does not resolve JSON Schema $ref; MCP 2026-07-28 now allows any JSON Schema 2020-12 keyword in inputSchema (SEP-2106), so hash the schema as served.

evidence.detail: Reference implementation: 'Cryptographic operations like hashing and signing depend on that the target data does not change during serialization ... By applying the rules defined by JCS ... constraining JSON data to the I-JSON [RFC7493] subset, and through a platform independent property sorting scheme.' Links 'Public RFC: https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc8785'.
Section 8.4.1: 'Before signing, the Agent Card content MUST be canonicalized using the JSON Canonicalization Scheme (JCS) as defined in RFC 8785.'
Trail of Bits: 'A pure-Python implementation of RFC 8785 (JSON Canonicalization Scheme)', version 0.1.4.
The RFC itself, as linked from the A2A spec and the rfc8785 package. Not fetched (host blocked), so the June 2020 Informational / Independent Submission status was not re-read here.

claims.claim: A Rule-of-Two violation then becomes a query over the BOM.
claims.check: Meta's 'Agents Rule of Two': date, exact definition.
claims.what_is_true: Meta AI published 'Agents Rule of Two: A Practical Approach to AI Agent Security' on the Meta AI blog on 31 October 2025, with no listed authors; Meta security researcher Mick Ayzenberg shared it. As quoted verbatim by Simon Willison: 'until robustness research allows us to reliably detect and refuse prompt injection, agents must satisfy no more than two of the following three properties within a session to avoid the highest impact consequences of prompt injection. [A] An agent can process untrustworthy inputs [B] An agent can have access to sensitive systems or private data [C] An agent can change state or communicate externally.' If all three are needed without starting a new session, 'the agent should not be permitted to operate autonomously and at a minimum requires supervision --- via human-in-the-loop approval or another reliable means of validation.' Later clarifications: [B] covers any sensitive system, and Meta relabelled the pairwise overlaps from 'safe' to 'lower risk'. The rule is defined per session and allows supervised operation. A static BOM can therefore flag configurations that make a violation possible (an agent whose inputs, data access and tools cover A, B and C with no approval gate recorded). Whether a given session actually violated it needs runtime evidence.
claims.suggested_rewrite: A Rule-of-Two check (Meta, October 2025) then becomes a query over the BOM. Flag any agent whose untrusted inputs, sensitive access, and state-changing or outbound tools cover all three properties with no approval gate on record. The BOM shows what is possible; session telemetry shows what actually happened.
claims.notes: MCP annotations alone cannot answer the query. openWorldHint mixes [A] (untrusted content) with [C] (external reach), and nothing marks [B]. The BOM needs explicit input-trust and data-sensitivity fields, which the author's fix does propose, and these should be recorded as producer claims, not verified facts.

evidence.detail: Willison, 'New prompt injection papers: Agents Rule of Two and The Attacker Moves Second' (2025-11-02). 'published on October 31st on the Meta AI blog'. Quotes the [A]/[B]/[C] definition and the supervision requirement. Update: Meta replaced 'safe' with 'lower risk'.
Meta's original post, linked from Willison's entry and cited in OWASP 2026 references as '(2025, October 31)'. Not fetched (host blocked).

OWASP AI Exchange: 'Agentic Rule of Two: until reliable model-layer refusal exists, an agent session should satisfy no more than two of: (A) processing untrustworthy inputs, (B) accessing sensitive systems or private data, (C) changing state or communicating externally. When all three are required, operate under human-in-the-loop supervision.'
'Meta AI. (2025, October 31). Agents rule of two: A practical approach to AI agent security [Blog post].'

claims.claim: Add a computed flag for any agent that combines untrusted input, private data and a way to send data out.

claims.claim: BOMs should link to in-toto attestations and SLSA provenance for AI artifacts; there is no SLSA-for-training equivalent.
claims.check: in-toto attestation predicates relevant to ML/AI and any SLSA or OpenSSF work on ML/model provenance as of Nov 2026.
claims.what_is_true: in-toto's vetted predicates are CycloneDX, Link, Reference, Release, Runtime Traces, SCAI Report, SLSA Provenance, SLSA Verification Summary, SPDX2/SPDX3, Simple Verification Result, Test Result and VULNS. None is ML-specific. OpenSSF Model Signing wraps its per-file manifest in an in-toto Statement with its own predicate type (https://model_signing/signature/v1.0), so model artifacts already have an in-toto-shaped signature that BOMs can link to. The SLSA draft spec has no ML or training track: its future directions list only a Platform Operations track, and its active workstreams are Build L4, Attested Build Environments, Dependency Ingestion and Tooling Modernization. The OpenSSF AI/ML WG's 'End-to-End (E2E) Model Lifecycle Provenance' SIG (issue #40) is 'developing a pipeline-agnostic framework for attesting and validating end-to-end model lifecycle provenance'. It complements OMS and builds on Intel's Atlas framework, whose Atlas CLI produces C2PA manifests for models and datasets with OMS signing and Intel TDX attestation. So no standardized 'SLSA for training' exists as of Nov 2026, but work toward one is under way.
claims.suggested_rewrite: BOMs should link to in-toto attestations (SLSA Provenance, Test Result, VULNS, SCAI) and to OMS model-signature bundles. Training has no standard equivalent: SLSA has no ML track and in-toto has no vetted ML predicate. OpenSSF's E2E Model Lifecycle Provenance SIG, building on Intel's Atlas, is the closest work in progress, so for now formulation stays self-reported.
claims.notes: Inference, not sourced: nothing stops a team from emitting generic SLSA Build provenance for a training job treated as a build. SLSA just defines no ML-specific requirements, such as dataset digests, hyperparameters or compute attestation. 'No SLSA-for-training equivalent' is accurate for standards but should acknowledge the in-flight work.

claims.claim: brox encodes MCP servers and their capabilities in its own brox.* properties.
claims.check: Does an AIBOM/SBOM tool named 'brox' exist? What does it emit?
claims.what_is_true: brox is real. It is a PyPI package, v0.1.0, the only release, uploaded 2026-02-13. Summary: 'Repo scanner that turns agent/tool/model changes into a PR capability diff and blocks unsafe power upgrades'. Author 'brox Contributors', Apache-2.0. Its repository and homepage links are an unfilled template placeholder (github.com/yourusername/brox). `brox scan` emits a 'CycloneDX-compatible' AI-BOM with specVersion 1.5. It lists MCP servers and their capabilities, prompts, LLM endpoints, agent frameworks and egress domains, all as custom brox.* properties. In the README example: (1) an MCP server carries brox.ai.asset.kind=mcp_server and brox.location.file=mcp.json; (2) capabilities are flattened into brox.capability.record strings ('cap=filesystem.write;scope=./data/**;evidence=mcp.json:12;asset=mcp_server:filesystem-server') on a pseudo-service named 'brox.ai.capabilities'. The same example gives the MCP server component "type": "service". That is not a valid CycloneDX component type in 1.5, 1.6 or 1.7, so the sample would fail schema validation.
claims.suggested_rewrite: No agent-native types. Neither has first-class types for agents, tools, MCP servers, skills, prompts or memory stores, so every generator improvises in its own namespace. brox writes MCP servers and their capabilities into brox.* properties (brox.ai.asset.kind=mcp_server, brox.capability.record=cap=filesystem.write;scope=...). cdxgen uses cdx:mcp:*, Cisco's AI BOM uses cisco-aibom:* and agent-harness-aibom uses harness-aibom:*. Fix: add typed components, and until then use one shared, registered property namespace instead of per-vendor keys.
claims.notes: The claim is accurate, but brox is a weak sole example: a single 0.1.0 release, a placeholder GitHub URL and no verifiable source repository. claims.claim: Another generator hashes each MCP tool's description and schema and flags unpinned tools; one AIBOM scanner reports what it actually scanned (coverage).
claims.check: Identify real tools that do this (e.g. MCP scanners or AIBOM generators on PyPI/GitHub).
claims.what_is_true: Both descriptions match real tools, but the document names neither, and one detail is overstated. (1) Hashing tool definitions and flagging unpinned tools. agent-harness-aibom (PyPI) gives each MCP tool a definitionSha256. Once a server is probed live, the hash covers canonical JSON of name, description and inputSchema, plus separate descriptionSha256 and schemaSha256 properties. Any tool not probed raises mcp_tool_not_pinned (severity low). Probing is opt-in (--probe-mcp) and HTTP-only (SPEC section 31, v0.12.0), so stdio tools stay name-only and get flagged. mcplock (PyPI, 2026-07-29) pins every tool with four hashes: content_hash (description + inputSchema), description_hash, schema_hash, and a separate annotations_hash. It treats a missing baseline as a failure, but it is a lockfile/CI tool, not a BOM generator. aibom-scanner's 'MCP server launched without a pinned version' (v1.3.0, 2026-10-13) means package-version pinning, not definition pinning. (2) Coverage. aibom-scanner (SaaSVista, PyPI; coverage accounting since v1.1.0, 2026-07-21): 'An AI Bill of Materials that silently omits what it could not parse is not incomplete, it is wrong. Every scan reports its own denominator.' It reports coverage_pct, readable_coverage_pct and incomplete_inputs, and --fail-on-incomplete-coverage exits with code 3. Its output is table, JSON or SARIF, not CycloneDX.
claims.suggested_rewrite: agent-harness-aibom hashes each MCP tool's definition (name, description, inputSchema) once it can probe the server live, and flags every tool it couldn't pin; mcplock does the same as a CI lockfile. [...] Fix: every claim references signed evidence by digest, and every BOM carries a coverage statement. aibom-scanner reports its own denominator for exactly this reason: 'An AI Bill of Materials that silently omits what it could not parse is not incomplete, it is wrong.'
claims.notes: Name the tools; 'another generator' and 'one AIBOM scanner' can't be checked as written. 'Hashes each MCP tool's description and schema' overstates agent-harness-aibom, which only hashes probed HTTP-transport tools. PyPI shows 0.11.0 followed by 1.0.0, with no 0.12.0 release, so the probing stage presumably shipped in 1.0.0. That is an inference: I could not inspect the wheel.

evidence.detail: Section 30: 'mcp_tool_not_pinned (security.py, severity low). Fires for any tool whose definitionScope isn't "probed"'. Section 31: 'A successful probe recomputes definitionSha256 over {"name", "description", "inputSchema"} ... New properties: descriptionSha256 ..., schemaSha256'. HTTP transports only; stdio deferred.

Hash model: content_hash = description + inputSchema; description_hash; schema_hash; annotations_hash 'deliberately not folded into content_hash'. 'A missing baseline is exit 2, not 0: exiting clean for an unpinned server would silently green-light it in CI.'

'## Coverage: what the scan actually read. An AI Bill of Materials that silently omits what it could not parse is not incomplete, it is wrong. Every scan reports its own denominator'. Also: 'MCP server launched without a pinned version'.
The v1.1.0 README already contains the coverage section; v1.0.0 (2026-04-09) does not.

claims.claim: Software-only MCP governance cannot guarantee policy enforcement; hardware-attested approaches process tool-call payloads inside TEEs (a PyPI package).
claims.check: Identify the package or project.
claims.what_is_true: I could not identify the PyPI package behind this sentence. I checked about 120 plausible names on PyPI, including mcp-tee, tee-mcp, attested-mcp, confidential-mcp, mcp-enclave, tee-gateway and mcp-attestation. The closest MCP-adjacent hits are unrelated: mcp-secure does software message signing, and attestmcp is an audit-trail proxy. The general technique does exist outside MCP. Lucid Computing's lucid-sdk (PyPI, 1.0.0, 2026-01-30) runs 'auditors' as sidecars inside a Trusted Execution Environment, where 'every result is signed by the hardware, allowing a remote Verifier to prove that the entire Auditor Chain was executed faithfully on genuine hardware'. It is not MCP-specific. 'Software-only MCP governance cannot guarantee policy enforcement' reads as a vendor absolute. My inference: a TEE moves trust to the hardware vendor and to whoever verifies the attestation, and it does not guarantee enforcement either (TCB bugs, side channels, unverified quotes).
claims.suggested_rewrite: TEE/hardware attestation binding. Policy enforced in software is only as trustworthy as the host running it. Some vendors now run policy and audit code inside TEEs and have the hardware sign the results (Lucid Computing's SDK, for example). CycloneDX can point at that evidence only through a generic 'attestation' external reference: nothing says which TEE, which measurement or which verifier, and nothing can require it.
claims.notes: The citation was lost, and the WebSearch budget ran out before any search executed, so the package may still exist under a name I didn't guess. A follow-up search could find it. Do not keep the absolute 'cannot guarantee' without a named source. The document's next clause, 'neither SBOM standard has a way to reference ... hardware attestation evidence', is overstated for CycloneDX (see evidence). SPDX was not checked here.

evidence.detail: 'Auditors typically run as sidecars within a Trusted Execution Environment (TEE). The SDK ensures that every result is signed by the hardware, allowing a remote Verifier to prove that the entire Auditor Chain was executed faithfully on genuine hardware.'

CycloneDX does have generic externalReference types 'attestation' ('Human or machine-readable statements containing facts, evidence, or testimony') and 'evidence' (present since 1.5). It has no TEE-specific fields and no way to mark evidence as required.

claims.claim: A March 2026 Oxford/Cisco paper proposed schema extensions to both CycloneDX and SPDX for capturing execution context and agentic decisioning (reported by Dark Reading).
claims.check: Existence, title, authors, date, venue.
claims.what_is_true: The paper exists: 'SBOMs into Agentic AIBOMs: Schema Extensions, Agentic Orchestration, and Reproducibility Evaluation', arXiv:2603.10057, submitted 9 March 2026 (cs.CR/cs.AI/cs.SE). Authors: Petar Radanliev (University of Oxford), Carsten Maple (University of Warwick / Alan Turing Institute), Omar Santos (Cisco Systems) and Kayvan Atefi (University of Hull). A journal version appeared in ACM Digital Threats: Research and Practice (DOI 10.1145/3798285, April 2026). It proposes a structured schema that extends SBOMs into agentic AIBOMs, covering runtime dependency capture, policy-constrained agentic orchestration and reproducibility/exploitability evaluation. Dark Reading (Ericka Chickowski, 'How CISOs Should Prep for Agentic-Ready AI BOMs', 20 May 2026) credits 'researchers at Oxford and Cisco' with proposing extensions to CycloneDX and SPDX that capture execution context and agentic decisioning. The doc's 'Oxford/Cisco' copies Dark Reading's shorthand and leaves out the Warwick and Hull co-authors. The same group published a follow-up, arXiv:2606.19390 (an AIBOM-driven CSAF-VEX framework, Frontiers).
claims.suggested_rewrite: A March 2026 paper by researchers at Oxford, Warwick, Hull and Cisco (Radanliev, Maple, Santos and Atefi, 'SBOMs into Agentic AIBOMs', arXiv:2603.10057; ACM DTRAP) proposed schema extensions to both standards to capture execution context and agentic decisioning, as Dark Reading reported in May 2026.

claims.claim: Research identified three 'AIRS' categories that remain unique and security-critical for model assurance (Packaging & Serialization Safety, Structure & Adapters, Runtime Probes), and current SBOM specs do not include them as first-class elements (arXiv).
claims.check: Existence, title, authors, date.
claims.what_is_true: I could not find the 'AIRS' paper in this pass, so its existence, title, authors and date are unconfirmed. The spec half of the claim does check out against the normative files. Neither standard has first-class fields for serialization-format safety, quantization, adapters, tokenizer integrity or probe results. In CycloneDX 1.7, modelCard.modelParameters contains only approach, task, architectureFamily, modelArchitecture, datasets, inputs and outputs. Only generic hooks exist: component 'mime-type' and 'pedigree', free-form 'properties', and externalReference types such as 'runtime-analysis-report' and 'dynamic-analysis-report'. In SPDX 3.0.1, AIPackage has 15 AI-profile properties (autonomyType, domain, energyConsumption, hyperparameter, informationAboutApplication, informationAboutTraining, limitation, metric, metricDecisionThreshold, modelDataPreprocessing, modelExplainability, safetyRiskAssessment, standardCompliance, typeOfModel, useSensitivePersonalInformation). All are optional and none covers those categories.
claims.suggested_rewrite: Three model-assurance categories have no first-class home in either spec: packaging and serialization safety (loader/serializer policy, unsafe-path findings), structure and adapters (quantization, adapters, tokenizer integrity), and runtime probes (portable summaries of probe configuration and outcomes). CycloneDX 1.7's modelParameters stops at approach, task, architecture, datasets and I/O formats; none of the 15 AI properties on SPDX 3.0.1's AIPackage touches serialization, adapters, tokenizers or probe results. [Restore the AIRS citation (title, authors, arXiv ID) or drop the 'AIRS' label.]
claims.notes: Not located: the shared WebSearch budget was exhausted and arxiv.org is blocked, so failing to find the paper here is not evidence that it was fabricated. claims.check: The paper or study, its numbers and date.
claims.what_is_true: I could not locate the 'large-scale measurement of generated AIBOMs on Hugging Face' in this pass. Three related facts are verified. (1) The schemas make every such field optional. CycloneDX 1.7's modelCard has no required properties; its considerations block offers users, useCases, technicalLimitations, performanceTradeoffs, ethicalConsiderations, environmentalConsiderations and fairnessAssessments. All 15 AI properties on SPDX 3.0.1's AIPackage, including limitation, energyConsumption and informationAboutApplication, are minCount 0. (2) The OWASP AIBOM Generator, the likeliest tool behind such a study, builds CycloneDX 1.6 AIBOMs from Hugging Face model metadata and 'Calculates AIBOM completeness scoring with recommendations'. Its code repository covers metadata for 74,970 models and 32,111 model cards as of 1 Oct 2023, but the README does not state the field-coverage findings.

Every model-card field is optional: CycloneDX 1.7's modelCard has no required properties, and all 15 AI properties on SPDX 3.0.1's AIPackage are minCount 0. So limitations, intended use and environmental impact are exactly what producers skip, and nothing scores it. [Add the Hugging Face AIBOM measurement study here, with its sample size and field-coverage figures, or cut the claim.]

'responsible-use' is not a field name in CycloneDX or SPDX, which suggests the wording comes from a generator's scoring categories. Lead, not retrieved: the Liang et al. paper reportedly found environmental-impact, limitations and evaluation sections among the least filled. claims.claim: In practice most training datasets in 2026 are described as 'CommonCrawl slice from date X' or 'internal data'.
claims.check: Source for this claim (the word 'safeguard' appears next to it).
claims.what_is_true: I could not retrieve the 'safeguard' source, and no retrieved source puts a number on 'most'. Primary provider disclosures do support the direction of the claim, and they are even coarser than 'CommonCrawl slice from date X'. Cohere's Public Summary of Training Content for Command A+ and family (v1.1, last updated 10 Sept 2026, filed under EU AI Act Art. 53(1)(d)) lists one large public dataset: 'The training data for the model includes text from Common Crawl'. Everything else is described generically: 'proprietary datasets accessed through partnerships or developed by Cohere'. Its most relevant crawled domains 'include publicly available content in a variety of languages, including educational, government, science and technology, code, and general-purpose content'. Data collection runs 'Up to June 2026', with no Common Crawl snapshot IDs. Anthropic's transparency hub describes Claude's training data as 'a proprietary mix of publicly available information from the internet, public and private datasets', plus 'synthetic data generated by other models'.
claims.suggested_rewrite: Dataset provenance is underspecified. Both CycloneDX and SPDX let you name a dataset, but neither requires verifiable provenance, and real disclosures stay coarse. Cohere's September 2026 EU training-content summary for Command A+ names one large public dataset, Common Crawl, and otherwise cites 'proprietary datasets accessed through partnerships or developed by Cohere'. Anthropic describes Claude's training data as 'a proprietary mix of publicly available information from the internet, public and private datasets'. None of that is actionable for downstream users.
claims.notes: The cited source ('safeguard') was not found. Two primary examples back the qualitative point but cannot establish 'most'. Open-data projects, not checked here, likely document their corpora in much more detail, so limit the claim to proprietary or frontier providers and argue from examples.

Section 1.3 'proprietary datasets accessed through partnerships or developed by Cohere'. Section 2.3 domain summary is generic. 'Latest date of data acquisition/collection ... Up to June 2026'.

claims.claim: Most SBOM generation tools do not populate CycloneDX ML extension fields automatically, and there is no required model-weight integrity field with a NIST-approved algorithm.
claims.check: Source (the word 'anchor-defense' appears next to it) and accuracy.
claims.what_is_true: The spec half is correct, per the normative schemas. In CycloneDX 1.7, component.required is ['type','name']; hashes and modelCard are optional. The hash-alg enum is MD5, SHA-1, SHA-256, SHA-384, SHA-512, SHA3-256/384/512, BLAKE2b-256/384/512, BLAKE3 and Streebog-256/512. So no weight digest is required, and nothing restricts algorithms to NIST-approved SHA-2/SHA-3. SPDX 3.0.1 is no stricter. Element.verifiedUsing is optional, and the HashAlgorithm vocabulary allows adler32, md2, md4, md5, md6, sha1, blake2b and blake3 alongside SHA-2/SHA-3. AIPackage requires only releaseTime, suppliedBy, downloadLocation, packageVersion and primaryPurpose, with no integrity method. The tooling half is broadly right but needs nuance. cdxgen 12.9.0 (CycloneDX project, published 22 Oct 2026) builds modelCard.modelParameters (task, architectureFamily, modelArchitecture, datasets, inputs/outputs) from Hugging Face and GGUF metadata, but only in its opt-in 'aibom' / '-t ai' workflow. Its README warns that filtering to machine-learning-model 'does not enable machine-learning model discovery'. The OWASP AIBOM Generator emits CycloneDX 1.6 AIBOMs from Hugging Face. Syft's README feature list names no AI-model ecosystem.
claims.suggested_rewrite: Model weight hash verification. CycloneDX supports component hashes but requires none: a machine-learning-model component needs only type and name, modelCard is optional, and the hash-alg enum still accepts MD5 and SHA-1 next to SHA-2 and SHA-3. SPDX 3.0.1 is no stricter: verifiedUsing is optional, and md5, sha1 and adler32 are valid algorithms. Default SBOM runs don't fill ML-BOM fields; even cdxgen discovers models only in its opt-in aibom mode, and dedicated tools such as the OWASP AIBOM Generator fill modelCard basics from Hugging Face metadata. Nothing mandates a weight digest, let alone a NIST-approved one.
claims.notes: The 'anchor-defense' source was not found. 'NIST-approved' here means the FIPS 180-4 (SHA-1/SHA-2) and FIPS 202 (SHA-3) families. That is background knowledge, since NIST pages are blocked, but SPDX's own vocabulary cites FIPS 202 for the SHA-3 entries. Background, also unverified here: SHA-1 is deprecated by NIST for most uses.

evidence.detail: Fetched. component.required = ['type','name']; component.hashes has no required constraint; hash-alg enum = ['MD5','SHA-1','SHA-256','SHA-384','SHA-512','SHA3-256','SHA3-384','SHA3-512','BLAKE2b-256','BLAKE2b-384','BLAKE2b-512','BLAKE3','Streebog-256','Streebog-512'].
Entries include adler32, md2, md4, md5, md6, sha1, blake2b256/384/512 and blake3, alongside sha224-sha512 and sha3_224-sha3_512.
'verifiedUsing - type: IntegrityMethod' has no minCount, so it is optional.

'aibom: Generate CycloneDX AI/ML BOMs from source, Hugging Face URLs/purls, Modelfiles, or GGUF artifacts (-t ai defaults)'; '--component-type ... is a filter, not an inventory enabler: passing a type such as machine-learning-model does not enable machine-learning model discovery'.
