claims.claim: EU AI Act Article 53 requires consent and licensing provenance per data source.
claims.check: Article 53(1)(c) and (d) text and the AI Office template for the public summary of training content (July 2025): what is actually required.
claims.what_is_true: Article 53 does not require consent or per-source licensing provenance. It requires the following of GPAI-model providers. (a) Technical documentation for the AI Office. Annex XI section 1(2) covers type, provenance and curation methods of training/test/validation data, number of data points, scope, main characteristics, how data was obtained and selected, and measures to detect unsuitable sources and biases. (b) Documentation for downstream integrators. Annex XII section 2 covers type, provenance and curation methodologies of the data; the licence named in Annexes XI/XII is the model's licence, not the data's. (c) A policy to comply with Union copyright and related-rights law, in particular to identify and comply with, including through state-of-the-art technologies, rights reservations (text-and-data-mining opt-outs) under Art. 4(3) of Directive (EU) 2019/790. (d) A sufficiently detailed public summary of the content used for training, following the AI Office template. Cohere's filed summary reproduces the template (July 2025) field by field: provider/model identification, modalities, size bands and latest collection date; 2.1 publicly available datasets, including a list of the large ones; 2.2.1 commercially licensed data, asking only whether transactional licensing agreements with rightsholders were concluded (Yes/No/Other) and for which modality; 2.2.2 other private third-party datasets, listed if publicly known; 2.3 crawlers, purposes, behaviour, collection period and a summary of the most relevant domain names; 2.4 user data (yes/no); 2.5 synthetic data; 2.6 other; 3.1 Code of Practice signatory status and measures honouring TDM opt-outs; 3.2 illegal-content removal. No field asks for consent, and licensing appears only as a category-level yes/no. Obligations (c) and (d) are not covered by the Art. 53(2) open-source exemption. Chapter V has applied since 2 Aug 2025.
claims.suggested_rewrite: Licensing and opt-out provenance per data source. The EU AI Act asks for less than you'd think. Art. 53(1)(c)-(d) makes GPAI providers keep a copyright policy that honours text-and-data-mining opt-outs and publish a training-content summary on the AI Office template: data-source categories, the large public datasets, the most relevant crawled domains, and the opt-out measures applied. Licensed data is a yes/no; nothing asks for consent. But per-source licence and opt-out status is exactly what a provider needs to fill that template and defend its copyright policy, and neither standard enforces structured capture of it.
claims.notes: EUR-Lex and the Commission's template page are blocked here. The Article 53 wording was checked against a German secondary rules catalog, and the template's fields against Cohere's filed form (a primary instance). That consent is a GDPR lawful-basis concept rather than an Article 53 duty is my inference from its absence in Article 53 and in the template. The template's July 2025 publication date comes from the task brief and was not re-checked.

evidence.detail: Filled AI Office template. '2.2.1 Datasets commercially licensed by rightsholders or their representatives: Have you concluded transactional commercial licensing agreement(s) with rightsholder(s) or with their representatives? Yes/No/Other'. '3.1 Respect of reservation of rights from text and data mining exception or limitation ... including the opt-out protocols and solutions honoured'. '2.3 ... Summary of the most relevant domain names crawled'. No consent field.

euaiact 0.1.0 (RiskDataScience GmbH), a rules catalog keyed to the consolidated text EUAIACT_2026_07_27. P_AIA_053_001_C: 'Strategie zur Einhaltung des Unionsurheberrechts ... Rechtevorbehalte nach Artikel 4 Absatz 3 der Richtlinie 2019/790 identifizieren und einhalten, unter Einbeziehung aktueller Technik'. P_AIA_053_001_D: 'Ausreichend detaillierte Zusammenfassung der Trainingsinhalte nach AI-Office-Vorlage erstellen und öffentlich zugänglich machen'. (c) and (d) are not exempted by Art. 53(2). Annex XI 1(2) and XII 2: 'Typ, Herkunft und Aufbereitungsmethoden der Trainings-, Test- und Validierungsdaten'. Chapter V applies from 2025-08-02.

'The General-Purpose AI Code of Practice is a voluntary tool ... designed to help industry comply with the AI Act's obligations for providers of general-purpose AI models'; GPAI obligations had 'imminent entry into application on August 2, 2025'.

claims.claim: EU AI Act Article 13 needs a system-level intended purpose.
claims.check: Article 13(3)(b) text.
claims.what_is_true: Correct in substance, but scope and timing need stating. Article 13(3)(b) requires the instructions for use of a high-risk AI system to describe its characteristics, capabilities and limitations of performance. Item (i) is the system's intended purpose; the catalog renders it as 'den konkreten bestimmungsgemäßen Zweck des Systems einschließlich maßgeblicher Einsatzgrenzen', i.e. the specific intended purpose including relevant limits of use. The other items cover tested accuracy and metrics, robustness and cybersecurity; foreseeable circumstances affecting performance; risks under intended use and foreseeable misuse; explainability capabilities; performance for specific persons or groups; input-data and training/validation/test-data information; and output-interpretation information. It is a system-level duty on providers of high-risk systems only. Under the consolidated text after Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, Chapter III sections 1-3 apply from 2 Dec 2027 for Annex III systems and from 2 Aug 2028 for Annex I systems. SPDX 3.0.1 has purpose fields only per artifact: SoftwareArtifact primaryPurpose/additionalPurpose, AIPackage informationAboutApplication and DatasetPackage intendedUse.
claims.suggested_rewrite: Missing system-level intended purpose. For high-risk AI systems, Article 13(3)(b)(i) requires the instructions for use to state the system's intended purpose, alongside its accuracy metrics, robustness, cybersecurity and foreseeable risks; SPDX carries purpose only per artifact (primaryPurpose, informationAboutApplication, intendedUse). After the 2026 Digital Omnibus, this applies from 2 December 2027 for Annex III systems.
claims.notes: The official text is blocked here; the wording was checked against a secondary rules catalog. The application dates come from that catalog's table and match today's earlier same-session check of the Digital Omnibus (Reg. (EU) 2026/1744).

evidence.detail: Rule AIA_013_003_B ('Leistungs- und Risikoinformationen', ART_013/3/b) requires 'anleitung_bestimmungsgemaesser_zweck: Die Anweisung beschreibt den konkreten bestimmungsgemäßen Zweck des Systems einschließlich maßgeblicher Einsatzgrenzen' plus accuracy/metrics, robustness and cybersecurity, foreseeable circumstances, risks, explainability, group performance, data information and output interpretation. Application table EUAIACT_2026_07_27: HOCHRISIKO_ANHANG_III_ABSCHNITT_1_BIS_3 = 2027-12-02; ANHANG_I = 2028-08-02.
primaryPurpose and additionalPurpose (SoftwarePurpose) are per-artifact properties.
intendedUse is a per-dataset DatasetPackage property; there is no system-level intended-purpose element.

claims.claim: ISO/IEC 42001 audits will demand exactly this evidence shape (benchmark identity, harness, scores, evaluator identity, attestation link).
claims.check: What ISO/IEC 42001 requires regarding AI system evaluation evidence.
claims.what_is_true: ISO/IEC 42001:2023 sets requirements for an AI management system (governance, risk management and a catalogue of AI controls). It does not define an evidence schema. Google Cloud, which is certified, says 42001 'outlines and provides the requirements for an Artificial Intelligence Management System (AIMS), specifies a set of best practices, and details AI management controls', and that it 'does not mandate specific AI controls'. The OWASP AI Exchange says '42001 is about extending your risk management system - it focuses on governance ... ISO 42001 doesn't go into the lifecycle processes. For example, it does not discuss how to train models, how to do data lineage, continuous validation, versioning of AI models'. Its annex guidance covers operation and monitoring (B.6.2.6, 'on a high abstraction level') and mentions data provenance only briefly (B.7.5). Anthropic (certified by Schellman, announced 13 Jan 2025) calls it 'the first international standard outlining requirements for AI governance'. Auditors will therefore expect documented evaluation and monitoring evidence, but nothing in 42001 requires benchmark IDs, harness config hashes, evaluator identity or attestation links.
claims.suggested_rewrite: ... so attestations become comparable across producers. ISO/IEC 42001 won't hand you this schema: it is a management-system standard that, in Google Cloud's words, 'does not mandate specific AI controls.' But a 42001 auditor will ask how each AI system was verified and how it is monitored, and a signed, structured eval record is the cleanest evidence you can put in front of them.
claims.notes: The ISO text is paywalled and blocked, so this characterization rests on a certified provider (Google Cloud), OWASP and Anthropic. I did not re-check specific Annex A control numbers, such as the verification-and-validation control.

evidence.detail: Fetched. 'ISO/IEC 42001:2023 outlines and provides the requirements for an Artificial Intelligence Management System (AIMS), specifies a set of best practices, and details AI management controls that can help manage AI risks.' 'The 42001 standard does not mandate specific AI controls'.

Fetched. '42001 is about extending your risk management system - it focuses on governance ... ISO 42001 doesn't go into the lifecycle processes. For example, it does not discuss how to train models, how to do data lineage, continuous validation, versioning of AI models'.
'ISO/IEC 42001 (AI management) briefly mentions data provenance ... in section B.7.5'.
'ISO 42001 is the first international standard outlining requirements for AI governance'; certification issued by Schellman Compliance, LLC (ANAB-accredited).

claims.claim: Model registries (Hugging Face, Ollama, Azure ML, SageMaker) are not scanned at the pull step; the most common mistake is treating ML framework packages as the complete AI dependency inventory.
claims.check: Source and support.
claims.what_is_true: I could not retrieve the 'anchor-defense' source, and no retrieved source measures what the 'most common mistake' is. Three facts support the risk itself. cdxgen's README says '--component-type' 'is a filter, not an inventory enabler: passing a type such as machine-learning-model does not enable machine-learning model discovery'; models are discovered only in its opt-in aibom / -t ai workflow. Unit 42 (Sept 2025) showed pull-by-name trust failing: re-registered Hugging Face namespaces served replacement models through Vertex AI Model Garden and Azure AI Foundry catalogs. The adjacent sentence in the doc ('no standardized provenance or attestation fields') is overstated, though. Two of the four named registries already have standard purl identities. The 'huggingface' type uses the model revision Git commit hash as its version, with huggingface.co as default repository. The 'mlflow' type covers 'MLflow ML models (Azure ML, Databricks, etc.)' with the tracking URI as repository. CycloneDX 1.7 also has generic 'distribution-intake', 'attestation' and 'digital-signature' external references plus component signature and pedigree. What neither spec has is required registry provenance or attestation, or pull-time verification semantics.
claims.suggested_rewrite: Model registries (Hugging Face, Ollama, Azure ML, SageMaker) are a blind spot. purl already gives Hugging Face (pkg:huggingface, versioned by revision commit) and MLflow-based registries such as Azure ML (pkg:mlflow) a standard identity, and CycloneDX has generic attestation and distribution-intake references, but neither spec requires registry provenance or a verified pull. Default SBOM runs inventory torch and transformers, not the weights they load: cdxgen's own docs warn that filtering for machine-learning-model 'does not enable machine-learning model discovery'. Unit 42 showed why that matters in September 2025: a re-registered Hugging Face namespace could feed a malicious model into the Vertex AI and Azure AI Foundry catalogs.
claims.notes: The 'anchor-defense' source was not found, and 'most common mistake' is an unquantified practitioner claim, so present it as the author's view. I did not retrieve evidence about registry-side or proxy scanning at pull time, so the doc should not assert a universal 'not scanned'.

evidence.detail: 'This is a filter, not an inventory enabler: passing a type such as machine-learning-model does not enable machine-learning model discovery'; AI-BOM via 'the aibom command or the -t ai project type'.
type 'huggingface' ('Hugging Face ML models'); version is 'model revision Git commit hash'; 'The default repository is https://huggingface.co.'
type 'mlflow' ('MLflow ML models (Azure ML, Databricks, etc.)'); 'The repository is the MLflow tracking URI. There is no default.'
externalReference types include 'distribution-intake', 'attestation', 'digital-signature' and 'model-card'; component has 'signature', 'pedigree', 'omniborId' and 'swhid'. All are optional.

'Model Namespace Reuse': deleted or transferred Hugging Face namespaces can be re-registered; demonstrated against Hugging Face-backed catalogs in Google Vertex AI and Azure AI Foundry. From today's earlier same-session search-based pass; unit42 is blocked for direct fetch.

additional_findings.finding: Cline's post-mortem (24 Feb 2026) is the authoritative root-cause source. Within 30 minutes of Khan's disclosure, Cline removed the vulnerable workflows and started rotating credentials, but 'the wrong token was deleted while the exposed one remained active'. npm's org-level token page 'showed zero active tokens' but did not list the exposed token. The VS Code Marketplace and OpenVSX tokens were rotated on 9 Feb, and no unauthorized releases appeared there.
additional_findings.relevance: Cite it next to the GHSA. It explains why the publish happened 8 days after disclosure and directly supports the article's no-long-lived-tokens control.

additional_findings.finding: The triage workflow file carries the comment 'SECURITY: These permissions are intentionally restrictive ... even if a malicious user attempts prompt injection via issue content, Claude cannot modify repository code'. The same file gives Bash to any GitHub user (allowed_non_write_users: "*").
additional_findings.relevance: A primary-source quote showing the team treated GITHUB_TOKEN scoping as the security boundary and missed the shared Actions cache. Strong evidence for the AIBOM and tool-inventory argument.

additional_findings.finding: Before the fix, publish-nightly.yml restored node_modules from actions/cache using a predictable key, ${{ runner.os }}-npm-${{ hashFiles('package-lock.json') }}, in a job with VSCE_PAT and OVSX_PAT in its environment. Cline removed these cache steps between 9 and 10 Feb.
additional_findings.relevance: Shows the exact cache-sharing weakness behind the article's 'must not share a cache with release workflows' control.

additional_findings.finding: The provenance anomaly was machine-detectable. Versions 2.2.3 and 2.4.0 were published by 'GitHub Actions' trusted publishing with SLSA provenance attestations; 2.3.0 was published by npm user 'clinebotorg' with none. StepSecurity flagged it at 11:40 UTC, 14 minutes after publish, as having been published outside the trusted-publishing pipeline.
additional_findings.relevance: A concrete case of provenance verification catching a compromise. It strengthens the article's 'verify signatures/provenance' and signed-AIBOM recommendations.

additional_findings.finding: Tarball forensics: my SHA-256 comparison shows cline-2.3.0.tgz differs from 2.2.3 only in package.json. The tar headers record the owner 'codespace/codespace' and timestamps of 11:18-11:20 UTC on 17 Feb. That is consistent with the package being repacked in a GitHub Codespaces-style environment minutes before the 11:26 UTC publish, but this is my inference from the metadata.
additional_findings.relevance: Independent confirmation that only the install hook changed. The repacking detail is optional colour and should be labelled as inference.

additional_findings.finding: Microsoft Threat Intelligence confirmed through Defender 'a small but noticeable uptick in installations of OpenClaw initiated by Cline CLI installation script' during the window of about 8 hours (11:26-19:30 UTC).
additional_findings.relevance: Independent evidence that the hook actually ran on real endpoints. Better than download counts for describing impact.

additional_findings.finding: Timeline: Khan reported privately on 1 Jan 2026 and got no response. The attacker's issue #8904 landed on 28 Jan (Raptor forensics). Public disclosure followed on 9 Feb and the publish on 17 Feb. The vulnerability was exploited in the wild while the private report sat unanswered.
additional_findings.relevance: Supports the governance angle: nobody owned or inventoried the AI agent in CI, so the vulnerability report went unanswered.

additional_findings.finding: If the author wants an OpenClaw risk example, CVE-2026-25253 is GHSA-g8p2-7wf7-98mq: 1-click RCE via gatewayUrl token exfiltration in OpenClaw's Control UI, CVSS 8.8, fixed in 2026.1.29, advisory published 2 Feb 2026. It does not apply to the OpenClaw version Clinejection installed (2026.2.15).
additional_findings.relevance: Lets the author keep an accurately scoped OpenClaw point, for example in the tool or registry layer section, without misattributing it to the Cline payload.

additional_findings.finding: Endor Labs (Henrik Plate) assessed the impact as low. The install 'does not include the installation/start of the Gateway daemon', and the immediate damage was likened to 'a prank', with a warning that the same technique could deliver destructive payloads.
additional_findings.relevance: Balanced framing for the payload paragraph that keeps the 'next time it won't be benign' argument intact.

additional_findings.finding: Michael Bargury's write-up 'Agent Compromised by Agent To Deploy an Agent' (19 Feb 2026), the Cloud Security Alliance research note (Mar 2026) and Krebs on Security (8 Mar 2026) all cover Clinejection.
additional_findings.relevance: Credible practitioner and mainstream citations for the 'agent installs an agent' framing. CSA (https://labs.cloudsecurityalliance.org/research/csa-research-note-clinejection-prompt-injection-cicd-cache-p/) is the safer source for the 'one of the first' claim.

additional_findings.finding: Research limitation: the shared web-search budget ran out partway through. The Cline post-mortem, Khan's post, the StepSecurity blog and the Endor Labs post were read only through search-result excerpts, because their hosts are blocked for direct fetch.
additional_findings.relevance: Before publishing, the author should open these pages and confirm the exact quotes. A follow-up run can continue the search.

additional_findings.finding: AWS-2025-016, 'Memory Dump Issue in AWS CodeBuild' (25 Jul 2025), is the real root-cause document. A pull request built automatically by CodeBuild could extract the repository access token from build-environment memory. AWS says a threat actor did this to the AWS Toolkit for VS Code and AWS SDK for .NET repositories. AWS added memory-dump protections for unprivileged builds and advises against automatic PR builds from untrusted contributors when the token has write access.
additional_findings.relevance: Turns the vague 'overly permissive token' into a concrete CI lesson that parallels the article's Clinejection 'isolate CI' control.

additional_findings.finding: The payload was swapped in at build time. The amazonq/v1.84.0 scripts/package.ts contains a downloader that runs only on STAGE=prod Linux release builds and fetches extensionNode.bk from the 'stability' ref into src/extensionNode.ts. The tagged src/extensionNode.ts is clean, and 1.85.0's package.ts is byte-identical to 1.83.0's.
additional_findings.relevance: Strong support for the AIBOM thesis: source review, or an SBOM built from the repo, would miss it. Only build provenance would show it.

additional_findings.finding: AWS fixed it quietly. The 1.85.0 changelog entry (19 Jul 2025) reads only 'Miscellaneous non-user-facing changes'. Public acknowledgment came only after 404 Media's 23 Jul story.
additional_findings.relevance: Concrete backing for the article's 'how would you know?' hook.

additional_findings.finding: CVE-2025-8217 is rated Medium (CVSS v4.0 5.1, v3.1 4.0), CWE-506, and titled 'Inert Malicious script injected...'. CISA's ADP assessment lists Exploitation: none.
additional_findings.relevance: Calibrates impact language: the vendor treats it as an inert near-miss.

additional_findings.finding: mcp-remote was patched before disclosure. Through 0.1.14 it called open(authorizationUrl) directly. 0.1.15 (11 Jun 2025) added sanitizeUrl, and 0.1.16 (17 Jun 2025) hardened it. The CVE and GHSA went public on 9 Jul 2025.
additional_findings.relevance: Gives the precise mechanism and timeline, and supports recording a minimum safe version (0.1.16 or later) in the AIBOM.

additional_findings.finding: Neither CVE-2025-6514 nor CVE-2025-8217 is in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog (version 2026.10.30, 1,766 entries).
additional_findings.relevance: Supports dropping any implication of in-the-wild exploitation.

additional_findings.finding: mcp-remote's upstream changed in 2026. npm metadata shows the repository field moving from geelen/mcp-remote to punkpeye/mcp-remote from v0.2.5 (26 Aug 2026). The listed npm maintainer is now 'punkpeye' (a glama.ai address), releases go out through GitHub Actions trusted publishing (OIDC), and the latest version is 0.15.2 (20 Oct 2026). The README credits Glen Maddern as original author.
additional_findings.relevance: A live example of the maintainer and registry drift an AIBOM should record. Worth checking before recommending mcp-remote by name.

additional_findings.finding: Wiz's 'CodeBreach' research, publicized January 2026, described a separate AWS CodeBuild webhook-filter misconfiguration in AWS-managed GitHub repositories, including aws-sdk-js-v3, that could have enabled repository takeover. AWS fixed it and said no inappropriate code was introduced. This comes from secondary coverage only.
additional_findings.relevance: Shows the same CI-pipeline weakness recurring in AWS repos after the Amazon Q incident; an optional follow-on example.

additional_findings.finding: The attacker's own access story is unverified. They claimed 'admin credentials on a silver platter' after a late-June PR, but GH Archive shows no June 2025 activity by lkmanka58 on the repo. Their downloader commit 678851b reused the message and author date of a commit by another account, atonaamz.
additional_findings.relevance: Cite AWS's token explanation rather than the attacker's narrative.

additional_findings.finding: The MCP spec 2026-07-28 (released 28 Jul 2026) removed the initialize/initialized handshake and the Mcp-Session-Id header ('stateless protocol core'). tools/list responses now carry ttlMs/cacheScope cache hints and SHOULD come back in a deterministic order.
additional_findings.relevance: Update the 'after initial handshake' framing. Cacheable, deterministically ordered tool catalogs are a natural point to hash and pin tool definitions, which supports the article's Step 5.

additional_findings.finding: The registry's moderation policy says: 'The MCP Registry does not make guarantees about moderation, and consumers should assume minimal-to-no moderation.' It explicitly won't remove 'Servers with security vulnerabilities'.
additional_findings.relevance: Quotable primary evidence for the article's 'registries... usually have minimal vetting'.

additional_findings.finding: The registry 'is not intended to be directly consumed by host applications'. Hosts should use downstream marketplaces or subregistries, which add curation and ratings.
additional_findings.relevance: Official backing for the article's allowlist / approved-registry control.

additional_findings.finding: For remote servers the registry 'does not verify that you control the remote URL, regardless of authentication method'.
additional_findings.relevance: Namespace verification is not endpoint verification. An AI-BOM should record each remote MCP URL and its operator, because there is no package to hash.

additional_findings.finding: MCPB is the only package type with a mandatory SHA-256 (fileSha256), and 'The MCP Registry does not validate this hash; however, MCP clients do validate the hash before installation'.
additional_findings.relevance: A concrete in-ecosystem precedent for the article's hashing/pinning recommendation, and a note on where verification actually happens.

additional_findings.finding: Registry version metadata is immutable ('Once published, version metadata is immutable (similar to npm)'), and 'deleted' servers remain retrievable with include_deleted=true.
additional_findings.relevance: An AI-BOM can reference an exact registry entry and version for provenance, and investigators can retrieve removed entries.

additional_findings.finding: As of the main-branch docs fetched on 1 Nov 2026, every registry doc page still says it is 'currently in preview', and the API has been frozen at v0.1 since 2025-10-24.
additional_findings.relevance: The article should not imply general availability. The preview carries no data-durability guarantees.

additional_findings.finding: Postmark's official npm package @activecampaign/postmark-mcp was first published on 2025-11-26, about two months after the unscoped impostor 'postmark-mcp' (created 2025-09-15, unpublished 2025-09-25) was pulled.
additional_findings.relevance: The attack exploited an unclaimed brand name on npm, a namespace-squatting lesson that fits the article's Registry layer.

additional_findings.finding: Official MCP server READMEs recommend unpinned installs: Postmark's 'npx -y @activecampaign/postmark-mcp' ('recommended — no clone required'), and the reference filesystem server's 'npx -y @modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem'.
additional_findings.relevance: Explains why rug pulls reach agents on their next launch, and supports pinning exact versions (npx -y pkg@x.y.z).

additional_findings.finding: CVE-2025-54136 (Cursor <=1.2.4, published 1 Aug 2025): after a user approved an MCP server config, an attacker could silently swap in a malicious command 'without triggering any warning or re-prompt'. Fixed in Cursor 1.3.
additional_findings.relevance: A CVE-backed rug-pull case to cite next to postmark-mcp. It shows why re-approval on change (Step 5) matters.

additional_findings.finding: Invariant's mcp-scan (now snyk-agent-scan, an 'Agent supply chain security scanner') implements tool pinning: it 'detects changes to MCP tools via hashing' to catch rug pulls.
additional_findings.relevance: An off-the-shelf reference implementation for the article's 'Pin tool schemas' step.

additional_findings.finding: The MCP maintainers' post 'Tool Annotations as Risk Vocabulary' (16 Mar 2026) says: 'An untrusted server can lie. A server can claim readOnlyHint: true and delete your files anyway.'
additional_findings.relevance: Primary support for relying on runtime controls rather than a tool's self-declared metadata.

additional_findings.finding: The official MCP SDKs shipped with DNS-rebinding protection disabled by default until TypeScript SDK 1.24.0 and Python SDK 1.23.0 (CVE-2025-66414/66416, published 2 Dec 2025).
additional_findings.relevance: The SDK name and version belong in the AI-BOM, because one SDK default reaches every server built on it.

additional_findings.finding: If you want to say 'persistent backdoor', cite Anthropic's Sleeper Agents paper (14 Jan 2024). It found backdoors 'can be made persistent, so that it is not removed by standard safety training techniques, including supervised fine-tuning, reinforcement learning, and adversarial training'. Those backdoors were deliberately trained in, not injected through 250 documents.
additional_findings.relevance: Gives correct sourcing for 'persistent' and keeps it separate from the 250-document study.

additional_findings.finding: AgentPoison (Chen, Xiang, Xiao, Song, Li; NeurIPS 2024) poisons agent memory and knowledge bases and measures action-level attack success against an autonomous-driving agent, a ReAct QA agent and EHRAgent.
additional_findings.relevance: Directly supports 'manipulating agent decision outcomes', which PoisonedRAG (a QA-only study) does not. Its headline numbers (around 80% ASR at under 0.1% poison rate) are from the abstract, which I didn't re-fetch.

additional_findings.finding: OWASP LLM04:2025, which the article already cites, names 'Frontrunning Poisoning' and 'Split-View Data Poisoning' as training-data techniques and references Carlini's 'Poisoning Web-Scale Training Datasets' talk.
additional_findings.relevance: A citable label and lineage for the Wikipedia edit-then-revert example.

additional_findings.finding: OWASP LLM03:2025 lists 'Vulnerable LoRA adapters' and says LoRA/PEFT 'introduce new supply-chain risks', for example a malicious adapter merged into a base model or loaded by vLLM or OpenLLM.
additional_findings.relevance: A PEFT-specific source if the author keeps 'PEFT' in the heading. It also fits the Models layer of an AI-BOM (adapters as components).

additional_findings.finding: Aikido Security registered npm 'react-codeshift' as a placeholder on 14 Jan 2026, after an AI-hallucinated `npx react-codeshift` command spread through AI-generated agent skill files into 237 repos (per a README citing Aikido's 'Agent Skills Spreading Hallucinated npx Commands').
additional_findings.relevance: A recent real-world case that ties slopsquatting to SKILL.md-style agent artifacts, which is the article's own Data/Tools theme.

additional_findings.finding: npm security replaced 'unused-imports', 'eslint-comments' (27 Oct 2025) and 'transform-react-remove-prop-types' (29 Oct 2025) with security-holding packages. These are AI-plausible shortenings of real ESLint and Babel plugin names, and they match what I recall of Koi Security's PhantomRaven report (Oct 2025). Verify that report before citing it.
additional_findings.relevance: Possibly the strongest in-the-wild slopsquatting evidence for A4-06 and A4-07, but on npm, not PyPI.

additional_findings.finding: The Anthropic poisoning write-up itself notes that triggers could be embedded 'in specific websites to make models unusable when they retrieve content from those sites'.
additional_findings.relevance: Links the pretraining-poisoning result to retrieval and agent contexts in the authors' own words.

additional_findings.finding: The article's reference line '(Slopsquatting rates: 21.7% open-source / 5.2% commercial.)' mislabels the figures. They are package-hallucination rates, and the overall rate across all 16 models was 19.7%.
additional_findings.relevance: Fixes a terminology error in the reference list.

additional_findings.finding: The 2024 'huggingface-cli' proof-of-concept package no longer exists on PyPI: the JSON API returned Not Found on 1 Nov 2026.
additional_findings.relevance: If the Lanyado proof of concept is cited, link Lasso's write-up rather than PyPI.

additional_findings.finding: A September 2026 npm package, 'astropy-fits-js', is a benign proof-of-concept marker for a coordinated package-hallucination disclosure to Anthropic via HackerOne.
additional_findings.relevance: A current (2026) sign that vendors are handling hallucinated-package reports through bug bounty channels. Useful context, not an attack.

additional_findings.finding: Method limitation: the shared web-search budget ran out on this task's first search, so verification relied on direct fetches from anthropic.com, raw.githubusercontent.com, registry.npmjs.org and pypi.org. Items marked 'background' (the PoisonedRAG 90% abstract wording, the Spracklen 5.2%/21.7% and repeatability figures, Carlini et al. details, the Lasso download count, PhantomRaven, the Seth Larson coinage) should be confirmed with a follow-up search.
additional_findings.relevance: Tells the editor which facts still need a second source.

additional_findings.finding: Picklescan, the scanner Hugging Face runs on pickles, has had 59 GitHub security advisories (58 CVEs) against v0.0.20 (February 2025), fixed between v0.0.21 (26 February 2025) and v1.0.4 (2 March 2026). Almost all are detection bypasses: unlisted dangerous callables (pip.main, ctypes, pty, profile.run, numpy.f2py helpers, pkgutil.resolve_name), ZIP header and CRC tricks, and file-extension mismatches (for example CVE-2025-1716, CVE-2025-1889, CVE-2025-10155, CVE-2025-10156, CVE-2025-10157).
additional_findings.relevance: Strong evidence for 'Ban pickle in production': blocklist scanning is a speed bump, not a control.

additional_findings.finding: CVE-2026-24747 (GHSA-63cw-57p8-fm3p, CVSS 3.1 8.8, published 27 January 2026): a crafted .pth file can corrupt memory in PyTorch's weights_only unpickler, with possible arbitrary code execution, in versions below 2.10.0. Fixed in torch 2.10.0.
additional_findings.relevance: Updates the CVE-2025-32434 story: weights_only=True is a mitigation, not a sandbox. Keep torch patched and prefer SafeTensors.

additional_findings.finding: Hugging Face's July 2026 incident write-ups (disclosure 16 July, technical timeline 27 July 2026) describe an autonomous AI agent getting code execution in production dataset-processing workers. One path was a Jinja2 template injection: an fsspec reference:// spec in a malicious dataset config had a numeric offset field that 'was actually a Jinja2 template', and the renderer evaluated it. The other was an HDF5 'external raw storage' read that leaked /proc/self/environ and the worker's source code. The agent then harvested credentials and moved laterally.
additional_findings.relevance: A 2026, in-the-wild case of the same bug class as CVE-2024-34359 (template injection in ML artifact metadata or config), run by an agent against an AI platform's supply chain. It fits the article's thesis directly.

additional_findings.finding: Keras 'safe_mode' has been bypassed repeatedly: CVE-2025-1550, CVE-2025-8747, CVE-2025-9905, CVE-2025-9906, CVE-2025-12058, and CVE-2026-1669 (HDF5 external storage and ExternalLink honored when loading weights). Fixes landed between Keras 3.9.0 and 3.13.2. By contrast, PyPI's advisory feed lists no vulnerabilities for safetensors 0.3.1 or 0.4.5.
additional_findings.relevance: Shows that non-pickle formats with 'safe' loading flags still execute code. Supports the GGUF point and the case for SafeTensors.

additional_findings.finding: Hugging Face transformers now defaults to weights_only=True for .bin checkpoints and refuses torch.load on torch below 2.6, citing CVE-2025-32434. The restriction 'does not apply when loading files with safetensors'.
additional_findings.relevance: Mainstream loaders are now safe by default. The residual risk sits in custom loaders, weights_only=False and trust_remote_code.

additional_findings.finding: Safetensors joined the PyTorch Foundation (Linux Foundation) on 8 April 2026. It is 'the default format for model distribution across the Hugging Face Hub', and Hugging Face is working with PyTorch so Safetensors 'may be used within PyTorch core as a serialization system for torch models'.
additional_findings.relevance: Updates the 'Hugging Face created SafeTensors' framing: it now has vendor-neutral governance and may become PyTorch-native.

additional_findings.finding: Trail of Bits' safetensors audit also flagged that 'PyTorch conversion utility is vulnerable to arbitrary code execution' (finding 8), and recommended adding a magic signature and a version number to the format to prevent polyglots.
additional_findings.relevance: Converting legacy pickles to SafeTensors must itself run in a sandbox, which is a useful caveat for the 'mandate SafeTensors' step.

additional_findings.finding: MITRE ATLAS case study AML.CS0031 'Malicious Models on Hugging Face' documents ReversingLabs' nullifAI find: reverse shells, Picklescan evasion through deliberately corrupted pickles, and Hugging Face's response.
additional_findings.relevance: A stable, citable source for the nullifAI paragraph, which currently has no reference.

additional_findings.finding: model_signing's main-branch changelog lists unreleased verification fixes: dangling symlinks, symlinked directories and empty files escaping the signed manifest, certificate EKU not enforced, and config reuse silently skipping unsigned files. The latest PyPI release is still 1.1.1 (10 October 2025).
additional_findings.relevance: If the article mandates signature verification, readers should pin a verifier release that contains these fixes and keep allow_symlinks off.

additional_findings.finding: Hugging Face scanning partners: Protect AI (22 October 2024), JFrog (4 March 2025) and VirusTotal (22 October 2025). VirusTotal hash lookups cover 2.2M+ public model and dataset repositories, and 'No raw file contents are shared with VirusTotal'.
additional_findings.relevance: Context for hub-side controls and their limits (hash and pattern based), which supports enterprise-side verification and intake.

additional_findings.finding: Sigstore's model-validation-operator, a proof of concept, adds an init container that validates model signatures (Sigstore, PKI or public key) before Kubernetes workloads start. Model and signature paths must be set explicitly.
additional_findings.relevance: A concrete, if early-stage, enforcement point for the 'verify before load' recommendation.

additional_findings.finding: OWASP LLM04:2026 Supply Chain (4 Aug 2026) recommends 'an up-to-date, signed inventory of components using a Software Bill of Materials (SBOM), extended to models, adapters, and datasets with AI BOMs (AIBOMs) and ML SBOMs'. It adds a caveat: 'Signing proves integrity and origin, not safety (a validly signed model from a compromised or trusted-but-malicious supplier can still be backdoored)'.
additional_findings.relevance: Direct OWASP backing for the article's 'signed AIBOM' thesis, plus the caveat the article should acknowledge.

additional_findings.finding: OWASP AI Exchange (Oct 2026): 'Agent component integrity: Maintain a per-agent bill of materials (model versions, MCP servers, skills, plugins, libraries, configuration files). Sign components at origin; verify signatures in the deployment pipeline and reject deployments that fail verification or do not match the approved BOM.' It names four properties of a usable BOM (accountable authorship; declared scope and explicit completeness claim; claims tied to evidence; controlled lifecycle) and warns that 'An AIBOM is not a control in itself'.
additional_findings.relevance: Mirrors the article's 'four pillars' and per-agent AIBOM recommendation. A stronger, citable OWASP source for that section.

additional_findings.finding: The EU AI Act was amended by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 (amended text applies from 27 July 2026). Annex III high-risk obligations now apply from 2 Dec 2027 and Annex I product-embedded high-risk from 2 Aug 2028. Legacy high-risk systems are caught only on significant design changes; public-authority systems by 2 Aug 2030. New prohibitions on AI-generated non-consensual intimate imagery and CSAM apply from 2 Dec 2026.
additional_findings.relevance: Corrects the article's implied 'currently binding' framing. Third-party encoding; confirm against EUR-Lex CELEX 32026R1744 before publishing.

additional_findings.finding: GPAI obligations under Art. 53 have applied since 2 Aug 2025; GPAI models placed on the market before then must comply by 2 Aug 2027; the Commission's GPAI fining power (Art. 101) applies from 2 Aug 2026. Art. 53(1)(b)/Annex XII requires providers to give downstream integrators architecture, parameter count, licence, integration means, maximum input/output size and the type, provenance and curation of training data.
additional_findings.relevance: The only binding AI supply-chain transparency duty already in force. Agent builders on top of foundation models are its beneficiaries and can feed it into their AIBOMs.

additional_findings.finding: prEN 18282, the draft harmonised cybersecurity standard for the AI Act (CEN/CENELEC JTC21/WG5), was 'ready to go for final internal review' in Oct 2026 and is expected early 2027. ISO/IEC 27090 (AI security guidance) was published in October 2026.
additional_findings.relevance: Presumption of conformity with Art. 15 will run through prEN 18282, so it is worth naming as the coming technical yardstick.

additional_findings.finding: OWASP still pins NIST AI RMF at v1.0 (2023) as of Aug 2026. It maps supply-chain risk primarily to GOVERN 6 (third-party & supply-chain policy), MAP 4 (map risks across all components, citing 'A signed SBOM, AIBOM, and ML-SBOM component inventory') and MANAGE 3 (manage third-party risks).
additional_findings.relevance: Better NIST anchors for an AI supply-chain argument than GOVERN 1.6 alone.

additional_findings.finding: Coalition for Secure AI (OASIS) released two frameworks, for AI model signing and for AI incident response, on 18 Nov 2025. OWASP cites it as providing 'a maturity model for signing ML artifacts'.
additional_findings.relevance: Industry consensus guidance that complements the OpenSSF Model Signing citation (URL as listed in OWASP's 2026 references).

additional_findings.finding: MITRE ATLAS catalogues AML.T0010 'AI Supply Chain Compromise', which OWASP LLM04:2026 pairs with ASI04.
additional_findings.relevance: A threat-framework ID the article can map AIBOM checks to (URL as listed in OWASP's 2026 references).

additional_findings.finding: OWASP moved the AIBOM Generator under the OWASP GenAI Security Project (blog dated 18 Dec 2025). The repository is GenAI-Security-Project/aibom-generator.
additional_findings.relevance: An OWASP tool for the 'adopt standards' step (URL as listed in OWASP's 2026 references; not fetched directly).

additional_findings.finding: Anthropic announced on 21 Jul 2025 that it would sign the EU General-Purpose AI Code of Practice, the compliance route for the GPAI obligations that started 2 Aug 2025.
additional_findings.relevance: Shows that the upstream (GPAI) transparency regime is live and that major model providers have opted into it.

additional_findings.finding: OWASP's AI Exchange explicitly extends AIBOMs to agents. It says 'In agentic AI this includes MCP servers and skills', and its agent component integrity control reads: 'Maintain a per-agent bill of materials (model versions, MCP servers, skills, plugins, libraries, configuration files). Sign components at origin; verify signatures in the deployment pipeline and reject deployments that fail verification or do not match the approved BOM. Monitor at runtime for unauthorised component changes.'
additional_findings.relevance: This is OWASP primary-source backing for the article's core thesis (an AIBOM covering MCP servers, skills and tool definitions, plus signing and drift detection), which is stronger than the current citations.

additional_findings.finding: The G7 SBOM-for-AI minimum elements list (seven clusters) includes 'SBOM author signature', 'SBOM generation context' (build/release/deploy/runtime), 'System data flow', model hash value and algorithm, dataset hash and provenance, and 'Vulnerability referencing' (CVEs plus VEX status). It has no MCP, tool-schema or agent-skill elements.
additional_findings.relevance: The author can map the four pillars and immediate steps to named G7 elements, and can state that the agent-tool coverage argued for goes beyond the G7 minimum (third-party encoding).

additional_findings.finding: k8s-aibom matured quickly after the July blog: v1.0.0 on 2026-08-17; v1.5.0 on 2026-09-22 added Sigstore/OMS model-signature verification (the 'verified' tier, which needs an operator-configured signer identity) and a kubectl plugin; v1.6.2 on 2026-10-22. NVIDIA AI Cluster Runtime adopted it under ADR-019 and installs it by default on its h100-gke-cos-inference recipe from AICR v0.20.0.
additional_findings.relevance: Current facts that make the 'Google released' passage concrete and show adoption beyond Google.

additional_findings.finding: k8s-aibom's limits, in its own words: 'Production-suitable for non-critical observation use cases'; 'This is not an officially supported Google product'; models downloaded at runtime are invisible ('runtime-model-fetch bypass'); and it only sees namespaces that are opted in.
additional_findings.relevance: Puts the 'reference implementation' recommendation in context. It is a runtime observer for the model and runtime layer, not a complete agent AIBOM.

additional_findings.finding: CycloneDX 1.7 (21 Oct 2025) added a top-level 'citations' array: 'A collection of attributions indicating which entity supplied information for specific fields within the BOM.'
additional_findings.relevance: This is the standard mechanism for the 'accountable authorship' idea in pillar 1 (who asserted each claim), which is another reason to name 1.7 rather than just 1.6.

additional_findings.finding: CycloneDX 2.0 is in development. k8s-aibom's schema-divergence register refers to 'the 2.0 RFC comments on CycloneDX/specification#990', and its v1.7 roadmap item 'aligns the document with CycloneDX 2.0 conventions'. SPDX 3.1 is listed as '3.1 (TBA)' in the spec's develop changelog.
additional_findings.relevance: 'CycloneDX v1.5–1.7' and 'SPDX 3.0' are current as of Nov 2026, but both formats have major revisions underway that readers should expect.

additional_findings.finding: The OWASP AIBOM Generator, from the OWASP GenAI Security Project's AIBOM Initiative, produces CycloneDX 1.6 AIBOMs for Hugging Face models and adds completeness scoring with recommendations. It is a build-time complement to k8s-aibom's runtime view.
additional_findings.relevance: Gives readers a free build-time tool alongside the runtime one, and explains why two OWASP AIBOM URLs exist: the GenAI initiative versus the OWASP AIBOM Project.

additional_findings.finding: OWASP's AI Exchange points to the 'OWASP CycloneDX Authoritative Guide to AI/ML-BOM' (https://cyclonedx.org/guides/OWASP_CycloneDX-Authoritative-Guide-to-AI-ML-BOM-en.pdf) for field-level encoding of model identifiers (PURL), dataset components, model cards, tokenizers and prompt templates, training and testing details, and EU AI Act mappings.
additional_findings.relevance: A better primary link for 'how to encode an AIBOM in CycloneDX' than the CycloneDX tool-center link the article uses. Its date was not verified.

additional_findings.finding: The OWASP AIBOM Project (owaspaibom.org) is an OWASP incubator project led by Aruneesh Salhotra and Yuvaraj Govindarajulu. Its official OWASP page, owasp.org/www-project-aibom, redirects to owaspaibom.org.
additional_findings.relevance: Exact attribution for the Foundations Guide citation and the executive-summary link.

additional_findings.finding: 1.7 changed nothing structural in ML-BOM. modelCard, componentData, performanceMetric and inputOutputMLParameters are identical to 1.6 apart from wording (model cards date from 1.5). The document's line 'The ML-BOM depth in 1.7 (training lineage, framework versions, model-card object) is a real improvement' is therefore wrong.
additional_findings.relevance: Fix or delete the sentence; credit model cards to 1.5.

additional_findings.finding: The 1.7.1 patch also fixed a second JSON-to-XML loss. modelCard considerations user, useCase, technicalLimitation and performanceTradeoff were maxOccurs=1 in the 1.7.0 XSD and became unbounded in 1.7.1. The JSON-only 1.7.2 patch changed nothing in JSON; the 1.7.2 XSD added relatedCryptographicAssets to protocolProperties. The current master XSD is version 1.7.2.
additional_findings.relevance: Shows the format-parity issue was real but has been patched. Cite the version precisely (1.7.0 vs 1.7.1+).

additional_findings.finding: JSF supports multisignature ('signers') and signature chains ('chain'), so CycloneDX signing is not inherently single-party.
additional_findings.relevance: Contradicts the document's 'Signing is bytes-level and single-party'. Reframe it as no claim-level, multi-party attestation composition and no Sigstore/DSSE alignment.

additional_findings.finding: The official cyclonedx-cli signs and verifies only XML BOMs (XML-DSig enveloped). cyclonedx-python-lib supports neither signature nor modelCard.
additional_findings.relevance: Concrete primary evidence for 'JSF is rarely used' and for weak ML-BOM tooling support.

additional_findings.finding: Sigstore cosign natively supports 'cosign attest --type cyclonedx', producing an in-toto Statement with the CycloneDX predicate in a DSSE envelope.
additional_findings.relevance: The de facto signing path to cite instead of a vague 'ecosystems sign with Sigstore/DSSE'.

additional_findings.finding: Services have no 'hashes' field (components do), and the dependency object has additionalProperties:false with no 'properties', so there is no sanctioned extension point on edges.
additional_findings.relevance: Strengthens the tool rug-pull (no definition digest) and typed-edge arguments with schema-level specifics.

additional_findings.finding: Formulation's taskType enum (copy, clone, lint, scan, merge, build, test, deliver, deploy, release, clean, other) has no train or fine-tune value in 1.5 through 1.7.
additional_findings.relevance: Precise support for 'formulation is self-reported narrative' and for the gap in training-pipeline semantics.

additional_findings.finding: Library support for 1.7 lagged. cyclonedx-python-lib added isExternal only in v11.12.0 (2026-08-13), about ten months after the 1.7 release, and added 1.7.1 support in v11.8.0 (2026-06-04).
additional_findings.relevance: Supports the point that optional spec features go unpopulated in practice.

additional_findings.finding: The CycloneDX AI/ML-BOM Authoritative Guide is First Edition (initial release 2026-03-03), Revision 1 dated 2026-06-10, from the CycloneDX AI/ML Working Group.
additional_findings.relevance: Use for a dated, precise citation of the guide.

additional_findings.finding: ECMA-424 2nd edition (CycloneDX 1.7) was approved by Ecma's 130th General Assembly in Geneva on 10 December 2025.
additional_findings.relevance: Lets the piece describe 1.7 itself as an international standard.

additional_findings.finding: Search budget note: the shared web-search budget ran out partway through this check. Remaining facts were verified by direct fetches of normative schemas and CycloneDX and Sigstore repo files. Only B1-07 (the exact AI/ML guide wording) was materially affected.
additional_findings.relevance: Explains why B1-07 is unverifiable rather than resolved. A follow-up search for the guide's 'Tokenizers and prompt templates' section would settle it.

additional_findings.finding: The CycloneDX 2.0 draft changes the document root in breaking ways. 'specFormat' replaces 'bomFormat', 'inventories' replaces top-level 'components'/'services', the schema is modular JSON Schema 2020-12, and its title is now 'CycloneDX Transparency Exchange Language'. New root sections include threats, risks, controls, blueprints, perspectives and definitions.
additional_findings.relevance: Any AgentBOM extension aimed at 2.0 must target this structure, not 1.7's.

additional_findings.finding: The 2.0 draft has no 'agent' component type; component types gain 'service' but not 'agent'. Agents are modelled as a party kind 'agent' ('Autonomous or semi-autonomous agent that can plan and execute. Includes AI agents.'), a party role 'agent', or a blueprint asset type 'agent'.
additional_findings.relevance: This confirms the 'no agent-native component types' gap carries into 2.0, and undercuts issue #1015's assumption of an agent component.

additional_findings.finding: The 2.0 draft's supportingData guidance says supporting material 'should be minimized and, where it contains secrets, personal data, or working exploit code, referenced through contents.url behind access control rather than inlined, redacted or defanged'. It explicitly anticipates 'a prompt and completion pair from a language model assessment' as evidence.
additional_findings.relevance: A primary source for the 'Transparency vs. attack map' section and for AI red-team evidence in VEX.

additional_findings.finding: The 2.0 technique vocabulary labels a bare vendor claim 'attestation' ('A determination asserted by a party... rather than derived from direct analysis'). Undisclosed methods are labelled 'unknown'. A schema rule stops 'proven-exploitable' or 'exploited' from being a bare assertion.
additional_findings.relevance: Strengthens the 'attribution isn't verification' argument with spec text: 2.0 can say when a claim is only someone's word.

additional_findings.finding: Dependency-Track v5 has reached GA and the default branch is now v5 (main is 5.3.0-SNAPSHOT). v4 is in maintenance on 4.14.x and reaches end-of-life in December 2026. The v5 docs say 'All versions of the CycloneDX BOM specification are supported for upload', but the code accepts only 1.2 to 1.7.
additional_findings.relevance: Update the ecosystem-fragmentation point, and don't repeat the docs' 'all versions' line uncritically.

additional_findings.finding: cdxgen v13 moved to the npm package @cdxgen/cdxgen (latest 13.6.0, 2026-10-31) and already accepts --spec-version 2.0. However, its bundled 2.0 schema is an older draft titled 'CycloneDX Transparency Expression Language', with no behaviors, blueprints or exploitabilityLevel. Its '2.0' output therefore targets an earlier draft than the current 2.0-dev branch (inference from the bundled file).
additional_findings.relevance: Tools claiming 2.0 support today are generating against a moving draft. Worth a caveat when citing cdxgen 2.0 support.

additional_findings.finding: cdxgen issue #4589 reportedly describes the 2.0 schema as 'ratified'. This contradicts the spec repo ('to be announced') and the announcement ('Ecma International approval anticipated in December').
additional_findings.relevance: Don't cite secondary tool issues for 2.0 status; use the spec repo and the CycloneDX announcement.

additional_findings.finding: CycloneDX issue #895 is the community 'Agent BOM' proposal that WasmAgent/agentbom implements. Issue #1015 builds on it.
additional_findings.relevance: A better citation than the vendor libraries for the state of agent-specific CycloneDX work.

additional_findings.finding: The draft's paragraph 'ML-BOM is the manifest. Consequential AI risk often materializes after the manifest ends: during retrieval, inference, tool use... audit or recovery' appears to closely paraphrase the framing of CycloneDX discussion #973 (AACIF), but has no attribution.
additional_findings.relevance: Attribute it or rephrase it to avoid presenting borrowed wording as original analysis.

additional_findings.finding: SPDX 3.1-RC1 was tagged 2026-01-24. Its changelog says /Core/RelationshipType 'has grown from 59 to 76 entries'. It also relaxes the AIPackage and DatasetPackage requirements (#1158), deprecates autonomyType in favour of Core isoAutomationLevel, and deprecates datasetSize and Dataset intendedUse.
additional_findings.relevance: Confirms the draft's '59 to 76', 'autonomyType deprecated' and 'requirements relaxed' statements and dates the RC to January 2026.

additional_findings.finding: The generated 3.1-RC1 ontology has no AI agent, prompt or RAG classes, and the string 'prompt' never appears in it. Agent's subclasses are still only Person, Organization and SoftwareAgent. The post-RC1 develop ontology adds AI/InteractionTemplate ('An artifact that defines the structure, formatting, and variable placeholders for AI model interactions'), plus Core/Action, DefinedProcess and Role.
additional_findings.relevance: Contradicts the draft's 'SPDX 3.1 (release candidate published in January) adds AI Agent, Prompt and RAG classes' and its 'AIAgent subclassing SoftwareAgent' passage. It supports the draft's other line: 'I saw no agent, tool or prompt classes in the RC1 changelog'.

additional_findings.finding: In the spec site's version index, the 'latest' alias belongs to v3.0.1. Version 3.1 exists only as v3.1-RC1 and v3.1-dev, and the 'v3.1' alias points to dev. 3.1 was therefore not final as of 2026-11-01.
additional_findings.relevance: Every 3.1 statement in the piece should be labelled RC or draft.

additional_findings.finding: The 3.1 development spec adds clause 7 'Signing' and clause 8 'Attestation'. Signing uses ITU-T X.590 JSS in a top-level 'signatures' property and covers the whole document only. Attestation lets SPDX 3 JSON serve as an in-toto predicate of type https://spdx.dev/Document/v3.
additional_findings.relevance: Updates 'SPDX 3.0 has hashes but no signature mechanism ... DSSE/in-toto envelopes that neither spec defines'. That is true for 3.0.x, but 3.1 is defining both.

additional_findings.finding: The generated 3.0.1 JSON Schema does not enforce AIPackage's five 'external property' requirements: ai_AIPackage requires only spdxId (plus creationInfo from Element), and DatasetPackage adds only dataset_datasetType. The SHACL shapes in spdx-model.ttl leave them out as well.
additional_findings.relevance: Strengthens 'not machine-verifiable': an AIPackage with no version or supplier passes the official 3.0.1 validators. This is my inference from the generated artifacts.

additional_findings.finding: safetyRiskAssessment uses the EU general product-safety risk methodology (Article 20 of Regulation (EC) No 765/2008). The spec states that this categorization 'differs from the one proposed in the EU AI Act's provisional agreement'.
additional_findings.relevance: Qualifies the draft's 'great for EU AI Act': SPDX's risk enum is not the AI Act's risk tiering.

additional_findings.finding: After RC1, the develop branch's RelationshipType grew to 82 values, adding for example performedBy, runsOn, hasInstall, finetunedOn, pretrainedOn, evaluatedOn and validatedOn. usesTool and invokedBy are now SHACL-constrained to LifecycleScopedRelationship.
additional_findings.relevance: '59 to 76' is RC1-specific. The new fine-tune, pretrain and eval edges partly answer the draft's 'no typed ML lineage relationships'.

additional_findings.finding: Every SPDX 3.0.1 Relationship carries optional startTime and endTime ('the time from which an element is applicable / valid') and a completeness value.
additional_findings.relevance: Corrects the draft's 'edges carry no ... validity window'. The real gaps are permission, condition and grantor semantics.

additional_findings.finding: The 3.1-RC1 Service profile's SoftwareService ('Software provided as a service over a network') has only three properties: serverAuthenticationProtocol, provider and serviceHostingCountry. In develop these change to serverKeyValidationProtocol, serviceHostingCountry and additionalInformation. Neither version has endpoint, trust-boundary or capability fields.
additional_findings.relevance: Refines the draft's '3.1 adds a Services profile': the profile is named 'Service' and is still thin for MCP and inference endpoints.

additional_findings.finding: 'SPDX gives you DEPENDS_ON, CONTAINS' uses SPDX 2.x relationship names. SPDX 3.0 and 3.0.1 have 59 camelCase relationship types, including usesTool, invokedBy, delegatedTo, trainedOn, testedOn, configures and hasDataFile.
additional_findings.relevance: Fixes a contradiction with the draft's own credit to SPDX's relationship vocabulary.

additional_findings.finding: SPDX 3.0.1 ships Extension/CdxPropertiesExtension ('A type of extension consisting of a list of name value pairs'), which can carry CycloneDX-style properties.
additional_findings.relevance: A standard hook for round-tripping CycloneDX properties, relevant to the draft's conversion-loss and extension-mechanism arguments.

additional_findings.finding: The 3.1-dev references cite 'ISO/IEC 18670:2025 ... SoftWare Hash IDentifier (SWHID) Specification V1.2', where 3.0.1 cited the draft ISO/IEC DIS 18670.
additional_findings.relevance: SPDX's swhid content identifiers now rest on a published ISO standard, which supports the 'content addresses as identity' recommendation.

additional_findings.finding: SPDX 3.1-RC1 makes AIPackage's releaseTime, suppliedBy, downloadLocation and packageVersion optional; only primaryPurpose stays required. The Package inheritance remains, but the mandatory version/supplier/downloadLocation semantics are gone.
additional_findings.relevance: Outdates the document's 'Package-centric inheritance is a straitjacket... forcing version/downloadLocation/supplier semantics onto weights and corpora' (line ~1041) for 3.1.

additional_findings.finding: The 3.1 development branch adds Core Role and RoleRelationship (relationshipType hasRoleIn, givenRole, assignedBy: Agent). The Role 'authorization' property describes 'permissions, rights, privileges, or benefits granted to a Role', but it is a free-text xsd:string.
additional_findings.relevance: The closest SPDX gets to the document's structured authorization record. It's worth citing as 'a hook, but free text, not machine-enforceable'.

additional_findings.finding: On develop, the RelationshipType vocabulary now carries 71 SHACL rules. Examples: 'When relationship is configures, class must be LifecycleScopedRelationship'; 'When relationship is createdBy, to must be an Agent'. There are none in 3.0.1 or RC1.
additional_findings.relevance: First semantic validation of edges. Relevant to the 'edges carry no qualifiers' and conformance-gap arguments: typing is improving, though still no permission, condition or validity qualifiers.

additional_findings.finding: 3.1-RC1 adds the pretrainedOn, finetunedOn, evaluatedOn, validatedOn and runsOn relationship types (17 new entries in total).
additional_findings.relevance: Partly answers the document's 'neither has typed edges for fine-tune...' for training-data lineage. Merge, distill, quantize and convert edges are still absent.

additional_findings.finding: RC churn is already visible. RC1's Software/artifactSize is gone on develop (replaced by byteSize), and the RDF namespace moved from https://spdx.org/rdf/3.1/terms/ (RC1) to https://spdx.org/rdf/3/terms/ (dev build). Zephyr's experimental SPDX 3.1 output already writes software_artifactSize.
additional_findings.relevance: Concrete evidence for the document's advice to design against 3.0.1 now and map to 3.1 later. Building on the RC is risky (see also https://raw.githubusercontent.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/main/doc/develop/west/zephyr-cmds.rst).

additional_findings.finding: 3.1-RC1 adds a Core 'intendedUse' property (PR #1109), defined as 'a free-form textual description' (xsd:string), and deprecates Dataset/intendedUse in its favour.
additional_findings.relevance: Bears on the document's 'missing system-level intended purpose (EU AI Act Art. 13)' point. Intended use can now attach to any element, but it is still unstructured text.

additional_findings.finding: Official SPDX Python tools (spdx-tools 0.8.5, 13 March 2026) fully validate only SPDX 2.2/2.3. SPDX 3.0 support is experimental and write-only. The SPDX python-model README adds that the higher-level tools 'doesn't yet support SPDX 3'.
additional_findings.relevance: A strong, citable primary source for the 'installed base is still on 2.x' claim.

additional_findings.finding: Microsoft's sbom-tool 'does not accept open-source contributions'. Homebrew now tracks unreleased tag v4.1.13 because 'the last GitHub release no longer builds due to security issues'.
additional_findings.relevance: Context for the tooling-reality argument: the SPDX 3.0 conformance gap is unlikely to be fixed by outside contributors.

additional_findings.finding: The normative SPDX 3.0.1 and 3.1-RC1 JSON schema and SHACL/OWL model files are published on the spec site's gh-pages branch, alongside versions.json, which shows 3.0.1 as 'latest'.
additional_findings.relevance: Cite these normative files instead of the '?utm_source=chatgpt.com' spec links in the draft, and use them to back every class or field claim.

additional_findings.finding: MCP spec 2026-07-28 standardizes OpenTelemetry trace-context propagation through _meta keys (traceparent, tracestate, baggage), via SEP-414.
additional_findings.relevance: Gives a standard join key between MCP tool calls and OTel traces, which is exactly what binding observed runtime to a declared BOM needs.

additional_findings.finding: MCP 2026-07-28 loosens inputSchema/outputSchema to any JSON Schema 2020-12 keyword, including $ref, with resolution requirements (SEP-2106). It also makes tools/list results cacheable with ttlMs and cacheScope (SEP-2549).
additional_findings.relevance: Tool-definition hashing must hash the served schema without resolving $ref. ttlMs gives a natural re-check cadence for detecting rug-pulls.

additional_findings.finding: OTel GenAI defines a gen_ai.main_agent entity with a required, stable, provider-assigned gen_ai.main_agent.id, and an opt-in gen_ai.tool.definitions_ref (a URI to externally stored tool definitions). All GenAI conventions are at Development status and now live in open-telemetry/semantic-conventions-genai.
additional_findings.relevance: Ready-made hooks for carrying a deployment/BOM identity and a pointer to hashed tool definitions in traces.

additional_findings.finding: The A2A protocol spec (latest release 1.0.0) requires RFC 8785 JCS canonicalization of Agent Cards before signing. It excludes the signatures field and applies explicit field-presence and default rules.
additional_findings.relevance: Strong precedent for the proposal to canonicalize and hash tool and agent definitions, including how to handle defaults before hashing.

additional_findings.finding: The draft ECMA-427 2nd Edition, due at the December 2026 Ecma General Assembly, adds an informative Annex B of cross-type qualifiers: checksum, download_url, file_name, repository_url, vcs_url, vers.
additional_findings.relevance: Lets pkg:huggingface purls pin the exact weight file and its digest without a new type, a concrete fix for the format/quantization ambiguity.

additional_findings.finding: Five open MCP SEPs propose new tool annotations: #1913 Trust and Sensitivity Annotations (co-authored by GitHub and OpenAI), #1984 Comprehensive Tool Annotations for Governance/UX, #1561 unsafeOutputHint, #1560 secretHint and #1487 trustedHint. A Tool Annotations Interest Group is forming.
additional_findings.relevance: The BOM capability fields should track these proposals so they don't fork the vocabulary MCP is converging on for trifecta and Rule-of-Two detection.

additional_findings.finding: MCP's Enterprise-Managed Authorization extension, built on ID-JAG and Okta's Cross App Access, was declared stable on 18 June 2026. The New MCP Roadmap (22 Aug 2026) says enterprise authorization now includes issuer validation, issuer-bound credentials and CIMD as the preferred client registration path.
additional_findings.relevance: Concrete identity artifacts a BOM authorization block can reference today, ahead of DPoP and WIF.

additional_findings.finding: OMS (model-signing) has an unreleased 'digest' subcommand that computes and prints a model's digest 'to easily pair the attestations with a model directory'. In v1.0 the subject digest is a SHA-256 over all sorted per-file digests.
additional_findings.relevance: Gives AgentBOM a standard content identifier for local models that matches what OMS signs.

additional_findings.finding: The OWASP GenAI LLM Top 10 2026, published 4 August 2026, includes 'Model Namespace Reuse' as LLM04 Supply Chain Scenario #5 and cites Unit 42 (Saraf & Balassiano, 3 Sep 2025).
additional_findings.relevance: A citable, fetchable secondary source for the namespace-reuse attack class that the author can cite alongside Unit 42.

additional_findings.finding: Meta's Rule of Two was clarified after publication. [B] covers access to any sensitive system, not only private data, and Meta relabelled the pairwise intersections from 'safe' to 'lower risk'. Willison argues that untrusted input plus state change is not safe even without [B].
additional_findings.relevance: Affects how a computed Rule-of-Two flag should treat the A+C pair. Consider flagging A+C separately rather than treating it as compliant.

additional_findings.finding: Hugging Face docs: transferring or renaming a repo automatically redirects the old URL to the new location.
additional_findings.relevance: Explains the transfer variant of namespace reuse. Supports recording the resolved commit SHA and the resolution path, not just the requested name.

additional_findings.finding: Cisco's Model Provenance Kit (PyPI cisco-ai-provenance-kit 1.0.0, 4 May 2026) ships a Model Provenance Constitution that defines in-scope lineage relations: fine-tuning, distillation, quantization, pruning, merging and LoRA merges.
additional_findings.relevance: A ready vocabulary for the typed derivation edges the author proposes (finetunedFrom, distilledFrom, quantizedFrom, mergedFrom, adapterOf).

additional_findings.finding: CycloneDX 1.5, 1.6 and 1.7 allow only these component.type values: application, framework, library, container, platform, operating-system, device, device-driver, firmware, file, machine-learning-model, data, plus cryptographic-asset from 1.6. Neither 'service' nor 'tool' is valid, yet brox's README sample and OWASP AOS's AgBOM CycloneDX example both use them. agent-harness-aibom documented the same mistake in its v0.1.2 and fixed it by moving MCP servers to bom.services[].
additional_findings.relevance: Concrete proof that improvised agent BOMs already produce schema-invalid CycloneDX. This is a stronger hook than 'custom keys don't interoperate'.

additional_findings.finding: The CycloneDX property taxonomy says 'Unofficial sub-namespaces and names MUST NOT be used under the cdx top-level namespace'. The registered cdx sub-namespaces are ai-ml, composer, device, esbuild, gomod, lifecycle, maven, npm, pipenv, poetry, python and rustc. cdx:ai-ml reserves cdx:ai-ml:prompt but defines no properties for it, and there is nothing for agents, MCP or tools. Even so, cdxgen 12.9.0 emits cdx:mcp:*, cdx:agent:*, cdx:skill:* and cdx:tool:*. None of genai, harness-aibom, brox, cisco-aibom or trusera is a registered top-level namespace.
additional_findings.relevance: Gives the 'one shared property namespace' fix a concrete, existing home: register an agent/MCP sub-namespace under cdx:ai-ml with the CycloneDX Core WG.

additional_findings.finding: CycloneDX has had externalReference types 'attestation' and 'evidence' since 1.5 (1.7 definition of attestation: 'Human or machine-readable statements containing facts, evidence, or testimony').
additional_findings.relevance: Narrow the document's 'no way to reference hardware attestation evidence' to 'no TEE-specific way (TEE type, measurement, verifier) and no way to require it'.

additional_findings.finding: modelCard.properties in the XML schema: the bom-1.7.xsd at the git tag '1.7' lists modelCardType children as modelParameters, quantitativeAnalysis and considerations (no properties). The master-branch bom-1.5/1.6/1.7.xsd files now also include properties.
additional_findings.relevance: The 'JSON but not XML' bug the document cites appears fixed on master but not in the tagged release files. Reword to 'fixed upstream, not in the tagged 1.7 schema'. The OWASP AIBOM Generator writes exactly this field (genai:aibom:modelcard:*).

additional_findings.finding: Tool-definition digests from today's tools are not comparable. agent-harness-aibom hashes json.dumps(sort_keys=True, separators=(',',':'), ensure_ascii=False) with SHA-256. That is not RFC 8785; my inference is that it can diverge on float formatting and on key order for non-BMP characters. mcplock keeps annotations_hash deliberately separate from content_hash (description + inputSchema), so that a destructiveHint flip shows up as its own critical finding.
additional_findings.relevance: The document's RFC 8785 proposal should fix both the canonicalization and the field scope, and decide whether annotations are folded into the main hash or kept separate.

additional_findings.finding: The MCP Registry launched in preview on 2025-09-08, and its v0.1 API froze on 2025-10-24. The latest dated server.json schema is 2025-12-11. fileSha256 is required for MCPB bundles and optional for other package types.
additional_findings.relevance: Precise, primary dates and fields for the registry-provenance gap, replacing the unverifiable 'smithmark' citation.

additional_findings.finding: Snyk's MCP tooling lineage: Invariant Labs' mcp-scan (first release 2025-04-07; v0.3.0 'detects changes to MCP tools via hashing') was renamed snyk-agent-scan. The PyPI mcp-scan entry is now a redirect, and Agent Scan feeds the Snyk Evo platform. The `snyk aibom` prerequisites name CLI v1.1298.3 (npm, 2025-08-14); `snyk aibom test` arrived in v1.1304.0 (2026-04-09).
additional_findings.relevance: Primary dates and lineage for the Snyk sentence, and an early precedent for hash-based rug-pull detection.

additional_findings.finding: SPDX's development model (spdx-3-model, develop branch) has an AI/InteractionTemplate class, a Core/Artifact for prompt/chat/training templates. It links from AIPackage or AIAgent via a LifecycleScopedRelationship ('configures', scope runtime). It is not on main and not in a released spec.
additional_findings.relevance: The document's 'neither standard has a type for prompts' may age quickly. Cite this as unreleased work in progress.

additional_findings.finding: agent-bom (koda-ai-studio, PyPI; 177 releases since 2026-02-19, v0.112.1 on 2026-11-01) also reports coverage: 'Review coverage warnings beside the verdict; incomplete evidence is not clean.' It scans MCP clients, servers and tools as well as CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md and .cursorrules, and outputs CycloneDX and SPDX.
additional_findings.relevance: A second, actively maintained example for both the coverage-statement fix and the third-party-tools-surface-MCP point.

additional_findings.finding: Cohere's 'Public Summary of Training Content for Command A+ and family' (v1.1, 10 Sept 2026) is a citable, filled-in instance of the AI Office template. It names Common Crawl as its only large public dataset, discloses licensed data as a Yes/No, and records Code of Practice signatory status and TDM opt-out measures.
additional_findings.relevance: A concrete primary example for the Dataset Provenance section, showing what Art. 53(1)(d) actually requires (B7-04, B7-06).

additional_findings.finding: The Art. 53(2) open-source exemption covers only 53(1)(a)-(b). Providers of open-weight GPAI models still owe the copyright policy (c) and the public training-content summary (d). Source is a secondary German rules catalog keyed to the 27 July 2026 consolidated text.
additional_findings.relevance: Matters for AIBOMs of open models: the training-data disclosure duty applies to them too.

additional_findings.finding: Under the consolidated AI Act after Regulation (EU) 2026/1744: Chapter V (GPAI, Art. 53) has applied since 2 Aug 2025; high-risk Chapter III sections 1-3 (including Art. 13) apply from 2 Dec 2027 for Annex III systems and from 2 Aug 2028 for Annex I systems.
additional_findings.relevance: Fixes tense and timing across the doc's legal mapping. Art. 53 binds now; Art. 13 does not yet apply.

additional_findings.finding: The purl spec defines standard identities for model registries: pkg:huggingface (version = model revision Git commit hash) and pkg:mlflow (covers Azure ML and Databricks registries via the tracking URI).
additional_findings.relevance: The registry-trust section should say the gap is attestation and pull-time verification, not identity; this also supports the doc's 'canonical model identity' proposal.

additional_findings.finding: cdxgen 12.9.0 (CycloneDX project, published 22 Oct 2026) ships a dedicated 'aibom' CLI that builds CycloneDX AI/ML BOMs from source, Hugging Face URLs/purls, Modelfiles and GGUF files, filling modelCard.modelParameters.
additional_findings.relevance: Updates the doc's tooling claims (B7-05, B7-09): ML-BOM population exists, but only as an opt-in mode.

additional_findings.finding: Google Cloud, which holds the certification: 'The 42001 standard does not mandate specific AI controls'.
additional_findings.relevance: A drop-in, citable line for correcting the ISO/IEC 42001 claim (B7-08).

additional_findings.finding: OWASP AI Exchange: ISO/IEC 42001 'doesn't go into the lifecycle processes', and specifically does not cover data lineage, continuous validation or model versioning.
additional_findings.relevance: Supports the doc's thesis that governance standards leave AI evidence formats undefined, which is the gap AgentBOM fills.

additional_findings.finding: Anthropic's transparency hub describes Claude training data as 'a proprietary mix of publicly available information from the internet, public and private datasets' plus synthetic data generated by other models.
additional_findings.relevance: A second primary example of coarse training-data disclosure (B7-04).

additional_findings.finding: MITRE ATLAS case studies on registry trust: AML.CS0027 'Organization Confusion on Hugging Face' (look-alike org accounts gained access to employees' uploaded models), and AML.CS0028 (Trend Micro found over 8,000 misconfigured container registries, about 70% writable, holding over 1,000 unique AI models pullable without authentication).
additional_findings.relevance: Citable ATLAS evidence for the registry and pull-step gap (B7-09). This data file is the deprecated v5.6.0 export and lacks the newer namespace-reuse case AML.CS0065.
